review_text: Javiara our tour guide and Manuel our driver were terrific. Javiara was waiting just outside the port - as described - and easy to find. We waited for about 15 minutes for other passengers to get off the ship. The morning was perfect with both volcanos out as we drove to the Petrohue falls. Javiara provided much information. We crossed our fingers that Osorno would still be out when we arrived to the falls but she was already behind clouds by the time we reached the falls. An opportunity to take a picture of Osorno by the lake was lost because so many of the ship's tour buses stopped at the pull off, so our bus didn't get any good pictures of Osorno. I would recommend to Javiara that anytime the Volcano is out - STOP THE BUS - so the tourists can take a picture. I am very disappointed by missing this opportunity. That aside, we had a short time in Puerto Varas - although there was a lot to see. We hurried to Fruttillar where we had more time to walk around a smaller town - than Puerto Varas. I would rather have had more time in Puerto Varas. .Frutillar has few shops but it does have an amazing bakery with German-inspired kuchen. All in all it was a fabulous full day trip. review_text: We did three tours with Atacama Magic: Valley of the Moon with Gustavo, Rainbow Valley with Denny, and Salt Flats Route with Felipe. We enjoyed all three tours. Communication is through What’s app and is very good. Pickup for the tours all went well and the drop off point was in front of our hotel. The Valley of the Moon tour involves driving a few minutes to the park, doing an easy hike in the park to see beautiful scenery, a quick stop at one other portion of the park, and then driving to an overlook nearby to watch the sunset with snacks. Rainbow Valley is about an hour drive each way and then a walk through the park to see the scenery. We also saw llamas and donkeys on this tour. Breakfast is provided. Both these tours are easy 1/2 day tours. The Salt Flats Route is an all day tour with lots of driving stopping at various points to take photos. Both breakfast and lunch are provided. We got up to about 16,000 feet on this tour. One caution - there are no public bathrooms on this tour. All three guides were very knowledgeable. We had a very positive experience with this tour company.

review_text: I was in Puerto Varas, Chile for a business event and had the opportunity to get out in the Patagonian wild for a few fantastic paddling days before all the work started. We were given nearly 50 choices of activities, but I chose Yak Expediciones' seakayaking offer because of the great location and the mixture of both nature- and culture-based elements. The trip was great because there was definitely plenty of paddling (10 km / 6 mi the first day and approx. 30 km / 18 mi the second day) but also other unique pieces to make it feel like a well-rounded experience! We visited a small, local hot springs resort on Llancahué Island for a relaxing break, saw lots of wildlife (like sea lions, birds, pelicans), and camped on the land of a local family, taking dinners in the house together with the matriarch. Technically speaking, the paddling was easy for me, although some heavy winds on the first day added some excitement in the form of hard paddling through high waves! (By the way, I love to go kayaking but I'm not a total river-rat, so this experience was suitable for a wide range of experience levels.) The weather for us was very comfortable - overcast, although I still got a lot of sun on my face. It was calling for rain, though, so an open mind, ready-for-anything attitude, and good waterproof gear is highly recommended :) For me, the natural look of the Pumalín Park and Lakes Region was the biggest draw, but it was the cultural elements - eating home-cooked food and hearing about personal life stories (in Spanish) from the host - which were absolutely the most memorable! Come paddle with Yak Expediciones if you want both an exciting sea kayaking experience and a taste of the local culture at the gateway to Patagonia!

review_text: We are travelling through Chile specifically to see the wildlife. The first time we arrived here there were no boat trips running as the sea was thought too rough. There is no harbour so people just have to walk into the sea to get into the boats. This means it has to be really calm to run the boat trips. The lady looking after the toilets (300 pesos a go) told us it would be a few days before the boats would be running. So we went elsewhere and returned a week later. We did enjoy excellent views of Skimmers on the beach though. On our second visit the boats were running. We put our name down on the list, 6000 pesos each, and waited for the next boat. Each boat takes 15 people and a loudhailer calls you when a boat is ready to depart. We waded into the sea about 8 inches deep and were helped on to the boat. Life jackets provided. Then we had a trip to the island but did not see any large concentrations of birds. Just a few Humboldt penguins and Peruvian pelicans and some sealions. review_text: Before my vacation I kept reading how Enotour was Chile's wine experts. With that comes an expectation that all aspects of a tour would be exceptional...especially when I paid US $380 for a full day private excursion. The vineyards I visited were Vina de Martino and Vina Perez Cruz and they were both awesome. The guides representing these places were informative and they were proud to show off their grapes (!) What I was disappointed in were the following. If Enotour calls themselves tour experts, and charges premium rates, they should also include the aspects of their organization too. 1. Communicate with the wineries - going forward, it would be helpful if Enotour communicated with the wineries in advance so there won't be duplicate information. Enotour should have checked to see what information would be highlighted and discussed. As a result, I found the information repetitive but was respectful when I heard the same discussion from the vineyard staff. 2. Be prepared - my Enotour guide should have researched lunch options in advance instead of the driver trying to find a possible place to eat. Did the guide ever touch base with the driver before the tour to make sure there were options? If this "Maipo Valley Full Day" tour is offered in their brochure, you would think Enotour has a list of places that worked for others. I understand about limited options in the wine region but I don't understand why we had to stop and ask a local person and turn the car around to go in the right direction. When we finally found a place 1 1/2 hours later, the local whole in the wall restaurant was certainly not as identified in the brochure "after enjoying a leisurely gourmet place". They didn't event have bottled water available. The "pear" drink that was available was sickening sweet and not thirst quenching. The food was passable as I was really hungry but felt it was not up to Enotour standards, 3. Know your audience - This might be picky but as part of my tour bottled water was offered. Most Americans (like myself) don't drink carbonated water and I consciously didn't bring any water with me from the hotel (the carbonation affects my stomach, just like soda and i can't drink it) and you would think there were have been water "sin gas" but there wasn't. When I brought this issue to my guide, there was no attempt to make it better. I am a seasoned traveler who has participated in other private tours overseas and the option is always given to you. A small ice chest would have also been nice to have the water cold too as other local companies would want to enhance their customer's experience. Instead of creating flashy brochures, Enotour might want to take a look at what they offer to tourists or change their pricing structure. Overall, my tour was not worth the money. I could have taken a local taxi and worked directly with the vineyards to get the same vino experience.

review_text: This is mostly a review to help with logistics. But simply put, this place needs to be on your bucket list! Despite the difficulty of the W trek, the remoteness and uniqueness of this place adds to its raw beauty. I strongly recommend you visit! Few things to note for this review: 1. This is the W trek West-to-East, which we did by ourselves (no tour company involved). I strongly recommend doing it this way if you are with someone; you can go at your own pace, and it is a LOT cheaper (we did it at less than half the price of what most tour companies charge!) 2. We booked the campsites using a helpful website called “torres hike”. You can book direct with the companies (Vertice and Fantastico Sur) that own the campsites to avoid torres hike’s booking fee, but I found the company websites slow and clunky. 3. We did this in early October. Timings may change in high season! And it will probably be busier. 4. I will review the refugios/campsites (Grey, Paine Grande, Frances, Chileno) separately here on TripAdvisor, although the first time I mention each one I will say how many stars they get. 5. The Refugios are in the same place as the Camps. A Refugio has dorms & bunk beds, and is where you eat if you bought meals in advance. The camp part is usually next to the refugio. 6. Between the 2 of us we carried our clothes, a tent, 2 sleeping bags, 2 sleeping mats (all of which we managed to rent the day before in Puerto Natales from Yagan House & Lili’s Patagonicos), plus a first aid kit, toiletries, and other bits & pieces. Day 1: Puerto Natales > Camp Paine Grande (5*) > Camp Grey (5*). We caught the 07.00 bus to Torres del Paine National Park with Bus-Sur. It stopped at Laguna Amarga first at about 08.30; everyone gets off here to have their national park ticket checked. Those who are doing day trips, the W trek east-to-west, or starting the O trek from here catch a shuttle to the beginning of the trails at Hotel Las Torres & Central Camp. We got back on the bus to go to Pudeto, the catamaran stop; this should only take about 40mins but we had to go slow for the ultra-runners. We still made it in plenty of time; the catamaran leaves at 10.30 and costs CHP 25000 or US$ 30, cash only! By 11.15 we were at Camp Paine Grande. After a quick toilet break and bag adjustment we headed off at 11.30. Signs state the walk to Camp Grey is 3.5 hours - this was roughly correct for us, but if you are not carrying your own tent, etc you will probably do it quicker. The walk itself is beautiful, although burnt trees are still scarred from a fire 10 years ago (partly why open fires are no longer allowed). The first 2 hours were difficult as we faced REALLY strong winds, to the point we sometimes had to stop, because lifting one foot may have meant falling over. The final 90mins were easier simply because there was less wind, though there are some uphill sections throughout. Once we reached Camp Grey we had a quick late lunch, put up our tent, then continued along the trail for another 45mins to see the “hanging bridge” (a wood, rope and metal suspension bridge) where you can get a good view of Lago Grey & the glacier. Once back, we had dinner, moved our tent into better shelter from the wind, then quickly fell asleep. Day 2: Camp Grey > Camp Paine Grande. We were supposed to fill our morning with a kayak session near the glacier (you can book this through the company direct, Big Foot Patagonia, online or at their office in Puerto Natales, and they also do an ice hike on the glacier) - unfortunately, it was cancelled as the winds were still too strong. So we trekked back the way we came on Day 1, meaning we ended up at Camp Paine Grande at 13.00. We completed it in just over 3 hours this time, as the wind wasn’t as strong as Day 1. Day 3: Camp Paine Grande > Camp Frances (4*) > Mirador Britanico (via Valle del Frances) > Camp Frances. This was our favourite day! We left Paine Grande at 09.30 and had a nice, although slightly wet, 2.5 hour hike to Camp Frances, where we could thankfully check in early to set up our tent. Once we had done that, packed our day bag and had lunch, we set off at 13.00 to hike the Valle del Frances. (Note that you can leave your big bag at the park ranger station at Camp Italiano, which is 1km before Camp Frances and also the start point for the hike into Valle del Frances. We decided to go to Camp Frances first to pitch our tent in case the weather got worse - thankfully it didn’t). From Camp Italiano, the hike is mostly uphill for the first 90 mins to Mirador Frances; you go through a lot of wooded areas so most of the time you are sheltered from any wind or rain. Once at Mirador Frances, you can turn back or continue to Mirador Britanico; this is about another 60mins, although we didn’t do the last 10mins because we got to a point where the forest opened up to an amazing view anyway. The hike to Mirador Britanico is still uphill but not as steep as to Mirador Frances. We then hiked back to Camp Frances, returning at 18.00. Day 4: Camp Frances > Camp Chileno (3*). This was our hardest day, both physically and mentally. By this point you begin to really feel the aches and strains from the previous days hikes, and it’s not made any easier by the fact that you have to walk approx 16km with all the weight in your bag. Most blogs I’ve read have put the timing of this walk at about 6-7 hours; we did it in 6.5 hours, including about 40mins of rest breaks. The first 3km of the walk, to Refugio Los Cuernos, is mostly downhill. It then alternates between uphill and downhill, but steadily increasing in elevation overall. The last 4km (roughly) were the hardest for us; after taking the left path at the fork for Camp Chileno or Hotel Las Torres, you cross some boggy ground before heading uphill for a good hour or so, and this is where the wind picks up again! At the top you reach Windy Pass (forget about using rain covers here - ours were ripped off), and then you’re less than 30mins from Camp Chileno. Watch out for horses for these last 30mins too - riders pass by delivering supplies to the camp. Day 5: Camp Chileno > Mirador Base Torres > Puerto Natales. And this was our second hardest day! Up at 5am, a quick breakfast at the Camp Chileno lodge (make sure you arrange this with lodge staff the night before), then off to Mirador Base Torres at 05.45. With our day packs, this took the recommended 2 hours - we might have been quicker had it not been for the fact we had to trudge slowly through amazing SNOWY landscapes! It was like that scene when they enter Narnia, except better! Anyway moving onto the logistics, the first hour was fairly easy with little uphills and downhills. The second hour, after you pass the turnoff for the park ranger station, was where it got hard with the constant uphill, and maybe even a little dangerous with all the snow covering the rocky trail. We knew we’d be a bit disappointed at the top, which we were (the Torres del Paine were shrouded in cloud and mist) but the scenery was just so breathtaking that the disappointment didn’t last. We had to be careful on the way back down - there were definitely a few slips and slides - but we made it back to Camp Chileno in about 1hr 45mins. After packing our tent and gear away, and a quick pick-me-up hot chocolate, we left Camp Chileno at 10.30 and descended all the way to Refugio Central, arriving at about 12.30, in plenty of time for the 14.00 shuttle bus (CHP 3000, cash only!) to Laguna Amarga. Then it was a short wait for our 15.00 bus back to Puerto Natales (we had pre-booked this, but at least one couple were able to get on without a ticket, with the bus driver saying they could pay back at Puerto Natales - doubt you could do this in high season though). I hope some of this helps with your planning 🙂

Despite the difficulty of the W trek, the remoteness and uniqueness of this place adds to its raw beauty. I strongly recommend you visit! Few things to note for this review: 1. This is the W trek West-to-East, which we did by ourselves (no tour company involved). I strongly recommend doing it this way if you are with someone; you can go at your own pace, and it is a LOT cheaper (we did it at less than half the price of what most tour companies charge!) 2. We booked the campsites using a helpful website called “torres hike”. You can book direct with the companies (Vertice and Fantastico Sur) that own the campsites to avoid torres hike’s booking fee, but I found the company websites slow and clunky. 3. We did this in early October. Timings may change in high season! And it will probably be busier. 4. I will review the refugios/campsites (Grey, Paine Grande, Frances, Chileno) separately here on TripAdvisor, although the first time I mention each one I will say how many stars they get. 5. The Refugios are in the same place as the Camps. A Refugio has dorms & bunk beds, and is where you eat if you bought meals in advance. The camp part is usually next to the refugio. 6. Between the 2 of us we carried our clothes, a tent, 2 sleeping bags, 2 sleeping mats (all of which we managed to rent the day before in Puerto Natales from Yagan House & Lili’s Patagonicos), plus a first aid kit, toiletries, and other bits & pieces. Day 1: Puerto Natales > Camp Paine Grande (5*) > Camp Grey (5*). We caught the 07.00 bus to Torres del Paine National Park with Bus-Sur. It stopped at Laguna Amarga first at about 08.30; everyone gets off here to have their national park ticket checked. Those who are doing day trips, the W trek east-to-west, or starting the O trek from here catch a shuttle to the beginning of the trails at Hotel Las Torres & Central Camp. We got back on the bus to go to Pudeto, the catamaran stop; this should only take about 40mins but we had to go slow for the ultra-runners. We still made it in plenty of time; the catamaran leaves at 10.30 and costs CHP 25000 or US$ 30, cash only! By 11.15 we were at Camp Paine Grande. After a quick toilet break and bag adjustment we headed off at 11.30. Signs state the walk to Camp Grey is 3.5 hours - this was roughly correct for us, but if you are not carrying your own tent, etc you will probably do it quicker. The walk itself is beautiful, although burnt trees are still scarred from a fire 10 years ago (partly why open fires are no longer allowed). The first 2 hours were difficult as we faced REALLY strong winds, to the point we sometimes had to stop, because lifting one foot may have meant falling over. The final 90mins were easier simply because there was less wind, though there are some uphill sections throughout. Once we reached Camp Grey we had a quick late lunch, put up our tent, then continued along the trail for another 45mins to see the “hanging bridge” (a wood, rope and metal suspension bridge) where you can get a good view of Lago Grey & the glacier. Once back, we had dinner, moved our tent into better shelter from the wind, then quickly fell asleep. Day 2: Camp Grey > Camp Paine Grande. We were supposed to fill our morning with a kayak session near the glacier (you can book this through the company direct, Big Foot Patagonia, online or at their office in Puerto Natales, and they also do an ice hike on the glacier) - unfortunately, it was cancelled as the winds were still too strong. So we trekked back the way we came on Day 1, meaning we ended up at Camp Paine Grande at 13.00. We completed it in just over 3 hours this time, as the wind wasn’t as strong as Day 1. Day 3: Camp Paine Grande > Camp Frances (4*) > Mirador Britanico (via Valle del Frances) > Camp Frances. This was our favourite day! We left Paine Grande at 09.30 and had a nice, although slightly wet, 2.5 hour hike to Camp Frances, where we could thankfully check in early to set up our tent. Once we had done that, packed our day bag and had lunch, we set off at 13.00 to hike the Valle del Frances. (Note that you can leave your big bag at the park ranger station at Camp Italiano, which is 1km before Camp Frances and also the start point for the hike into Valle del Frances. We decided to go to Camp Frances first to pitch our tent in case the weather got worse - thankfully it didn’t). From Camp Italiano, the hike is mostly uphill for the first 90 mins to Mirador Frances; you go through a lot of wooded areas so most of the time you are sheltered from any wind or rain. Once at Mirador Frances, you can turn back or continue to Mirador Britanico; this is about another 60mins, although we didn’t do the last 10mins because we got to a point where the forest opened up to an amazing view anyway. The hike to Mirador Britanico is still uphill but not as steep as to Mirador Frances. We then hiked back to Camp Frances, returning at 18.00. Day 4: Camp Frances > Camp Chileno (3*). This was our hardest day, both physically and mentally. By this point you begin to really feel the aches and strains from the previous days hikes, and it’s not made any easier by the fact that you have to walk approx 16km with all the weight in your bag. Most blogs I’ve read have put the timing of this walk at about 6-7 hours; we did it in 6.5 hours, including about 40mins of rest breaks. The first 3km of the walk, to Refugio Los Cuernos, is mostly downhill. It then alternates between uphill and downhill, but steadily increasing in elevation overall. The last 4km (roughly) were the hardest for us; after taking the left path at the fork for Camp Chileno or Hotel Las Torres, you cross some boggy ground before heading uphill for a good hour or so, and this is where the wind picks up again! At the top you reach Windy Pass (forget about using rain covers here - ours were ripped off), and then you’re less than 30mins from Camp Chileno. Watch out for horses for these last 30mins too - riders pass by delivering supplies to the camp. Day 5: Camp Chileno > Mirador Base Torres > Puerto Natales. And this was our second hardest day! Up at 5am, a quick breakfast at the Camp Chileno lodge (make sure you arrange this with lodge staff the night before), then off to Mirador Base Torres at 05.45. With our day packs, this took the recommended 2 hours - we might have been quicker had it not been for the fact we had to trudge slowly through amazing SNOWY landscapes! It was like that scene when they enter Narnia, except better! Anyway moving onto the logistics, the first hour was fairly easy with little uphills and downhills. The second hour, after you pass the turnoff for the park ranger station, was where it got hard with the constant uphill, and maybe even a little dangerous with all the snow covering the rocky trail. We knew we’d be a bit disappointed at the top, which we were (the Torres del Paine were shrouded in cloud and mist) but the scenery was just so breathtaking that the disappointment didn’t last. We had to be careful on the way back down - there were definitely a few slips and slides - but we made it back to Camp Chileno in about 1hr 45mins. After packing our tent and gear away, and a quick pick-me-up hot chocolate, we left Camp Chileno at 10.30 and descended all the way to Refugio Central, arriving at about 12.30, in plenty of time for the 14.00 shuttle bus (CHP 3000, cash only!) to Laguna Amarga. Then it was a short wait for our 15.00 bus back to Puerto Natales (we had pre-booked this, but at least one couple were able to get on without a ticket, with the bus driver saying they could pay back at Puerto Natales - doubt you could do this in high season though). I hope some of this helps with your planning 🙂

review_text: Franco was a great tour guide, he is well spoken, funny and very intellegent. I believe he does the morning tour on week days only. The four hour tour provided lots of information about what we were seeing, as well as a good historical, and political prospective on Chile. He is quite willing to answer any questions about Chile: food, politics ,culture, wine, resturaunts, musems, music(he has a band), nothing is out of bounds.. The pace was really great and I enjoyed our stop for ice cream mid-way through the tour. It was also a great opportunity to chat with others in our group. I would highly recommend this to anyone visiting Santiago. We have been to Santiago about 6 times and I wish we had taken the tour sooner. The tour operates on tips only, Franco recommeded no more than $10 per person. But that is up to the individul.

Miguel guided us expertly through all the tiny alley's, showed us amazing street art & more importantly, the stories behind them. The empanade stop was delicious, just go for it!! I couldn't not mention a large part of our tour: the dogs! From early on, we were joined by 2 strays that Miguel knew very well, then this increased by another 2 Miguel was also familiar with. Luckily the group was very fond of dogs so they were a great addition, with plenty of cuddles all round! (If you're not a big fan of dogs, Valpo might not be the place for you!)

review_text: ……..A real fascinating big well laid-out and immaculate-lii maintained wide open space on the edge of the Mapocho river and almost in the centre of the business district of Santiago de Chile, Entrance is free of charge and you can just wonder in at leisure and enjoy a safe and quiet ”walk in the park”, it’s very clean and there are benches strewn all over at well placed distances so you can walk look at all the fascinated modern sculptures take a break read a book and then continue. Some of the pieces on show are open for you to make up your own mind as to what the artist is trying to convey as someone once said “the artist learns to communicate and the public learns to make a connection” this is so true when you are wondering around here. There are even parakeets frolicking around on the green-lawns and chirping merrily in the trees. There is a nice sized exhibition centre where companies or businesses can display there good in this love-lii natural environment. Very interesting to see when you take time to read the little plaques in the flower-beds you will come to see that many of the plant species and trees are from different counties in the world. If you just want to take a break bring a picnic basket and do what many Chileans do during the day, they come to the park and relax and have a good time. This is a must visit park when in the area its rejuvenating and fun-filled……………

review_text: We hire a 6 night program with excursions and accommodation. The first day the problems left, we had to wait 2 hours at the airport to be picked up. When we arrived at the hotel in Puerto Chacabuco they did not want to deliver lunch because they said it had been delivered in a transfer, which was not real. Then we realized that the hotel has no pool or spa. WiFi internet does not work, we asked more than once to fix it but we were not taken into account. The food included in the package is buffet, but neither breakfast, lunch, nor dinner is of good quality, the menu is repetitive and little varied. When I ordered a bean coffee at breakfast, not a machine like they offer, they wanted to charge me as an extra (a small thing). In general you see few people with experience in reception and restaurant. Receptionists have no power or criteria to make decisions and solve problems. For some reason that I do not know the electric power tends to fail on bad weather days, apparently they do not have backup equipment or voltage stabilizer. The rooms do not have air conditioning, which is already a basic standard, considering that the rooms on the north side are very hot on sunny days. Maid service needs to improve, sometimes they don’t remove all the trash and they don’t change or leave the towels, not to mention that the towels are small and worn. TVs are old, none are smart TVs. They have a very basic cable TV system. The rooms also have no fridge, so it is not feasible to buy drinks and leave them there. They never gave us slippers even though they had to give to guests. On the other hand, the excursions are very good, so it is clear that the service is focused on that and not on the rest, less on the hotel, which is promoted as 4 stars in booking, but I consider that it does not give you for more than 2 stars (rooms and restaurant). It is also listed as being in the top 10% of hotels in the world according to TripAdvisor, which is misleading for the passenger, as it tends to be thought to be in the top 10, which is not effective. With regard to meals, I was left with the feeling that we overpaid for a service that is not properly used. The last day we were supposed to be taken to the airport at 12 noon because our flight was leaving at 15:40, that's what they offered. However, we were forced to leave the room before 10hrs, with no alternatives, that is, in addition to the non-compliance, we had to wait about 1 hour at reception because the transfer had changed schedule and did not warn, plus 3 hours at the airport for arriving early. A disaster of service. When I presented my claims to the hotel manager, he simply told me "it's his opinion", with high-handedness, intransigence, zero empathy, zero self-criticism and zero willingness to solve the problems of the passengers, while, he unraveled in attentions for people of the TV who were apparently invited to promote the place (it seems that he does not understand that the best or worst advertising is that of the paying passengers). I think it is better to have a hotel like Dreams de Coyhaique as your accommodation and from there hire excursion services. You would have much better hotel service and maybe even cheaper. I’m left with the feeling that we overpay for a service whose added value isn’t in the entire service value chain – we receive much less than we expected and what we pay for. Consequently, I recommend excursions, but for no reason recommend the hotel, it is a place I would never return to again.

review_text: What can I say?... I've spent 6 weeks traveling alone across Chile and this was definitely the highlight of the whole trip. To my person, I am 31 years old, have only minimal spanish knowlegde, have experiences in seakayak trips and of course like to spend time camping in the wilderness. So it seemed to be the perfect plan to do this trip. But in the end it exceeded my expectations. And this not only because of the stunning landscape and animals. But mainly because of the whole combination of wilderness, a perfect tour guide Juan who is experienced, knows the area by heart and is a reaaally warmhearted person who tries anything make this a perfect trip for you and of course the other locals who hosted us/me so openminded and cordially (even though my spanish was too bad to talk a lot besides the patient translations by Juan). The (pre)organisation was already really good and easy. Because I was traveling alone and it was already a bit off-season (april), I had the opportunity to do this trip as the only participant. Everything, concerning finding a date, gear, hostel in Puerto Varas, payment and what I should expect was so well organized and I never had doubts it could be a bad decision to do this trip. I could talk of course a lot about the trip itself, the waterfalls, hotsprings, the animals, the campsites, but as there are so many pictures on facebook for example - just take a look there. What you see is what you get! (at least a feeling of it - paddeling in those fjords is breathtaking). What you cannot see on the pictures is how warm you are welcomed by the locals and which makes this trip exceptional compared to trips that you do on your own just in the nature. Thanks a lot Juan for this wonderful opportunity you gave me. Next time I will stay at the car ;) Muchas gracias y saludos atentos! review_text: I would like to leave a few comments about the tours we did. Overall, everything went well and we had good support from Oasis, especially from the girl who served us, always calm and friendly, unlike the boy. The collaborating agencies that conducted the tours with us were also good. The Suenos Seller team was always attentive and close to solve doubts and help us with the refund of one of the tours that we were unable to make due to adverse weather conditions, always open and transparent communication. All guides were great, knew a lot about what they were talking about and knew how to organize the tours satisfactorily. Positive highlights for the guides Jonathan (I do not remember the name of his agency) and Carolina (Andes Travel), for the moristas Daniel (Andes Travel) and Gregory (the same agency Jonathan). As points to improve note that the driver Marcelo (Andes Travel) was extremely imprudent and did not seem to have experience with the route of the Salares, which led us to have to stand still for about 30 minutes waiting for a car with new brakes during the route. In addition, the Astronomical Tour was very disorganized, we tried to make the tour the day before and we were not warned if it would occur by 2:30, they appeared at our door at 23:00 by surprise, when we were already sleeping, that is, there was no communication. When we managed to make the tour there were too many people, about 28 people and this left everything more complex, the photo was not professional (the positioning angle of the photos was bad and there was no direction for who was photographed), only took 1 photo of us when we paid for 2, during the whole experience there were lights around. Music around and high, breaking the mood of the moment. The agency was Atacama Borealis. I am very grateful to all those involved who helped us realize the dream of meeting Atacama with as much support as possible.

review_text: We only found out about the Valparaiso street art tour late the evening before our last day. Unfortunately the 10.30am one was booked out but we couldn't the guy and ended up arranging a private tour for the afternoon. Jake, our guide was awesome - friendly, smiling, accommodating and informative. Jake took us through the streets and explained all the street art, who made it, what inspired them, the history and importance behind street art for Valparaiso, the different stages of graffiti for artists. Being an art lover it was fascinating and informative! After the 2 hour tour we also included a graffiti art workshop meeting two of Chile's most famous street artists, where they we're painting one of the world's largest graffiti works on the back of a skyscraper / apartment block. The artists then showed us techniques on how to paint, showed us how to write a 'tag' for our names and let us play around with colour and spraying techniques. It was heaps of fun. Jake also gave us recommendations on where to eat, drink and things to do. His English is perfect. Valparsio is all about the street art, to go here without doing this tour would be missing out on seeing the real Valparaiso. For $80 US for two people it's a must do (includes workshop and private tour). Review of: Valparaiso City History & Graffiti Tour

review_text: My wife and I had a great fishing day with Ben in late Jan. 2017. He picked us up in his 4x4 at our hotel. We drove in the direction of Torres Del Paine park until cutting off on a gravel road to a large estancia in sight of the Torres. We fished a small river (creek) about 10-15 meters wide that ran through a pasture area. Most of the time we were on the bank and not wading. Fishing was slow due to very low water conditions. The fish finally woke up and we each got some quality brown trout. Ben brought a good lunch and set up table and chairs for a nice rest at noon. The wind came up in the afternoon which made it quite a challenge to cast across the river (where the fish were hiding). I'm sure that and my poor casting ability cost me several more fish as I was unable to accurately cast to the proper spots. All in all a good day. Just wish I could get back there soon.

review_text: We did the Villarrica Volcano ascent with Politur after being recommended through our hotel. We were able to drop by the day before to fit hiking gear which I would totally recommend to avoid some stress in the early morning. There was a small hiccup with our hotel pickup arriving 30 minutes late but everything else went smoothly. The ascent was a tough climb but not as hard as we expected from reading other reviews. It took around 3 hours to reach the summit after taking the chair lift. The climb itself is not that interesting since it’s just over snow. But the mountaineering equipment make it feel like a real expedition. The views climbing up are stunning, the country is laid out before your eyes like a map, you can see over a 100 kilometres in the distance. Reaching the summit is very satisfying, the idea that’s it’s an active volcano makes it all the more exciting. Finally sliding down is a lot of fun. Totally worth doing. The guides were patient, encouraging and spoke good English.

review_text: We went on the 3 day/2 night tour of the Uyuni Salt Flats leaving from San Pedro de Atacama in Chile. Cruz Andina organised the tour, and when we crossed the border into Bolivia the company who took us on the tour was White and Green Bolivia, who transported us in their jeep. It was all well-organised and seamless. Alfio was our guide. The tour was in Spanish, and even though we only spoke basic Spanish we got by, particularly with the help of a bilingual tour mate! The accomodation was basic but very comfortable, and the food provided was great, my food allergy was easily accommodated for. Alfio was a wealth of knowledge, friendly and easy-going. He took lots of fun photos of us throughout the tour, particularly on the Salt Flats, which were an incredible and otherworldly site. Other particularly memorable moments were visiting Laguna Colorada with its many flamingos, soaking in the Termas de Polques and climbing the Italian Perdidas. The tour was also a convenient way to transit from San Pedro to Uyuni, and then depart from Uyuni to La Paz or somewhere else in Bolivia. We highly recommend this tour.

review_text: Lots of bad reviews here but we found the service to be very reasonable. The snow has come very late this year which gave us the chance to go and speak to Ski total before the big snow came and before the rush began. Arranged our contract for ski and snowboard equipment and clothing rental on Friday afternoon when the shop was empty; the employee spoke English and was very helpful. It is quite a lengthy process so I can see how people can get frustrated if they try and do it on the day they go skiing when the shop is very busy and everyone is rushed off their feet. Having made the rental contract we came back early on Monday morning once the snow had arrived and there was a certain level of organised chaos on account of the number of people who are there wanting fitted for boots, skis jackets etc. Once we had our kit there was a sign in table for transport to the mountain. Transport was very reasonably priced and we were given a bus number and taken to the transport area. There was somebody here checking tickets and helping people get in the right vehicle- all went very smoothly. The ride to the slopes took just over two hours as the road up to the mountains is treacherous and icy; our driver was great but you are limited by other trucks and cars struggling to make it up there ahead of you on the narrow track. Once up there we got 5 and a half hours of skiing before we got back in the van to descend. The way back only took an hour and a half as the track had been fully cleared of ice by the end of the day. Overall the experience could be more streamlined as if it was any busier it may have taken an age to get rental stuff sorted, contracts made etc before we got to the transport vehicles- avoid this by making the contract and exchanging details the day before you go when the shop is quiet. Expect a long ride to the slopes but this can't be helped. For us it was exactly what we required and we loved every minute of it. I normally ski in Kitzbuhel which is the benchmark for great service and seamless rental experience but the Santiago equivalent day trip including rental, transport and lift pass only cost us £110 each which wouldn't buy you lunch in Kitzbuhel so I guess you get what you pay for! I would recommend this company for the competitive price and reasonable service.

review_text: We had a wonderful time seeing the highlights of Torres del Paine National Park and the Milodon Cave. We were worried because the weather forecasted rain and clouds, but our guide, Daniel, and driver, Roberto, made sure we saw the towers! Daniel is enthusiastic and engaging when sharing his love for these beautiful natural treasures! His enthusiasm was infectious, and his positivity kept the group engaged. He mixed nature and history and took some great photos too! I really cannot compliment him enough. I wanted to share some praise for Roberto as well. While it seemed his English was more limited, he was still able to exude friendliness. I have been on many tours all over the world, but hands down, he was the best driver I have ever had on a tour! He had an eagle eye and spotted condors, rheas, and guanaca for us. While nearly all the group were sleeping, I was awake to witness how carefully he avoided potholes while not excessively swerving for everyone's comfort - he did this for over an hour and I know it was probably exhausting. Truly, he's awesome. In any case, Torres del Paine is an unmissable place, but Roberto and Daniel made this an unforgettable experience! review_text: The Expedition to Laguna San Rafael See with pictures @ http://run.kobish-il.com/LSR/LSR.htm The story starts 6 months ago when I decided to make a trip to Chile, the trip planning process included some discussions with friends and very shortly the important goals where defined, since I love Kayaking and heard about Laguna San Rafael and the San Rafael majestic glacier such an expedition was set as a corner stone... After consultation with Yosale Dror from my Kayak club (Optimist Sdot-Yam) I have made a decision to paddle in the unknown waters where tide range is 5 meters, currents are strong and weather is unpredictable with a professional guide. I have started looking for a guide and found Rolando Toledo from AguaHielo. Quitralco 411, Puerto Aisén, Chile Tel: +56 9 7605 3580 Mail: aguahieloexpediciones@gmail.com Besides the everlasting smile on Rolando’s face in the gorgeous pictures and videos, Rolando answered me in perfect English which for me is very useful, making the communication easy and fluent, we have set a date for the expedition on February 20th and I was waiting for it impatiently :). On January 21st My partner Giora and me were on a flight to Chile and after trekking in Torres del paine Jeinimini and more we arrived at Coyhaique and rented a nice pickup, first thing we did was driving to Puerto Aysen to meet Rolando and get acquainted We have met Rolando and indeed our good internet impression became an understanding we have made the right choice, we have made a short kayak paddling trip down the Rio Simpson made sure the equipment fits us and asked Rolando for a tip where to camp, to make a long story short our pickup (not 4x4) required some help, it was 21:00 (PM) and Rolando came in 15 minutes from call and towed us out.... what a man We agreed to meet on February 20th in Puerto Tranquilo where the expedition will start We made our way down the Caratera Austral had great time visiting Capillas de Marmul, Rio Baker (rafting in Puerto Bertrand) Cochrane (Festival), Villa O’Higgins (El Musco glacier), Chilechico red rocks (Rolando’s recommendation) and more... On the 19th we were in Puerto Rio Tranquilo and on the 20th afternoon Rolando arrived as agreed with his famous Bongo loaded with Kayaks, food and equipment Roland opened with a short plan review using a map The planned route was the following We packed quickly and headed Los Tres where we plan to get into the water tomorrow In Los Tres we met with Don Jaime and Sra Vera, we got a splandid Salmon based dinner (Lazanga, and on the plancha) And heard the stories on Salmon fishing, Jaime's Balsa (Raft), How the way to Puerto Grosse was opened using fire and water... vey very warm and homelike feeling Morning the Los Tres point is the merge of 3 rivers and due to the rain in the last few days water level is high and the current is fast (8 knots) looks chalanging but fun as well, we pack the Mexicano (Marco) is saying last goodbye to Vera and we go in, the feeling can not be described, the current the mountains the waterfalls so the best way will be to look at Edgardo singing down the river Rolando is leading making sure the path is clear from wood and eddies and soon we are getting into the pacific waters We continue to paddle and the wind is coming up, Rolando takes a decision to call it a day and we are heading a small lagoon very protected and nice, We lift the Kayaks 4 meters since tide is low and in minutes Edgardo and Rolando are setting the camp and start cooking Dinner is a great so a great day is behind us Second day weather looks nice and we start paddling we pass a Salmon farm and watch the jumping fish, the farms are nice but bring a lot of pollution... while paddling one can see the seagulls tonina dolphines and sea lions We pass the the strait of Golfo Elfantes, paddling down current avoiding the eddies and having grreeat fum, Patagonian weather is surprising so after a very good weather at day start we suddenly get strong head wind waves start rising and rain is striking our faces, Rolando is signing to get closer to the shore and is tieing one of the boats to his Kayak we are back in safety soon enough :), wind goes down we continue paddling and get to a very nice beach for the second night, good food, good wine, full moon light, huge campfire what more can we ask for Third day, we will start late because we want the incoming tide water current to take us into Laguna San Rafael, paddling against the current will not be a good idea :), since we are lucky not only tide current is at our back but also the wind, Rolando has a small sail but all us fly with the current and back wind into the laguna and get to see the floating glaciers Camping at Laguna San Rafael is convinient, meal is good as always and in the next morning we are hiking by foot to the San Rafael glacier mirador (lookout) a little rest from the long ~110 KM we covered in the last 3 days Afternoon short Kayak trip to the glacier during which we pickup some ice from the water for a special use Last day in the laguna consists of paddeling through the ice to the far side of the glacier and walking to its blue icy face, the expirience is so wonderful words will not be good enough and also the pictures only hint how great this is For dinner Rolando says he will fish, I must confese I wasn't optimistic but in an hour I witnessed the miracle Rolando got 4 large Robalo fish which Edgardo prepared in the oven.... how come we have an oven during an expadition? well Rolando being a very generous expedition manger got hard rain forecast and decided to rent the guarderia building for us and eventhough the rain was not that hard we got the luxurious building along with wine and very nice jokes Marko was telling we had great evening In the morning we took all the gear packed and loaded a small boat that took us back Great great expirience, many thanks to the profesionalism of Rolando and Edgardo and the nice team, Giora, Roberto, Francisco, Marko, Mauricio and me Kobi the writer of the above Bottom line very recommended expedition and if you decide to do it only with Rolando and Aguahielo

review_text: I was crammed for the whole day (12 hours) in the very back row of a minibus, a seat that felt more like a “little ease”, with 0.70 sq. ft., no room to stretch legs under the seat in front because of the back wheel. No switching around (some seats were more comfortable I think)! The Porvenir museum was an interesting stop. Penguins are visible only from a distance and as the guide insisted so much on not taking any food on the premises, I left my bag (with food but also with my binoculars) in the bus. I suppose the excursion would have seemed nicer if the material and physical conditions had not been so terrible. To top it all, the driver would either switch cold ventilation to very high or stop all ventilation, causing windows to fog up. To cut a long story short, certainly not worth 90 USD, + lunch and entrance fee to the park.

review_text: We went to Lauca National Park last year, in august. It was a wonderful experience. No better place to leave behind your troubles. Open plains, vulcanos, more than 500 alpacas and vicunas. We organised the tour through a little tour agency in Arica: Orange Travel. You can e-mail them at orangetravel@terra.cl. We went for the 3 day tour (Lauca National Park + Las Vicunas National Reserve). I strongly recommend the full tour through Las Vicunas (with Salar de Surire), because it is the road less traveled. We were alone in the park for the complete day, only alpacas and vicunas held us company. And our wonderful tour guide Oreol, who gave us the absolute best tour experience ever. He lives in Putre, not far from the parks. He knows the region, drove us around in his little bus and took his little dog with hem. He invited us to meet his friends on a barbeque while we watched the football game Chile-Argentina. That is when we fell in love with Chile. It was wonderful. If you go to Chile, don't miss out on this northern region. This was absolutely better than San Pedro de Atacama, where we saw more people than wildlife and nature. Take the less traveled road and head to Arica!

We were alone in the park for the complete day, only alpacas and vicunas held us company. And our wonderful tour guide Oreol, who gave us the absolute best tour experience ever. He lives in Putre, not far from the parks. He knows the region, drove us around in his little bus and took his little dog with hem. He invited us to meet his friends on a barbeque while we watched the football game Chile-Argentina. That is when we fell in love with Chile. It was wonderful. If you go to Chile, don't miss out on this northern region. This was absolutely better than San Pedro de Atacama, where we saw more people than wildlife and nature. Take the less traveled road and head to Arica!

review_text: This review is for the penguin and Magdalena Island tour. Overall a good tour with some great guides, but organization and communication needs to be improved. We waited at the bus-sur station from 640am~830am for what was supposed to be a 7-730am pickup. No communication from the organizers and it was unclear it the tour was going to happen or was canceled. Eventually the staff arrived, and it turned out a cruise ship caused problems that morning. We needed to check in at both the bus and the boat. The dock was so close it would have been nice it we had the option to walk rather than ride the bus just a few blocks. We eventually set sail ~1 hour late, maybe more, and had a smooth sail across to the island. On the way guides answered questions in both spanish and english, showing maps and talking about this area. We saw a whale, dolphins, seals, and sea lions. The island itself was fantastic! You have about an hour to walk a 1mile loop. The guides were great, taking photos and answering questions along the way! My issue with this tour lies with the "main" guide and the feeling of the morning's delay constantly being pushed onto the patrons. The entire walk we were hounded with reminders of the 1 hour limit (despite moving more than fast enough) and at the end as we were loading the boat, constant mentions of how late we were returning to punta arenas. The other passengers we sat with, along with my group, didn't appreciate that when it wasn't our fault we left port late that morning. If I had to do it over, I may check out Solo Expediciones where some friends of ours had a better experience.

review_text: Quebrada del Diablo (or Garganta del Diablo) is an awesome, AWESOME bike ride. From the entrance to the quebrada, it's about a 2 hour ride, twisting through rock walls and dirt hills. It's probably not for beginners, but with a bit of athleticism, you'll be fine. The views are gorgeous, but be careful, THERE ARE NO SIGNS! There are karns in some places, and footprints and horse hoof-prints to follow in others, but we eventually got lost. We found two other couples who were also lost, so we know it wasn't just us. We eventually found the river and followed it downstream over hills of sand until we found a way out onto the road. We definitely weren't on the trail, though. If you like to mountain bike, don't miss this! But be prepared and ASK about the path before you go! (I bet Juan Carlos, who is in charge of bike rentals at Apacheta in the plaza, knows!)

review_text: While visiting Santiago we were lucky enough to get to watch a soccer (aka, futbol) game (Chile versus Burkina Faso). On the morning of my flight, I texted and called starting at 9:14am when there was still no one to pick me up. I even called the number listed on the website. Multiple messages and calls but no response. I was getting very worried I would miss my flight! Finally I frantically ran to the bus station at 9:45. The bus station employees said that there was no bus that would get me to the Calama airport now on time, that I would need a taxi right now in order to make my flight. The bus station employee was nice enough to get me a taxi and I was able to make it to the airport for a 50,000 Chilean pesos ($85USD)! I made it in time just as the flight was boarding! Two days later I saw that there was a missed phone call from Lithium's number on my Whatsapp. I called back and spoke with Eva. I was very upset and explained that I nearly missed my flight and emergently had to pay $85USD for a private taxi. I was very stressed out and teary-eyed that I nearly missed my flight. review_text: I travelled to this winery from Santiago. With traffic, it took me about 45 minutes to get there. Once at the winery, I was assigned a guide who was fluent in Spanish and English and ran a joint language tour. Although the guide was friendly and knowledgeable, I wasn't over impressed with the tour, which dragged on a bit by virtue of being in Spanish and English. The composition of the group (primarily Spanish speakers) meant that the guide put more focus on the Spanish speaking group. He spoke in Spanish for minutes at a time, and then provided an abbreviated version of what he had just said to the English speakers. The net result was that the tour felt a bit long in the tooth and left me with the sense that I was only getting a fraction of the experience that Spanish speakers got. Additionally, I had anticipated more discussion of wine and more tasting opportunities, and instead got a tour of the wine making facilities and lots of stats on how much the winery produces each year. We only tasted three wines. Also a little disappointing was the fact that the grapes are harvested in March and the vines were empty. If you're the kind of person who'd like to see the grapes in full bloom, take this into account when planning your trip. The winery was still quite scenic, though. Overall, the tour was good, but not great.

review_text: Preparation: We rented a car in Copiapo for 2 days, it has to be a powerfull 4x4, with atleast 2.5 liter engine. (We bought 2 plastic tanks of 20 liters filled with gas, very important because there are no gas stations in the park area. You are going to sleep in very high altitude, prepare yourself, drink 2 liters of water a day and consider to take pills for prevention of altitude sickness (Acetazolamide). Day 1: Copiapo to Laguna Santa Rosa ( 2 hours drive with lunch stop) the altitude is 3,700m. We payed $5,000 entrance fee in the Conaf (per car). You can sleep in your tent or car, or sleep in the refugio, it is private and costs $10,000 per person, it has 6 beds, kitchen with gas and water, and inside toilet. The woman that works there is very nice and came few times to check that everything is fine. The Laguna is beautiful and has many flamingos . It is freezing after the sun down, take a warm sleeping bag and worm clothes. Day 2 : from Laguna Santa Rosa (2:30 hours drive) to Negro Francisco the altitude is 4,200, we got lost a little bit, there are no signs , just follow the electrical posts, the Laguna is amazing, breathtaking view if the water, mountains behind it and lots of flamingos. keep driving until the free big refugio there. If you keep going 5 more kilometers after the refugio you will see a nice view (the Conaf suggested us) . Then we continued to Laguna Verde (2.5 hr) 4,300 altitude. Don't take the shorter way that GPS suggets you, take the highway. We barely got out the huge holes in the dirt road (without 4x4 you're stuck) we came to the Laguna Verde at 19:00 and it was really windy but the amazing view made you forget about the cold. Then we continued with the road until Termas, the refugio there was overcrowded (max 10) and the water wasn't hot enough to get into the termas considering the strong wind. We headed back to the refugio at Volcano ojos, (small sign on the road) it is a free refugio, on the first level one private small room with 2 matresses , kitchen, (no gas and no water) big spacious room with bunk beds, enough room to put 10 mattresses on the floor, one more private room with one matress, second floor has 4 beds. The toilet is outside without a door and in a bad shape. It looks abondened, has no light, quiet scary to be there at night in the middle of nowhere. During the night we got altitude sicknes, terrible headaches, hard to breathe so we couldn't sleep, also it was freezing cold in there. We waited for the first light to get out of there. My suggestion is to sleep in Laguna Santa Rosa where the altitude is weeker. On the way back to Copiapo we drove to the salar de Maricunga.

review_text: While in Santiago, Chile we wanted to visit a winery and the Santa Rita got the most nods. It was a four hour tour that took us from the grape vines through the whole process of fermentation, storage, bottling and finally tasting. Our guide was a young man named Mattias that explained the whole process with knowledge and information that I had never experienced before. The winery itself is in a beautiful old building that once was the estate of a woman that saved 120 soldiers during the war of independence with Spain. They now have a wine named 120 for these brave soldiers. Information like this just made the whole place come alive and the four hours passed incredibly fast. Too fast. Soon it was time to get back on the bus and back to the city. We did come away with a lot more knowledge of the whole process and appreciation of effort the winery puts into ensuring a wonderful tour.

review_text: This was one of the highlights of my life. I skied Portillo in August in the 1990's After my boyfriend who I was with on and off for 16 years broke up our relationship. At the time, I was heartbroken. But I had the most amazing 7 day vacation. Portillo is 22,838 ft above sea level. World Class Skiing. 100 percent above the tree line. Condors in the sky. It's located 160 km By vehicle from Santiago Chile. Opened in 1949, it hosted Alpine World Ski Championships in August 1966. It marked The emergence of Jean Claude Kelly. I got lucky. I skied beautifully, And the men there were gorgeous. Only the Finest from Chile and Argentina. Everybody there was divorced and many Had attended Columbia University in New York City. I was the only pretty blonde American Woman that was there from New York City. Enough said. I felt beautiful being so popular. The owner of the resort was American and I was always invited for dinner to eat at the Owners private table with him and his wife, who was Chilean. My boyfriend in New York asked me to go back with him the week after I returned to New York. I felt so beautiful from Skiing Portillo I was glowing for weeks. I spent 16 years of my life with my boyfriend in New York. We did not live together. We keep separate apartments but we had lunch with each other every day,and spent evenings together 3 times a week. He was a Magnificent man, but he Didn't want to get married because his parents had had such a terrible marriage And that was quite painful for him. I was told at a the age of 11, that I could not have children. We were a great pair until he got Horribly Sick. He married a nurse that he Had know as a friend for over 30 years. She takes care of him and his finances. He is now in a wheelchair. He was a Tribal Art Dealer, internationally And he had 3 other businesses, so he could never travel with me in August. He Was busy with the accountants. But we did travel together, often on business in London or in Paris. I met him when I was 29 years old and fell madly in love. He took me To 11 Cadogan Gardens for my 30th birthday. You will love Portillo, Chile. There is nothing in the world like it.

Anyone who enjoys watching birds should put this site on the "must" list for Punta Arenas.

review_text: I went in June a couple days after rainfall in Santiago. There's a small area to park at the bottom of the trail, but nothing official. But, it's well worth it during the winter still. As others have said, the first half an hour going up is a little bit harder than the rest of the trail. There's a beautiful lake half way up to the glacier, which was mostly frozen over. Up towards the glacier there was actual snow! Exciting stuff when you're coming from Santiago, hahah. There's a river following much of the trail. I'll definitely be heading back in the spring/fall!!! At the bottom of the trail there's the little guard-house where you pay the entrance fee and some bathrooms. There's also places to buy snacks, have lunch/dinner, and buy knick-knacks at the bottom, but I didn't really check anything out. The Baños/hotsprings were closed despite the sign saying it was open on those days and those times... but maybe it's closed for the season?

review_text: Valparaiso was already a very important city globally, especially before the operation of the Panama Canal, as it functioned as a commercial warehouse. It currently has one of the highest unemployment rates in Chile. Home to frequent earthquakes and some tsunamis, it still has several buildings (such as one of its churches) damaged and unavailable for visit, even after 14 years of the last major earthquake. It has one of the biggest camelodroms I've ever seen in my life, which works as an informal market. The city is distributed by hills, with huge population density, reminiscent of the Brazilian favelas, but without (so much) garbage on the streets or sewage at open sky. Ja Vina del Mar is a younger, more beautiful and more elegant city. The beach, however, is of more yellow sand, darker, and the water (of the Pacific) is frozen. Complete the landscape many stones on the beach and a more violent sea, which requires a lot of caution. review_text: Besides having the bad luck of entering the station with way less snow than expected (reason why the only track open was the Ski Lessons/Basic Track), I didn't have a positive experience overall, due to the main reasons below: - Crowd: Absolutely awful. Went up on a monday (29/07), already after the oficial winter holidays in Chile and off from the weekend and even so there was way more people I expected. Lines to get to the belts that take you to the highest point on the only open track as I said before could get up to 15 minutes. Basically you stay 15 minutes in the line, 2 more to reach the "top" and then 30 seconds to go down. All other rides had lines worse than that (Canopy, Tubing, etc.). - Infrastructure (Food and Drinks/Stores/Bathrooms, etc): Ok for the bathrooms (haven't seen if there was toilet paper available), but cleaningness was "OK". Stores. Food options are extremely limited and very expensive. You can definately have a healthier option paying much less if you bring food from home. One thing that bothered me quite a lot was the disorganization to get rental equipment (snowboard/skis, boots and accessories overall). Employees haven't been quite helpful and they behave to rush everyone out of the rental tent, which is very small to the amount of people they receive (specially if the site is in its first hour). Good to bear in mind that they do not provide clothing rental, equipment ONLY. Instructors: Had some basic classes and they went well. The instructors were fine and attentive. If you are focused on skiing/learning to ski, this is not the best option for you.

review_text: My visit here was one of the best mornings of my entire life - and I'm 53. We arrived around 9:30 AM and it was literally empty. You descend into a narrow valley, practically a fissure in the earth, surrounded by beautifully rugged red clay walls and mesas. And there awaits a bubbling river nestled into giant ornamental beach grass and tumbling down from level to level, connected by small, therapeutic waterfalls. And the water is deliciously warm - maybe 85 degrees! It's a magical experience floating on your back down the stream, and then letting a natural jacuzzi massage your trek-weary muscles. Be sure to find the falls where you can sit, cross-legged, behind the waterfall. It's magical. NOTE: The best price we could get for this excursion from San Pedro was 40K pesos each, plus 15K entry fee. So we hired a cab, which drove us there, waited two hours, and drove us back for a total of 40K pesos . . . one third the price. No guide is needed! Don't miss it . . . and enjoy!

review_text: I had a really great day out on this tour lead by Alvaro. It was unexpected as originally I had booked to go to Portillo but that tour wasn’t able to go so the tour company offered me this one instead. I had a really lovely day as the tour was filled with expected and unexpected stops. On our way to cajon del maipo, we stopped at a few photo moments, along with a cafe in the morning to get coffee. At the reservoir there is about a 30 min walk to the main sight. The walk was not hard but the elevation and altitude made the air feel thinner so I was a bit out of breath. Once there the views are breathtaking. On our way back we stopped at a quick bathroom stop where there were some alpacas and farm animals. From above we were able to see condors which was very exciting. We then stopped at a unique chocolate shop, and then a wine and cheese tasting. After this we got delicious empanadas - you get to choose what you want inside which is ideal for a picky eater like me. That really concludes the tour. It’s then back to Santiago. We got back around 4.45pm. Highly worth the day trip. It was beautiful to see all the mountains, and the stops along the way were fun. Thanks Alvaro!! Review of: Cajon Del Maipo Including Wine with Picnic and Empanada

There are no other exhibits here other than three ship replicas so even the non-museum lovers will enjoy this experience as will kids.

review_text: After a lot of research on trip advisor, I picked Cruz Andina for a round trip tour to Salar de Uyuni from San Pedro Atacama. I was very impressed by the tour and have nothing negative to point out. 1. Booking: I booked with them over email. Responses were prompt (albeit in Spanish). All details were clearly provided particularly regarding the requirements and documents needed to procure a visa at the border 2. Confirmation at SPA: I reconfirmed with them the day I arrived in SPA and paid the outstanding balance. They provided clear detailed instructions for the tour and guided me through getting Bolivian currency and necessary photocopies of documents for the visa 3. Pickup and travel to border: Pick-up was promptly at the scheduled time. They took us by shuttle to the Bolivian border. They even reviewed the customs and immigration forms we filled out - question by question. I speak very limited Spanish and they were helpful in talking to the Bolivian immigration officers on my behalf at the border. After clearing immigration, we transferred to 4x4s for the rest of the tour 4. Driver/Guide: Our driver and guide was Jose Luis. A genuinely great chap, he was a calm and patient driver - we always felt safe with him. He arranged for our food and explained all the sights to us. Though he spoke almost no English, he spoke slowly and patiently and I had little trouble understanding what he was saying. 5. Accommodation and Food: I spent a little bit extra to get private rooms instead of shared rooms. While the hotels were fairly basic, I had no complains - I had a private room with clean private baths, hot water showers available and towels etc. provided. Through the trip the food was great - homemade style simple food - soups, pasta, stews etc. Simple but hearty and satisfying 6. Sights: The sights you see are to die for. They are unreal and it feels like you are in the middle of a Planet Earth or Nat Geo documentary All in all, I would recommend Cruz Andina to anyone considering a trip to the Salar.

Confirmation at SPA: I reconfirmed with them the day I arrived in SPA and paid the outstanding balance. They provided clear detailed instructions for the tour and guided me through getting Bolivian currency and necessary photocopies of documents for the visa 3. Pickup and travel to border: Pick-up was promptly at the scheduled time. They took us by shuttle to the Bolivian border. They even reviewed the customs and immigration forms we filled out - question by question. I speak very limited Spanish and they were helpful in talking to the Bolivian immigration officers on my behalf at the border. After clearing immigration, we transferred to 4x4s for the rest of the tour 4. Driver/Guide: Our driver and guide was Jose Luis. A genuinely great chap, he was a calm and patient driver - we always felt safe with him. He arranged for our food and explained all the sights to us. Though he spoke almost no English, he spoke slowly and patiently and I had little trouble understanding what he was saying. 5. Accommodation and Food: I spent a little bit extra to get private rooms instead of shared rooms. While the hotels were fairly basic, I had no complains - I had a private room with clean private baths, hot water showers available and towels etc. provided. Through the trip the food was great - homemade style simple food - soups, pasta, stews etc. Simple but hearty and satisfying 6. Sights: The sights you see are to die for. They are unreal and it feels like you are in the middle of a Planet Earth or Nat Geo documentary All in all, I would recommend Cruz Andina to anyone considering a trip to the Salar.

review_text: My daughter and I decided to visit the park but weren't sure where to start. We walked to the Pio Nono entrance to go up on the funicular. It was about 1 pm. We encountered a 90-minute wait. So instead we took a five-minute taxi ride for $5 up to the Plaza Tupahue. From there, we could walk 30-40 minutes up a steady, slight incline to the Cerro San Cristobal (a giant statue of the Virgin Mary is at the top) or take the teleferico to the top (where the Virgin Mary is). We didn't have time to walk. So I paid $5 per round-trip ticket. We waited 10 minutes in line to ride one stop to the top. It was a scenic ride. The line to board the teleferico to ride down looked long. But they separate the line into two - the line for three or more was about 45 minutes. The line for the two of us was about five minutes. We rode down to the bottom station, Pedro de Valdivia. The park was filled with Chilean families. If we had more time, we would have explored the various nooks and crannies within the park. Alternatively, if you are a jogger, you can start at the entrance near the Pedro de Valdivia teleferico stop and make your way up the slight uphill incline to the Virgin Mary. It takes me about 45 minutes. The park's gates open at 7 am.

Then, we decided to spend 2 (amazing) days with Miguel Fuentealba (ISO100 owner and field guide) with our guide. Approximately 40 minutes after he picked up us at the very first day, he suddenly stopped the car and said "Look, a cougar will jump from that rock!!!" Unbelievably, suddenly a cougar jump from behind the rock and also cross the road in front of our car!!! At the same day he tracked some footprints and was able to find two young brother cougars... Amazing!!! He do all the cougar track with a huge respect for the animals and for their habitat... We have seen some guides in Paine with have no real respect for the wildlife. Miguel is a real example of guide with a great sense of respect and love to nature. Besides that, he is a lovely person, has a great knowledge of the region and all its major attractions. Also, he has another major skill, he is wildlife photographer!!! So, we got several advices for the best shots and videos of the local animals!!! Two amazing days in the company of this awsome guide and human being. We have seen 8 different pumas (cougars) in Torres del Paine in the company of Miguel Fuentealba. We do not have words to thank him!!! For sure, we want to come back to Patagonia and Torres del Paine, and of course, enjoy the company of Miguel (ISO100). We have met guides all over the world, and we can assure that Miguel is an outstanding one! Thanks, "Chê"... We hopw to see you again soon... HASTA PRONTO!!

review_text: I am giving this a mixed review for a few reasons. First I want to say that the guides were absolutely wonderful. None of my issues have to do with them, as they were really accommodating, informative, friendly and flexible when we hit the bad weather. So context: my partner and I were in Puerto Varas only because we had come over the Cruce Andino from Argentina. We had a day to kill, and when I did several google searches for what to do in Puerto Varas - this is what came up (and that was reinforced when this was the main thing being sold at the tourist desk in our hotel). However, the day we did this it was pouring rain. That was not a problem when seeing the waterfalls - absolutely beautiful. But it was so foggy that when we got to the top of the volcano, you could see nothing. The tour even just stopped there, we took a funny pic with the whiteout, then got back in the van. So my take on this tour? If it is bad weather then don't do it - not worth it. But I'd also add: I didn't look into the cost of renting a car and doing this ourselves. That may have been a better idea, as it turns out there are other walks in the national park we could have done if we had the time/opportunity. So mixed review: good tour guides, worthwhile if there is nice weather, but if you have the opportunity to rent a car and do it yourself, that's probably a better option. review_text: When we stopped for a short visit at Concha y Toro, we knew it would be quite a large, impersonal winery. We didn't go on one of the tours (although we did see hordes of people doing so), but instead stopped for a quick bite and wine tasting at the wine bar. We wanted to try the flagship wine, Don Melchor, as well as the Almaviva, and both were offered by the glass. There were actually two vintages of the Don Melchor on offer, so we were able to do a vertical tasting. The wines were great, but the experience itself not so great. (If possible, try to find these wines somewhere else and skip the visit entirely.) The service at the wine bar was awful, the wines are served without any explanation (and in small, cheap glasses), and they simply forgot to bring one of the items we ordered. This could be such a nice tasting experience to go with the high quality of some of the wines, but they have missed the opportunity.

review_text: We went with Flamingo tours and were collected from our hotel. The bus was full so we had to squeeze into two seats right at the back of the bus. It was a very tight space and not a very comfortable journey to get there. The guide was good explaining everything in Spanish English and French. First stop on a trip was to the rainbow valley. The guide walked us around the site and explained all of the geology which was very interesting. We then were given breakfast at the side of the van. We were then taken to see the petroglyphs. We had to pay an entrance fee for here. There were very basic toilets there but no running water to wash hands. There were drawings of animals like llamas, flamingoes and foxes. Headed back to San Pedro and were dropped off in town so we could walk back to our hotel around 130 pm. It’s really sandy and dusty there as is everywhere in San Pedro.

review_text: We did a fair bit of research before choosing Chilean Wine Lovers as our guides for 3 full days in the Santiago area. Corresponding via email several months prior to our trip, Mauricio took the time to understand the type of experiences and sights we wanted do & see. From this he crafted 2 custom itineraries for each of the 3 days, that included wineries, sightseeing, gain some understanding of the culture, and architecture. He is also super flexible with the itineraries, when a road wash-out occurred that prevented us from going into the mountains, he easily created a day for us in Maipo Valley that was outstanding. For wineries he selected different types of experiences, One a small boutique winery just outside Santiago, where in true boutique fashion, all labels are made on site and applied by hand, The second was organic winery The House of Morande, a full vineyard tour, followed by private session on the learning the essentials and of wine tasting, This was followed by the best (and I mean the best) ever custom tasting menu paired with spectacular wines in the most incredible setting... If you only have time for one Winery this would be it... Finally we toured Underraga Winery, which was the largest of all the wineries and here we also toured the vineyards, the fermentation area and another wonderful .wine tasting... Underraga gives you the glass to take home...Each of the wineries were all beautiful settings, which added to the experience. We also had an impromptu picnic one day, several bottles of wine, traditional meat pies, the top of a mountain, overlooking Casablanca Valley - magical. We spent a few hours in Valparaiso and Vina Del Mar... and after seeing Valparaiso a Unesco world heritage, sight, I am both very glad that we had the opportunity and that we had a private guide...get so much more understanding of the people and the area with a guide...(plus where to go and where not to go...important in Valparaiso) We spent time in a small town that specializes in making pottery and had a wonderful traditional local meal there also.....also accompanied by outstanding wines, that Maurico brought with them. We also wanted to see Santiago, yes the traditional great places to see such as the Mercardo, but also the architecture, both old and new, as well as learning a little more about how the people of Santiago live... Mauricio accommodated all of this for us, including getting to see the "burbs" Mauricio, readily shares his tremendous knowledge and insight of the area, in such an personable way, and he loves what he does.. Before this trip we had never used the services of a private guide. I am now totally convinced this is the way to go, when you have a short time in an area, want some unique/memorable experiences, an understanding of the culture and people and do not speak the language. When I return, I would absolutely call Mauricio, it would be visiting an old friend.
