review_text: Perhaps it is adequate to book their service from airport to any downtown hotels, but I tried their round trip service from San Cristóbal Hotel to Santa Cruz, the Colchagua Valley to visit Clos Apalta. I had agree to a price of US$270 to start with, as the receptionist was explicit that he offered me a “good deal” and therefore the discounted price. I settled all payment at their counter at once. To my surprise, their staff called me at San Cristóbal the night before I was about to go to Santa Cruz, and said there was a mistake in pricing and the total price for this round trip service would be US$400 in total, so I still owed them another US$130. Since I didn’t have much of a choice, I reluctantly agreed to top up the extra US$130. On the day of transfer, the driver again haggled with me about the price and said in fact the total should be US$560, so there was still a shortfall of US$160. I was very frustrated at that point, but not about the monies, rather the integrity and professionalism of this company. On my return trip, they insisted I pay US$560 or else they would not drive me back to Santiago, so I paid immediately, but what’s even worse was on my way back to Santiago Airport (as I was catching a flight to Atacama), the driver took a complete detour and we ended-up at somewhere in nether him nor me knew our whereabouts. What would originally took 2.5 hours from Santa Cruz to the airport eventually took 3.5 hours to get there, if I was not an Emerald member of the One World Alliance, I would have missed my flight because of this. So next time when you are dealing with this company Transvip, please be cautious.

review_text: Embalse El Yeso is a must-see destination if you are visiting Santiago. The picturesque views of the vast water and mountains are breath taking. In the visit, I was first picked up from a hotel of my choice to where the Turistik bus leaves to start to excursion. I would say that there were about 15 people in the tour. They can do the tour in English and Spanish also. The bus driver was Mario and he got us everywhere on time. My tour guide was Valentina and she was great. She spoke in both languages and it helped me compare words, since I am still learning Spanish. We first stopped in a town to get snacks and go to the bathroom. Then we did some more driving and got out of the bus to start walking to Yeso. We had about an hour to explore and take pictures. I recommend walking to the very end first and then working your way back to the bus, because that is where you'll have the best mountain/reservoir photo shoot. Once you return to the bus there is juice, cheese, and crackers waiting. After that, we stop at a restaurant in the mountains. When I went there was a buffet of a lot of typical Chilean foods such a Pastel de Choclo. The late lunch wasn't included but it was worth it and the bathrooms at the restaurant are clean. On the way back Valentina helped show me where to go, so I would be able to get home quickly. She was very nice and I had a great experience. I would definitely recommend this to anyone (the hiking, well walking, was flat. don't worry) and you will for sure get amazing pictures. review_text: We were so excited for a unique experience to see Glaciar Jorge Montt. This is a once in a lifetime trip. We didn’t realize how hard it would be to find a reputable company to take us but Waeskar was willing. They just said they would look for more people to ride with us because we were only 4 and they wanted 6. Later that day, the day before our anticipated trip, they told us that we needed to find the other people or else pay for their spots. Not ideal and we even asked about getting a commission if we were to spend the rest of our evening hawking for this boat. Regardless, we did find 2 more people but there was no discount and we all rushed to depart by 9am the next morning. Unfortunately, our captain was 45 minutes late. We finally departed after that delay only to find out after nearly another hour that we didn’t have any gas. We had to turn around and go back, losing another hour. When we saw how much fuel they did have to load on the boat, it is baffling how they couldn’t have realized it was missing in the first place. We also had to stop 4-5 times during the journey to refuel. We did make it to close to the glacier, better late than never. There were some choppy waters which had everyone clutching the side of the boat and we had the aforementioned fuel stops, but we did dock near the glacier for a surprisingly good risotto, some soup and some cocktails. We did hike a bit but it wasn’t the hour we were expecting. We saw other boats getting closer to the glacier but ours did not get as close as theirs. On the way back, our guide, Tomas, kept coming to the back of the boat to drink pisco from the bottle the guests were supposed to enjoy. We made it back two hours later than expected and with the exchange rate, paid close to $900 USD for 6 people. The boat is nothing glamorous and the experience fell short of what we would expect for that amount of money. We did get close to the glacier but I think we would have been better off with a different tour company.

review_text: If you're in Santa Cruz, you can't beat this excursion as a way to see the beautiful countryside and create memories of a lifetime. We had rented an apartment from Ian Garrett while in Santa Cruz, and this excursion was his suggestion. So glad we did it! I'm a little nervous around horses (even though I'm a veterinarian), and I didn't know anything about how to ride. But Ian was a great teacher and the horses are incredibly responsive and well-trained. I quickly lost my fear as I learned to navigate the horse and appreciate the gorgeous scenery. We truly enjoyed Ian's company, and he was a great tour guide in general for our time in Santa Cruz (he gave us so many helpful insider tips). Ian packed a delicious picnic snack for us to enjoy at the top of the hill overlooking the valley, with locally made wine, jerky, cheese, and nuts. What a great way to spend Thanksgiving! Be sure to wear jeans, long sleeves, and a hat to protect yourself along the ride. Also make sure the toes of your shoes aren't too thick - I had a little trouble squeezing my hiking shoes into the stirrups. Review of: Horseback rides Santa Cruz, Chile

review_text: I was excited to have this tour booked because it was a very hot day. Too hot to be walking all over Santiago. Spending a few hours in an air conditioned bus seemed like the perfect ticket. The bus was clean and new but the bounce is incredible. Add that to the 60 (yes, 60) hairpin tours up the mountain and it's enough to make anyone sick. Several did! I'm glad I took dramamine. The driver and guide were nice but not a lot of information was provided. There was a lot of downtime at places where there was nothing to do. The tour could have been reduced by an hour or more. We spent over an hour at a completely empty ski resort. I guess we were supposed to hike, but I didn't bring shoes for that as it was not mentioned in the description. No one did, so we just sat and waited . Then we moved to the sunset site. Cute little mountainside cafe with a perfect patio to see the sunset, but we had to wait about 90 minutes. The biggest disappointment was the tour was advertised as being in English, and while the guide did a great job of talking in English and Spanish, I was the only English one who spoke English. As a solo traveler, I took the tour hoping to meet other people, but there was no one else to talk to. It made the 7 hours even longer. Overall, it was just OK and a very long exhausting day. I think it would have been much nicer in spring when the mountains would still have snow but in the summer there really isn't much to see. Also, the empanadas are just cheese. You get 4 little ones. Since it was dinnertime, it would have been nice to just get 2 little beef ones instead. review_text: We booked this tour at 9:20 the night before which allowed us to negotiate the price down to lower than we had seen anywhere else. Speaking to others on the tour who had organised other tours with them, similar discounts had been offered for multiple bookings. Apart from the price, the thing that really attracted us to the company was the fact that their breakfast seemed more generous than the others’ including scrambled eggs, bread, juice, chocolate milk, coffee, tea and biscuits. As we waited with all the other geyser-goers in the street in the early hours of the morning, we watched as everyone was picked up and wondered where our van was. The guy at the front desk of our hostel said that this company are always later than others. We were worried that they were not going to come but they were just a little late. At the time we were concerned that this would mean that we would miss sunrise at the geysers but it was not a problem at all. In fact in retrospect I wished that we had arrived a little later because we still seemed about half an hour to forty-five minutes too early for the start of the sunrise. Getting into the jeep at this very cold hour of the morning, we were each given a blanket- a very nice touch. The guide, although not speaking much English, was super friendly and enthusiastic and seemed to genuinely enjoy guiding the tour. He was a one man band, guiding, driving and cooking our breakfast but this certainly did not detract from the tour in any way. The breakfast was fantastic and as we were eating fresh scrambled eggs and drinking hot chocolate that had been warmed in the geyser I was certainly glad that we had chosen the company that we did. But what really set them apart from the others was that, when all the other groups left about 15 minutes after sunrise we remained as long as we wanted, lingering over coffee and sharing stories whilst enjoying the geysers, now in perfect morning light, all to ourselves. This flexibility to stay at locations as long as we liked, rather than being herded around to a tight time schedule as all other tour groups seemed to be, made the morning a lot more relaxed and enjoyable. As an aside, dress warmer than you think is necessary- it gets really cold!

review_text: At Torres del Paine National Park, we enjoyed most spectacular views of irregularly shaped, rugged, snowy peaks diffusing into white puffy clouds. While we enjoyed temperatures in the 50•F – 60•F (10•C-15•C) range, days were misty, with constant drizzle, and gusty winds that forced us to straddle our legs while standing, so we would not get pushed by the wind. Patagonia branded wear was definitely inspired by this weather. On February 19, 2019, my husband and I hiked about 12 miles round trip to a glacial lake at the base of the Torres at about one kilometer of altitude. Our exhilarating expedition filled us with anticipation of spectacular views at every turn. We saw condors fly not much higher than us, and waters of many hues in distant lakes beneath us. Different accumulated minerals, we later learned, cause the different water colors.

review_text: On the whole, this was a well-organised trip from booking to embarkation through to the actual 3-day ferry journey itself (though the website needs improvement). For complete privacy, we chose an AAA cabin which, for a vehicle ferry, was well appointed and more spacious than we had expected. The briefings were thorough and the talks and films throughout the journey were good. The captain always announced things of interest to see. The staff were courteous and helpful. When we booked, what they failed to tell you on their website was that, for the eye-watering cost of choosing one of the few AAA cabins, you do actually get to eat in the separate AAA dining room with a better menu, tables with tablecloths and napkins, waitress service and free, good quality wines with all lunches and dinners – that’s a real bonus. The weather was mixed on our trip though fortunately the seas were largely calm. You take this trip to look at the scenery of the archipelago so the weather plays an important part of your enjoyment of it. In this region, you can’t predict the weather, so you have to take what comes. Tip: don’t book any onward travel too close to the expected arrival of the ship – if the weather’s bad, it can arrive many, many hours later than anticipated.

review_text: I took a day tour from Santiago to Vina del Mar and Valparaiso with Turistik. I enjoyed the tour and would recommend it. Previous comments suggest that the tour company was not organized; on the contrary, my experience with Turistik was efficient and pleasant. Firstly, i could not pay with VISA online because of a technical glitch. I called the Turistik office and was able to book via the phone with payment to be made at the tour bus. I was picked up at the hotel on time and the transfer to the tour bus was efficient and straight forward. The tour guide, Felipe, was engaging and interesting. He flitted between Spanish, Portuguese and English with little effort. He was easy to understand, and standard tourist and tour jokes notwithstanding, was informative and pertinent. I have read some Tripadvisor reviews which mentioned that not information or facts were provided, but in this case Felipe provided the right mix of history, facts and anecdotal content (more factual info and we would then complain that it was exhaustive with facts). the tour minibus (of say 25 people) was clean and comfortable. The other nice thing about this tour was the pickup and drop off at the hotel plus they did not try and sell you a bunch of souvenirs and knick-knacks. The tour provided a good overview of the 2 cities so that one could then venture out on one's own and make a more detailed and personal exploration. Our tour was made up of around 15 persons, which i think is better than a whole busload. All in all - a good tour package, an efficient driver, an interesting tourguide and 2 picturesque but contrasting cities. i recommend this tour. Dear Customer, We are pleased to read you had an enjoyable time with us. As mentioned, Viña del Mar and Valparaíso are two completely different cities, even though they are one next to the other. So it is a must for those who are traveling to Santiago and want to know a little more about the history of Chile in two beautiful cities located just 1 hour and 30 minutes from the capital. We hope to see you again in the future and we thank you again for your positive comments.

I didn't make a booking, but think that might be necessary in high tourist season.

review_text: There are boat trips available that take you closer to the glacier. If you absolutely want to make this boat trip you should book in advance. We just walked on the moraine and on the island that split the lake in half. We saw the Glacier in the distance and wondered why the boat trips were taking about three hours. When the boat arrived we saw why: boarding takes a lot of time, as they are shipping passengers to the bigger vessel in a small boat and the strong wind made the bigger vessel move quite slowly. If you are planning to see the Glacier Perito Moreno, skip the boat trip to Glacier Grey. Access to Perito Moreno is much easier and Grey is just as beautiful from afar, especially with all those bizarrely shaped icebergs bobbing in the lake.

review_text: We were in Australia with flights booked to Chile, how were we to get around? What was transport like? Hotels? Wine tasting and getting from one vineyard to the next (the reader may have guessed we’re into wine!)....... over to Google! Sent a simple email to Chile Private Tours and within hours Thomas replied. We told him when we were landing and when we were taking off and he put together a fantastic mix of wine and scenery and culture that although initially I thought a bit expensive - now it’s all over - I realise was great value for money. I won’t detail everywhere we went but all the places we went to were excellent. Our driver / host / wine expert / music lover Jorge, was fantastic, so helpful and professional giving a real insight into the country and culture. Again we did so much and all between boutique hotels and wineries that Thomas had planned. The penultimate day we were given a walking tour of Valparaiso by Thomas and then we met our chef for a cooking lesson - Pablo - bus to the market, buying tips for fresh fish and meat, veg - Chilean style - bus back to the cooking school all the Pisco sour, wine, ALL included. Brilliant afternoon and late into the evening. Last day to a final winery then Departures at Santiago aeropuerto! My advice - if you want to get a great taste of Chile, as the sportswear company says - just do it! You will really enjoy your experience. Feel free to ask any questions.

review_text: After reading quite a few reviews we decided to do our two night/three day tour with World White Tour and everything exceeded our expectations. AGENCY: The two ladies working at the office in San Pedro were super professional, kind and polite which made us feel very reassured from the beginning. Everything they promised did happen during the tour and even one of them was at the Bolivian border during our breakfast just before we jumped on the jeep. We thought the whole thing was very well organised and again helped us feel we were in the hands of people who cared. GUIDE: Casimiro was a very experienced and responsible driver, as well as a very knowledgeable guide. He literally tailored the trip for us so we could see things that weren't in the initial itinerary and worked around other groups doing the same trip which meant most of the time we were on our own and not with many other people at each stop. This is a big plus, especially when you want to see flamingos, which are very shy. Casimiro was super patient with us during the stops and didn't rush us once. He played great Bolivian music and let us play our own too. He also helped us take brilliant pictures and videos at the salt flat. I strongly recommend him as a guide. JEEP: It was a great jeep in good condition. We were a group of six (amazing people by the way, if you're lucky you will make friends through this experience!) and it felt comfortable and safe at all times. We constantly rotated seats so everyone got to be by the window and got good views during the drive. FOOD: Way better than expected. Generous portions and vegetarian options. Casimiro also gave our group a bottle of red wine on the 2nd night which was much appreciated. ACCOMMODATION: Basic but again better than expected and exactly as they advised when we booked the tour. We got our sleeping bags (which were good quality) included in the tour price. TOUR: The actual tour is just amazing. Impossibly beautiful landscapes that I never imagined could exist. It really is remote and untouched in some parts, which makes you feel deeply connected with nature and its wonders. I totally recommend this tour.

review_text: We loved our winery tour with Tom from Bodega Wine Tours. We've attended lots of wine tours in Australia and overseas, and this would have to be one of the best and most enjoyable. The tour is a bit different to what we are used to - normally rushing to 5 or 6 wineries in a day - but the Chileans like to do things a bit differently, and in this case I think it works! Firstly, Tom was very easy to deal with over email to make the booking and he even agreed to change his schedule so that we could visit Casablanca on a day normally reserved for Maipo. Tom reconfirmed the tour the day before and picked us up around 9:30am in a nice mini van with separate driver. The drive to the Casablanca valley took an hour or so while we chatted and before we knew it we were at the first winery - Veramonte - which as others have mentioned is a certified organic medium scale winery. Tom showed us the vines before we entered for our tasting. We sat down at a table and had our own dedicated host to describe the winery and each wine to us in detail. We tried 5 wines and each was a generous pour. All were very good quality - one of the nicest sauvignon blancs we have ever tried! Next we went to a microwinery called La Recova where you start the tour in the owner, David's, living room. This one is also organic, but not certified. Here we had a full tour of the winery wonderfully hosted and explained everything by David. We even got to try some of the not-quite-ready-yet wine from his tanks. After the tour David led us to a magnificent alfresco area where there were a range of delicious treats (cheeses, olives, oils etc) and three of his wines for tasting. An extremely generous pour of each was provided, with more offered if you wanted it. All three were delicious. Then David introduced us to a traditional Chilean sport (of which I cant remember the name!) but we all had a go and it was really fun and a unique touch which put this tour above any other. Then we went back to the house where we got to label a bottle of his wine ourselves (also a cool experience), which he then gifted to us. So lovely! The final winery was Vina Mar, a larger one with a lovely restaurant. The lunch is an additional cost, but even though its an upmarket restaurant the prices were extremely reasonable and the servings were a good size. We each just had a main and it was certainly sufficient. Tom also led us through a blind tasting to see what we had learnt - I think we all did pretty well! I booked this tour because of the good reviews and the price (it was one of the cheapest I could find) - and I'm really glad I did! even though US$105 per person might still seem a bit expensive to visit three wineries and pay for your own lunch, after having experienced the tour I now think its extremely good value. In this case quality definitely trumps quantity! If you like wine you must do this - it was a highlight of our month in South America!

review_text: Valparaiso is the oldest seaport in South America. You might be yawning now, but wait til you see this little city on the water! It is built straight up from the water on steep hills, and many places are or were only accessible by elevators. Some homes have actually been abandoned because their is no access as the elevators become a thing of the past. It is hard to describe, because it is so unusual. The houses are all different colors it is said, so that the sailors and fishermen returning home could see their house quickly from a distance, by its color. You need to see this quaint seaport!

On our way to El Tatio we passed a lagoon, around 8 AM, where flamingoes were feeding, and not a human soul around, since the latter had passed this spot when it was still pitch-dark. We arrived at the Geysirs by 9 AM when most people had left or were leaving, so we enjoyed some quality time with nature...It maybe true, that photographs are more stunning when the geyser' jets of water hit the very cold mountain air just at daybreak, but we don't travel for Instagram.

review_text: I very rarely (read never) can be bothered to write reviews on Tripadvisor, so this just goes to show how great Spicy Chile walking tours are!!!! I was somewhat sceptical when my friend insisted that we all did it, but I was definitely proved wrong. The format is as follows - Pick a route, meet a guide there at the listed time, walking tour round Santiago, tip what you think it´s worth at the end. Very simple, very effective. Our guide was called Rocio (Spelling, I don´t know, but she said we could call her Rose) was an incredibly friendly, knowledgeable bundle of fun, who instatly puts you at ease. Did I mention she´s the best guide? She speaks excellent English, and is a veritable fount of knowledge, on a variety of subjects ranging from culture, architecture, history, food, nightlife, wildlife, and everything in between. The tour we did was called Good Morning Santiago, taking in a real range of sights, sounds and smells, and includes a little cafe stop that serves excellent Empanadas. All of this is interspersed with humourous (Where appropriate) commentary, personal anecdotes and recommendations, and is crucially conducted at the general pace of the group, so you can stop and take pictures wherever you wish, ask for stops, or decline others, which is really nice! In fact, we liked this tour so much, that five of us came back and did Patrimonial tour today, which is pretty much the best proof of Spicy Chile being awesome I can offer! We visited all kinds of off the beaten track sights, which I would not have had a hope in hell of finding, even using a guide book and a map. It´s very interesting, as Rosio (again, same guide) really brought the history to life, and I can honestly say I was pretty much enthralled through out. Quirky, friendly, a great way to soak up the ambience of Santiago, and opens your eyes to all sorts of cool stuff to do for the rest of your stay! JUST MAKE SURE YOU LIKE WALKING! Both tours I did lasted for about 3 or 4 hours. It´s a fairly relaxed pace, but if you don´t do walking, it´s probably not for you. Although I don´t know why you would be looking at a walking tour if you don´t like walking. But I thought I´d better mention it anyway... What an awesome critic!!!! Thanks Harris!!! You made Rose super happy after your post!!! Hehehe!! Hope to see you back soon!!

review_text: We did two activities with Stamp's on two separate days. The first was a day trip from Santiago to Valparaiso. Everything about the trip was great; the tour bus was comfortable, and our driver, Jimmy, did a great job. Our guide, Frank, was awesome as well. He was very knowledgeable on everything about Chile; he spent much of his life in the US, so his English is excellent and communication was not an issue. He was also very friendly and made sure to pay attention to all the guests on the tour. The only critique I have of the tour was that the restaurant that we dined at in Valparaiso was not as good as I hoped; the food was not very good, although the ambiance was fantastic and it was overall still a good meal experience. The second tour we did was the Cajon Del Maipo tour. This was also excellent, and we had Frank as our guide once again. Our driver, Patricio, was very friendly and did an excellent job navigating the dangerous canyon roads. The reservoir was beautiful, and the guides set up a light picnic that included wine, which was a great touch. Overall, I would highly recommend a tour from Stamp's-- they did a great job!

review_text: Each time I looked up, which I tried to do as often as my footing would allow, I said "WOW!". The W is straight out of a movie with it's breathtaking landscape. We trekked east to west, doing to towers hike first. We were so tired by day 4 that we were thankful to have completed the most difficult hiking day first. TBH, if you have a reasonable baseline level of fitness (I am 52 and no longer a gym rat, but I am active) it's just not that strenuous. Super enjoyable with some huffing and puffing thrown in from time to time. :) Chile Nativo set us up with Nana as our guide, and she totally made the trip even more awesome for us. She was AMAZING! Our kids loved her, we loved her, she was super knowledgeable about the flora and fauna, she can spot a condor from 10 miles away, and she was a BEAST on the trail. She rocks! :) A few suggestions: I would say that hiking poles are a MUST for anyone over 50. We bought them in Puerto Natales (~$20 each) at our guide's suggestion and I am SO thankful that I had them. Some parts of the trail are pretty steep and my knees would never have forgiven me if I didn't have the poles to assist. You can drink the water straight out of the rivers and lakes, so skip the heavy filter bottles. We all had medium size Nalgenes, and they were perfect. Unless you are an epic sweat-er, plan to wear the same thing every day (except underwear), to keep your pack light. Lots of thin layers up top is key. The wind can take you from sweating to shivering to sweating on the same hike. We were there end of Dec and were very fortunate with no rain and good weather. I wore (all synthetic!) a short sleeve T, a thin long sleeve T, a thin running jacket, and a waterproof windbreaker. The top 2 layers went on and off as needed and I was super happy the whole time, even when the wind was howling at 40MPH. Hats MUST have a strap. A wool beanie or a buff is a better idea. Sunglasses at all times! SUNSCREEN people! And don't forget your hands. The backs of my hands are the only place that got sunburned, and it's not fun. Crocs for after hike were awesome cuz you can fit socks under them for warmth but it feels like you're barefoot. And they dry quickly after you wear them in the shower, which you will want to at the refugios. The refugios are cool! Not going to be your best night sleep ever, and keep in mind that they are on a very local septic system, but still a fun experience. The food is what the food is. Not a deal breaker. The smaller size quick drying towels from REI were perfection. Dry by morning, and they double as a "bedroom" curtain on your bunk in the refugio. Staying in the same room with other adults was not my new fav (but I would do it again for this hike!!) and the towel trick helped me sleep. Bring tip money. Each refugio has a tip jar, and they do work hard to make it a good experience for the guests. Plus, you'll want to tip your transport people, and of course, your awesome guide. BOOK IT!!! :)) Review of: W Trek Torres del Paine

review_text: We visited as part of a private tour to do stargazing and check out the countryside. The Elqui Valley does not disappoint - you have beautiful and progressively more rugged countryside as you drive in, lots of vineyards and lots of pisco distilleries (along with a very nice small winery in Cavas) and charming little mountain towns. At night, the stars are to-die-for - so clear and so dark, you can see things here that aren't visible much of anywhere else. The guided tour approach is a good one if you aren't fluent in Spanish, because in the valley few people speak any English. Be sure to check out the crafts in the village of Horcon (go no earlier than lunchtime), the Los Nichos pisco distillery, and the Restaurant Solar (all the cooking is via solar ovens!). If you can, stay in a dome at Elqui Domos (it calls itself a hotel, but it's really a collection of cabins) and pay for the personal astronomy tour they offer - way better than what you'll get at one of the public observatories, and the sky is darker there.

review_text: I hate to give my first low review from my trip but I have to. Portillo is catered for skiers. Don't bother going here, especially if you're a snowboarder. As far as what was good, they do an excellent job of grooming the trails with the minimal snow that they got. I cannot complain about the amount of snow because that's out of the resort's control. I will complain in regards to the fact that I read Portillo snow was going to be similar to that found in Colorado-I've been to CO and its no where near as good. It's more like East Coast conditions with frozen granular in the morning and slush by 12pm if the sun is out. Also, the food at Uncle Bob's was delicious although ridiculously expensive even for resort standards- $39 for 2 burgers, fries and 2 waters. As for the "resort" the trails are no better than a small mountain in upstate NY. Yes, the views are far more beautiful but this is not the place for an advanced/expert skier/rider. I suppose I could have worked on riding switch because I was bored within 2 hours of riding here. Not to mention the amount of skating and walking a rider has to do because of the pitch between trails. AND the steepness getting off the chairlift causing a snowboarder to really practice skating fast downwards. And I can't even begin to describe how the t-bars are the only access to the steep stuff. Visit here for the day to check out the oldest resort in South America. ONLY stay here for the week if you've for kids who are not very experienced-it's perfect for that. Just like a cruise ship with everything laid out for the week. It's best for families and should be avoided for serious skiers/riders. Choose Valle Nevado or La Parva instead.

review_text: Vina Casas del Bosque is in the center of the Casablanca Valley, just about an hour west of Santiago. It is a modern, young winery that focuses on the production of mostly white wines, with Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and Chardonnay being the main targets. The winery grows Syrah and Pinot Noir too, and it makes Carmenere and Cabernet Sauvignon-based wines grown in Maipo and Rapel, two other wine-producing areas of Chile.While the facility is modern and efficient, the production methods are somewhat unconventional. The resulting white wines are mostly young, fresh and pleasant, but not intended to age. They should be consumed within the first year or two. The basic wines are labeled "Reserva" as opposed to most other wineries around the world where this label means something special. Gran Reserve is the next level up and then there are a few wines produced in small quantities and greater care. These latter ones deserve attention and with time will likely grow into mature and enjoyable wines.

review_text: We self drove to the lakes from San Pedro, an easy drive. The entry fee is CLP10,000 per person. The salt lakes are home to local bird wild life. There are 3 lakes here and one is available for swimming - so sunblock to keep chemicals out of the water. Good modern bathroom facilities, outdoor showers to wash salt water off and change rooms are provided. All clean and well maintained. We couldn't resist the water. Although not as salty as the Dead Sea, the water has a similar effect of making it very easy to float. However, different to the Dead Sea, the water is thermal. Walking into the lake the floor is quite warm, then in shelves off into quite deep water which is cool on the surface and from the lower levels warm water rises in pockets. It was a lovely relaxing experience soaking in the lake with amazing views of the chain of volcanoes in front of us. A perfect desert setting. By the time we got out it was lunch time, so we took advantage of the shady areas provided. You have to bring your own food and drink with you. Recommend a visit.

review_text: To "fully appreciate" the beauty of this city is to come up this tower with two levels of observatory on levels 61 & 62 with the upper one being "open sky" (although not a "wide-open" one where you can kind of feel the openness above unlike some of the observation floors I've been to like those of Marina Bay Sands in Singapore, Umeda Sky Building in Osaka & Palacio Municipal in Montevideo). In any case, I was actually somewhat amazed by "how green" this big metropolitan city down below was with its urban part of so-so-many buildings of 20-or-so-stories "nicely balanced" by its nature part of plenty of trees & tree-lined streets among those buildings (really a "greener view" than that of many other cities of the world I've seen from above); and at a "fair proximity" to the Andes Mountains (the east side of the city pretty much stretching to the foot of that mountain range), it was great to see a few "snow caps" on top of them although yes not as awesome as the big snow slopes I saw in some postcards of this tower (but which I guess was just a natural view in January which is summer in South America). And apart from enjoying the views, it was also great to learn from the info displays (on Level 61 the 1st level of the observatory) about the city's "premier sites" such as Plaza de Armas, La Moneda Palace & Cerro San Cristobal (actually a very good view of that hill from here and close enough to get a "tiny glimpse" of the big Virgin statue on the top if you look carefully). The only feature lacking on these two floors I would say as compared to the observation floors of other similar towers of the world is the "distances to other well-known cities" (which I'm kind of used to seeing them looking up above an observation floor). If coming by metro, Tobalaba Station (either Line 1 or Line 4) is where to get off at pretty much right beside this tower (with actually a big shopping mall directly below that you enter from like the overpass just a short walk from the street after coming out of the station), and yes it was "absolutely worthwhile" for me the admission of about 15,000 chilean pesos (which is a little less than 25 US$) not just for the phenomenal views of the city & beyond (as mentioned above) but also given the fact that this is the "tallest building" of the entire South American continent!

review_text: The Atacama Desert plays host to some of the most stunning landscapes anywhere in the world. If you are into scenery on an epic scale you won’t be disappointed. I based myself in San Pedro which was ideal for getting to all of the major attractions, and with planning you can easily do two sites in a day. San Pedro is also a lovely little town ideally set up for tourists with good facilities, places to eat and loads of great little shops. I stayed at the Hostal Katari which at 195,000 pesos (about $220) for 5 nights was very good value (lovely room, clean and friendly staff). I chose to self-drive which was fine, Chilean drivers being respectful and accommodating. This gave me the chance to get out early to the sites and avoid the crowds. It also gave me a chance to drive some of the most spectacular roads in the world. The route east to the Argentine border is utterly otherworldly and south through the Atacama salt flats and up into the mountains was magical (go see the Salar de Agunas Calientes and Laguna Miscanti whilst you’re there) Most sites are ticket only admission but with a bit of patience you can arrange this yourself online. The major sites are also staffed (who were very helpful and patient as I don’t speak Spanish), and have toilets. Prices are reasonable around the $10-$15 mark and very good value. The El Tatio geyser fields are well worth a visit as long as you can tolerate the atrocious roads! And the ruins at Pukara de Quitor about 5km out of town should not be missed. I’d also recommend a swim in the Laguna Cejar which is also home to flamingoes and Valle de la Luna is a must see. San Pedro also offers a huge array of organised tours on minibuses. These range from a couple of hours to full days out. If you don’t want to drive or want the benefit of the knowledgeable guide these are well worth it. I did the Valle de la Luna tour with Whipala which was excellent. A truly incredible place!

review_text: My partner and I travelled with navimag during Mid May which is the low season so the ship was downgraded to a smaller sized one. From reading the reviews below we were aware of what was on offer. We thought the food was very good and there was a lot of it- you will never go hungry. Although it does cycle around the same theme of potato and some type of meat. The living quarters were very comfortable with not too many people and a tv that is constantly playing movies. There is a section of the trip that you sail on the open seas which can be rough and a few people were very ill during this time, however they do offer seasick pills. Fortunately I didn't get sick and had a great day on deck outside. Our arrival date was also delayed because of bad weather, this is a positive because the captain chose not to sail on the open sea when the waves were very large for the safety of his passengers and cargo. There was amazing scenery and wildlife to be seen along the trip including smoking volcanos, mountains, whales, sea lions and dolphins. It really was a great experience that everybody on board agreed was special. As for the animal cruelty... Chile is no different to the rest of the world. This is really an insight into how cows and animals that end up on our plate are treated worldwide. It is not specifically a Chilean thing, I think it is important to unveil how animals are actually treated around the world.

review_text: It took me a couple runs to do this right. It´s 2 to 2.5 hours round trip, so don´t leave at 5pm and chance it. Lessons learned: when in doubt, stick to the widest trail possible. Don´t go off on the single track if you plan to do the loop, and only the loop. At one point, when the trail narrows, you will be guided by arrows made of stones, or sticking out of the ground. Follow the arrows, and don´t expect it to be 100 percent clear. Also, I HIGHLY recommend RYM Expeditions (or RYM Adventures). It is a bike shop at about 160 or 170 Caracoles. I ride a lot at home, and was insistent on finding a shop where the bikes are maintained, and include the fixings - lights, helmets, repair kits, spare tubes, etc.) they include all the fixings, and the bikes are well-maintained, for the same prices as the other places. 3k per 6 hours. I have no skin in the game, as you can see from my reviews. But once I found this place, I ended up renting from them every day for a week. They also have photos on their computer, which will point out all the turns you need to make for whatever ride you want to do (not just the quebrada del diablo). No cost to enter the trail.

The apartments are small, but clean and nice. We stayed at the 1st floor it was not too loud, but if you're at the 5th floor it will get noisy! Skiing was very good (we are beginners), and the views are breathtaking. I'm giving it 3 starts based on what you get for the price you pay (for everything from meals to accomodation). If you don't mind the waits for everything from eating to buying tickets then go for it. I would streamline so many simple processes that would be so simple to do. For example check-in and check-out. For check-in I spent 25 minutes and there was only 1 person in front of me checking in!!! Just have all the packages ready and give all the relevant information before people arrive by email, or in paper.

review_text: Bolivia Desert Crossing to (Salar do Uyuni)/ Travessia Deserto da Bolivia ao Salar do Uyuni I made the crossing to Salar do Uyuni across the Chilean border. My friend and I made the trip alone. It was 4 intense and magical days. We find an exuberant beauty with many surprises and adventures along the way that we will never forget. However, I would stress that our trip could never have been so special had it not been for our guide GILMAR, our guide, cook, photographer and driver, who was waiting for us on the Bolivian border. Gilmar is a sensational and unique person. He introduced us to everything and made the trip even more charming, fun, solicitous, charismatic, always with a smile on his face. For sure, a true friend we made in Bolivia. We realized that we were very lucky to take a trip with him, during the trip we came across other people who were traveling with us and who complained a lot about their guide / driver. And talking to our fellow travelers, we realized that despite being from the same company, their guide did not even half of what our guide did and was always scowling. It seems like a simple detail, but a good guide makes all the difference, after all we spent 4 days traveling with him . I recommend requesting Gilmar's services if you make this trip. The company we chose is one of the best, it went well. But their highlight for sure is Gilmar. Fiz a travessia com destino ao Salar do Uyuni pela fronteira do Chile. review_text: This is a good way to get s great view and see how large Santiago is. I was going to take the vernacular rail but line was too long so decided to walk. The path in the lower section is well paved becoming dirt track further up. The are water fountains and taps along the path should you forget your water bottle. There are lots of facilities at the top including the Virgin Mary statue. I was going to walk back down but spotted a bus down from the cable car entrance which costs £1.40 for a ride down to the bottom stopping at a few points along the way. This meant I got to see some different views from the foot path and some more pics so would recommend doing s different route down.

Access is down a long series of steps. There are changing facilities but you keep your possessions with you depositing them in open lockers by the side of each pool. It cost just 5,000 per person, but it is time limited to three hours. We found this more than enough time if all you want to do is sample the experience of a thermal spring.

review_text: We had been up since 6 am to prepare for our bus journey from El Calafate across the Patagonian Steppes with all the awkward time-wasting of having to pass the borders of 2 countries that probably hate each other more than most on earth. The journey was dull, the weather miserable, but as we approached the National Park, the rain diminished and patches of blue started to appear. Our 1st stop to catch a distant view of the Paine Massif (Cordillera) was at a view point close to this rather large lake. As we wrapped ourselves, collected the camera, and descended from the bus, that segment of the sky immediately above our heads turned blue, the sun burst through, and the drizzle miraculously ceased. It was an unforgettable moment. The lake was much more densely blue than the sky. I was told that this was because unlike most of the other lakes that feed into the Paine or Serrano Rivers, after which they are carried through the Seno Ultima Speranza fjord to the Pacific Ocean, Sarmiento is a closed lake. Another possible explanation is that it is especially rich in the rock flour and microbial life occurring in most lakes within the park. Finally, it is notable for the thick rim of carbonate that provides its uppermost level and lips with a white chalky surface, arising partly from thermal activity and partly from natural evaporation. Although we did not attempt them, I have seen splendid videos showing the trails that run round the lake at a higher altitude, offering remarkable views as well as intensely windy conditions.

review_text: We did the "O" trek in 7,5 days in December 2016. We organised everything ourselves beforehand, reservations of refugios/camping sites through Vertice Patagonia and Fantasticosur (these two companies own the campings/lodges around the trek). We did everything from Norway online, even ordering the bus from Puerto Natales to the park entrance. We did not carry tent/sleeping bags/food, we hired tent and sleeping bags they nights we did not sleep in the refuigios, and we had full board all nights, except at Los Perros which do not have such facilities. We bought a nice waterproof map before we left, but we did not use this. The best map was the one we got at the park entrance. The trail is very well marked, you dont even need the map. The nature is fantastic, ice bergs, glaciers, blue lakes and spectacular mountains. But be prepared for rain, we had one one day without rain. Remember waterproof gloves! And remember that you have to walk counterclockwise on the "O" trek. Despite what people are writing on the internet, no special permit is required (previously only 80 persons people allowed on the "O" at a time, this is not longer applicable). The one you get at the park entrance is enough. You should prepare to carry a backpack of approx 10 kilos, without food and tent.

review_text: My last vacations were in Puerto Montt with my family. We decided to visit Angelmo for our lunch in the first day of stay. Angelmó is a big market located near downtown Puerto Montt, just in front of Tenglo Island, here you can find lots of restaurants with typical food from the south and handcraft. I can define Angelmó as a delicious experience, you can try the typical, cheap and delicious "churrascas" (a kind of bread/sopaipilla but bigger) for only $150 CLP, also there is a big variety of ceviches, curanto, milcao, pichanga sureña, etc.and all of this for a very affordable price, being a perfect place for have lunch in Puerto Montt. Also, between Angelmó and Tenglo Island there are lots of sea lions, making this a southern experience even more beautiful and special for the tourists.

review_text: This trek is a must for hike lovers, one of the most beautiful sceneries in the world. The W consists of different trails of astonishing beauty that takes you up and down mountains, through valleys, across rivers, side by side clear blue lakes, while rounding Los Cuernos mountains, Torres del Paine or Paine Grande in the Chilean Patagonia. I was worried about the weather, especially because we travelled at the beginning of the fall and we come from a tropical country. Out of five days hiking, we had four wonderful sunny days and one rainy day (so we could experiment the full Patagonian weather) with temperatures between minus 5 (at night) and up to 15 degrees in the day; however, for what we learned, weather is very unpredictable and you should come prepared with layers and waterproof jackets. During the five days we hiked around 80 kms. If you don’t have time to do the full W, I would recommend the trek to Mirador Las Torres (21 kms from our base camp) and Valle Francés (25 kms from Refugio Los Cuernos to Refugio Paine Grande). We booked our excursion with Ecocamp Patagonia and were not disappointed. They took care of everything as we spent two nights at refugios and five in Ecocamp location. It was great to be able to disconnect from daily stress and spend seven days surrounded by this wonderful natural landscape.

review_text: After discovering about the block to allow non tour cars into the valley of the moon after 1pm we decided to drive to Tatio geyser at dawn instead. As the tour operators apparently start early from hotels we held back until 6am. By this time it’s light and easier driving. The drive out to the geysers is filled with great views and wildlife so take your time and enjoy them. There are tall cactus, flamingos in a small road side lake, lots of geese and other birds too, Vicunas, amazing colours on the mountains and volcanoes as the light comes up. We stopped many times on the way, allowing tour buses to pass by. The road is sometimes treacherous as the stones are like marbles underneath. The potholes can be pretty big too. Watch for springing vicunas especially after dawn. We did see a donkey who had been knocked down which is so sad. Speed is a problem with some tour operators and has unfortunate consequences. The geysers are amazing. We took a plunge in the hot spring. Felt invigorated afterwards. It is at a high altitude so good to help with getting used to the thin air if you are heading to the salt flats of bolivia after SP.

review_text: This 100 year old house,palace, museum built by Italian architects and next owned by a Very successful Croatian businessman has an interesting history to its development and where it finds itself today in the historical life of Valpo. ( I am advised that if one has been to Valparaiso twice you may refer to the City as Valpo). I passed by here several times over the past few Canadian winters but today I entered for the first time and was quite surprised by what I saw and learnt about something I took for 'just another building'. To my surprise on entering I noted something I expect to see back home, a special discount for Seniors, which meant entry for $1.00 Cdn / 500 pesos. The Museum is loaded with painting assigned to various levels of the house, one or two get a few sculptures. In some respects there are so many it almost becomes overwhelming to your senses. However that is lessened when you devote some time to the absolutely fantastic detail of the workmanship evident in the details of the wood .. Absolutely Beautiful. Just when that abates you step into the Master Bathroom. Considering the period of construction I thought perhaps I has passed through a time warp. The shower is something else - -- I Want one of those. You can get quite a bit of detailed info on Wikipedia by doing a Baburizza Palace Search. When you have finished you can stop by the resturant for a drink, lunch. A definite Recommend when in Valpo.

Well worth a family visit.

review_text: Highly recommend: both Valparaiso (the city) and “Ruta Valparaiso” (Cristian Blanco and the Ruta V. private tour company). I was a fairly demanding and detail-oriented organizer of a small group of people disembarking from a cruise ship. I corresponded for a few months with Cristian via e-mail over the course of a few months, to develop and settle on a concept for our small group’s tour that would be best tailored to our specific circumstances. Cristian was prompt in communication, patient, and fully responsive to areas of inquiry. Although (due to the itinerary of our cruise) Valparaiso was our final destination, the specifics and terms of the tour we had developed with Cristian and R.V. were well and completely worked-out, so that on the morning of debarkation, there were no worries and there was complete clarity. The result, was a seamless transition “from the custody” of the ship, into the care of the Ruta Valparaiso van/driver/tour guide at the exit Valparaiso Marine Terminal. (You might hear "the terminal" and think "scary, busy" place, but it is actually pretty easy to move around in, and it has some seats, some decent souvenir shopping, and a fairly orderly luggage collection method, so don't foresee it as an overly arduous experience.) At the terminal, the R.V. tour guide and vehicle had professionally-drawn placards that clearly identified them as for our specific small tour group. The signs were easily recognized by all members of our group. Getting our baggage stowed onto the van was straightforward and quick. At that point, our R.V. tour guide, Danae took over; she did a fine job taking us on our desired combination tour of Vina del Mar and Valparaiso, followed by a transfer to the Santiago Airport (or in the case of two from our group, a drop off in Santiago at their hotel). Danae took us to see highlights in both Vina del Mar and Santiago, and her extensive knowledge and clear love for her cities showed through. We enjoyed seeing Vina del Mar; however, I’d be remiss if I didn’t comment that we were simply “blown away” by Valparaiso. The word is overused, but the place is unique. It’s a mind-blowing, visually arresting place – be prepared to get and keep your cell-phone camera working. Very much appreciated Danae’s backup in that regard, as her pictures captured what we didn’t manage to, and more. In our group, we had some folks with slightly limited mobility as well as a couple with a toddler in a stroller: given the almost never ending sets of stairways and hills in Valparaiso, you'd think it would have produced some grumbling, but the place was so interesting and different (as in - when you round a corner, you really don't know what is going to be on the other side), that it really kept issues of the walking-challenged to a minimum. (That, and, the van did a good job of dropping off and picking up - visualize if you will a game of chutes and ladders on a set of hillsides. If after looking at some of the city pictures, you can't visualize what I am saying, don't worry; you will after being there!) Some final advice on tour design: due to our circumstances, we only had about 5 hours total before having to leave for the airport. If I had to do it again, I’d probably trade off an hour less of Vina (fine, but less interesting) for an hour more of Valparaiso. Or, bite the bullet and spend all of the little time we had in Valparaiso. Or best, find a way to spend an overnight there: Ruta Valparaiso clearly knows how to expand an itinerary with worthwhile events, to make best use of more time as it becomes available. Well done, RV! Thank you very much for your detailed comments regarding your experience with us! Your comments are very interesting and I believe very useful to those who don´t know what to expect upon their arrival. We´re very pleased that you were blown away with our city and you´re welcome to be blown away again any time you wish to return. The doors are open for you! Danae sends her best to you and thanks you for mentioning her. Our very best from the Ruta Valparaíso Team!

review_text: I was afraid I couldn't stand the W trekking in Torres del Paine, but with the FlaviaBia program, it was perfect! Pre-physical preparation is necessary, but we had all the guidance from the team on how to assemble the backpack and all the appropriate clothing. On the eve of the trail they went to the hotel to give final directions and check if there was nothing missing. We stayed 3 days in the shelters (1 in Paine Grande and 2 in Grey) in a room with 6 bedbeds, edredon and pillow very good. Shower with hot water and good food. FlaviaBia also provides excellent food (super-filled burritos, nuts, drink, electrolytes and fruit) on the first and last day. Then you can do the French Valley (day 1 - 21km), go to Refugio Grey (2 - 11 km), splendid ice hikking + pensil bridge (day 3 - 12km), sailing to the excellent Hotel Grey (day 4) and finally the trail to the base of the Torres del Paine (day 5 - 21km). All this with the company of a very special guide, Tomas, who gave all the tips on how to go up and down the rocks in a technical way, with rhythm, using the sticks and without wasting energy!! It was 5 intense days, but to contemplate the landscapes of Chilean Patagonia, it is a unique experience and no one leaves there as they entered.

review_text: My daughter and I hiked the W from Torres Del Paine to Grey Lago. I am in my 50's and a long distance runner in good shape. I am not inexperienced backpacker. I found the uneven rocky surface challenging because I am so wary of turning my ankle and losing running training. Hiking boots above the ankle were a must for me. I wore them a lot to prepare for the trek but I did not find a place that mirrored the uneven surface. I ended up with a bruised knot above my right ankle from the boot digging into my skin from foot leaning inward over V shaped trail and uneven rocks. That was pretty painful on day 3 but it improved with duct tape wrap for day 4. I am petite and that also presented a challenge when climbing rocks on parts of the trail. I cannot see an unfit person enjoying anything but a day hike (but youth may be able to make up for some of it). We were blessed by perfect weather during our stay. Perfect weather does include a small burst of sleet the first day, a bit of sprinkling here and there and very heavy and challenging wind gusts or parts of the trail. It just made the rewards that much sweeter. We stayed in shelters during our trek. Shelter Torre Norte was a bit like teen camp. The expected bunk beds and hall bath facilities were basic and fine. We had 6 girls to a room. There was hot water in the showers and no line any time we saw. The dinner in this shelter was not even edible although many were managing. Mystery meat and cold vegetables that tasted nothing like anything I'd ever had made us dive for the granola bars back in the room. Of all the bad food we had on the trek this was the worst. Our lunch provided by Shelter TN was typical of all of them but still the worst. Staff was nice enough but not outstanding. The next shelter we visited was Domo Frances. This was our favorite. The gal that seems to be in charge (yikes--I forgot her name!) was very helpful and enthusiastic. The shelter is the smallest that we visited and we enjoyed meeting the fellow trekkers and the food was the best we had on trek. The domes were newer and the only clean place we experienced after campers came thorough. Paine Grande was big, loud (constant door slamming), dirty and old. We were scheduled to camp at this stop and were dreading it because it was so windy and cold. The unexpected vacancy in the shelter made us happy with even the gross accommodations. The front desk girls were nice and helpful there. Vertice Gray was the last shelter for us. It was great when we arrived but the bathrooms were disgusting by 2 hours later. I believe they must be crashed by campers that are supposed to use the building next door. Seriously gross bathrooms--sanitary products (used) left in showers, tp that missed the trash can all over the floor, slushy floors from shower water, mud and tracked in dirt all over the entire floor of bath. This is too bad because the staff housekeeping was left to clean it and they do a good job. (We were witnesses to how clean it was upon arrival.) The staff was nice at this shelter and the rooms were nice. Two sets of bunks to a room. There are a few things that would have made our trek easier and more enjoyable. These are tips for anyone ready to trek the W-- Make sure to have cash in pesos. You must pay the park entrance fee in cash. We did not know this and through a series of traveling challenges ended up at the entrance short of about $1 (for two of us). They would not let us in. Finally, a kind volunteer gave us a dollar of her own money. They will accept dollars or pesos but no credit cards. You also will be asked to tip throughout the trek and may want cash for snacks or drinks at shelters. Next, we were not prepared for co-ed living. A warning would have been nice. I realize that this is not a surprise to many hostel frequenters but we did not expect co-ed rooms. It can be awkward. It is hard to find bottled water at the shelters. If you have a water bottle or bladder to fill you will be fine but expect to haul it around with you. You can refill in bathrooms and we're told the water is fine straight from the streams. (We still filtered.) There was some internet at Torre Norte and we could buy time at Domo Frances in the dining area. However, there was not internet at other shelters. It would have been great to have it at Gray because we had lots of down time and had finished our reading. I noticed many others with the same predicament at end of trek. If you suffer from any hay fever/allergies, travel will plenty of meds. Especially at Paine Grande our allergies really flared up. Medication was a great relief. The catamaran (Grey III) trip back to leave park and see glacier along the way was a nice surprise. The boat staff was excellent and the sights were amazing. I highly recommend this. A couple of ways fixes in the shelters would make them much more comfortable for hikers. More (or any) hooks in the shower areas would be great and helpful. Paper towel dispensers that actually work would be a plus. In every shelter but the Domo Frances, the dispensers were full but not working so nobody could dry hands. I was beginning to think it was intentional so paper was not scattered around! The other think would be to put felt pads on the door frames of doors that slam. An easy fix especially needed at Paine Grande. Yes, these views are from a traveler that prefers a soft bed and a blow dryer. However, anyone that is a few years away from middle school camp might agree with my experience. This is a stunning park and the trek is a don't miss. Just be aware of the challenges and you will have a great time. The park is safe and you do not need a guide to follow the circuits.

review_text: We were debating between Salar Andino and Towanda Tours for our 3-day, 2-night Salar de Uyuni trip from San Pedro de Atacama to Uyuni - ultimately the choice came down to two factors for us: 1. Salar Andino only charged us 100,000 CLP for the trip, compared to 115,000 with Towanda Tours; 2. Salar Andino has offices on both sides of the border, so you know that the company is owned entirely, so you are not handed off to an unknown company when you reach the Bolivian border. I think that Towanda Tours had a specific company they work with on the other side, so it's still not a bad choice. Both tour companies choose to stay the first night at a lower altitude in Villamar, which is a safer option with a lowered risk of altitude-sickness (still a high altitude, and the sickness can affect anyone, no matter how fit you are). Again both companies follow a similar route, and during the wet season spend the second night in Uyuni as the salt-flats are flooded (do not choose a company that states they stay on or near the salt-flats the second night, it's untrue or unsafe either way). We traveled with Salar Andino in the middle of February 2018, right in the heart of Carnival. For those who are already nervous about traveling within Bolivia due to frequent reports of unsafe or intoxicated driving, Carnival is a season which increases the risk (a lot of drinking goes on during this festival). Many companies choose not to tour Salar de Uyuni at this time to minimise this issue, yet when we traveled with Salar Andino, our driver Eddy was a safe driver through and through. On top of this, many of the other tour groups we saw along the way also seemed to have very friendly, and safe drivers with them. The route is not a covered road, so expect a bumpy trip along many of the routes - Eddy our driver was one of the 'slower' drivers who slowed right down to navigate some bumpier areas, when we were overtaken by other drivers speeding over the holes and uneven surfaces - this was one of the more reassuring points for us - he was not in a rush. The food provided by this company varies little from the other tour companies (when everyone arrives at the accommodation or lunch spot, their is a big kitchen run by locals, and they provide essentially the exact same meal for each group - the only differences were the types of fruits given for dessert, or a flavour of yoghurt for breakfast etc. During one dinner we were not given a dessert, while other table had - it just just depends what your company has previously organised with the kitchen.) The food that is brought with you in the car is not usually what you consume - it is to replace what you eat at the remote locations, a great exchange, I think, which lessens the need for delivery vehicles to these destinations. We were asked at the beginning of the tour if we were vegetarian (we are not), so it is good that they are aware of different preferences, should we require a vegetarian meal. The accommodation was completely fine the first night, yet the second night in Uyuni had much to improve on (hot showers were not working on certain floors, and it is a bit of a dark and dingy place - not Salar Andino's fault though). We were worried about altitude sickness before starting the tour, because San Pedro de Atacama's many tours were cancelled due to the rain, so we did not have ample opportunities to acclimatise well beforehand. We carried with us a prescription from New Zealand from a travel doctor for some Diamox (check with your doctor - makes you pee more, tingling fingers, and soda tastes flat), which we think did help with the adjustment, plus we purchased some coca candy (available from many convenience stores in SPdA), and the tour companies all have either coca tea or leaves to drink or chew to help. One girl in our group had a really bad headache and nausea, which the tour guides were quick to make her a hot coca tea, and I offered some iBuprofen to help with the headache. She was mostly ok the next day, just really tired. We all experienced varying symptoms (headaches, dizziness, breathlessness when walking). The sites that are visited are beautiful, which Salar Andino cannot take credit for, yet you are given plenty of time at each place to take photos, breathe in the fresh air, and stretch your legs. There are not many toilet breaks, so take the chance to use a bathroom each time you have the option to. At one point we were still two hours away from our accommodation, so a lovely Brazilian girl we were traveling with took turns with me to hold a towel up for each other while we peed (sorry, TMI? It's a valid point of concern, so...), as there was no shelter in site for miles around. Not everyone is keen on taking a quick dip in the thermal pools, and it is only recommended to spend up to 15 minutes in there, as the heat alters your blood pressure (I think), and may make any altitude symptoms worse (especially as when you are traveling from San Pedro to Uyuni, the highest point of the trip is straight after you swim/have lunch. We had many concerns before traveling the Salar de Uyuni tour, yet essentially all of them were catered for with Salar Andino. We recommended them to a couple we met before we left (just based off customer service in their office in San Pedro), and when we met up with them again in Uyuni, they had had just as good of an experience. The only difference they experienced is that the pick-up vehicle arrived 15minutes early in San Pedro, and expected them to be ready, therefore rushed them. review_text: I booked a tour of Tierra del Fuego National Park with the optional End of the World Train for our cruise ship stop in Ushuaia with Patagonia Shorex. Due to weather conditions we had a change of itinerary but a quick email to Jamie and the change of date was not a problem for the tour to still go ahead. We had a slight mix up with the meeting place after disembarking our ship, Jamie had told us one place to meet and the tour bus was in another place but after we finally connected, our group finally set off. After taking the group to the train for our ride he arranged to pick us up at the other end for our tour through the park - what stunning scenery. Our guide, Lucas (??), was very engaging with a wicked sense of humour; he gave us so much information on the history of the area, how it became to be set up, and the early indigenous Indians of which we knew relatively little. He also gave the group the option of doing a walk through the area to the lookout overlooking Bahia La Pataia which we thoroughly enjoyed. His knowledge of the local flora and fauna was outstanding, he found birds in trees that even with him pointing them out, we had trouble locating. Dealing with Jamie was very easy, he answered all emails promptly and his handling payments from the group was great as I, being the tour organiser, did not have to do it. If you do not like overpriced crowded ships tours, I can highly recommend Jamie and his group of guides and drivers. Review of: Full-Day Tour to Petrohue Falls Through the Lake District , Chile thanks for your preference, it was a pleasure

review_text: This is a fascinating and spectacular otherwordly landscape, well worth the 2 hour drive from San Pedro de Atacama. Of all the fantastic Atacamean landscapes that we saw, this one was our favourite. A one hour walking trail leads down to the rocks bordering on the aquamarine blue salt water lake. It is not a difficult trail but feels strenuous due to the altitude of 13,000 feet. CAUTION: Do not go directly to Piedras Rojas without tickets, as they will not let you in. It is suggested that you purchase tickets in advance online, but we could not do so due to glitches in the system, and we met others who had the same problem. Thus, we set out and stopped at the visitor centre in Socaire, 90 km south of San Pedro, to purchase tickets for cash. In our case, we had to go through a routine to demonstrate that we couldn't buy the tickets online before they consented to sell them to us for cash. Glorious state of Chile, please reform your ticket purchase practices, as it is not fair to be hit-and-miss when buying tickets for these amazing attractions!

review_text: I took this excellent tour with Turismo Layana and the terrific guide was Christian. It was a very early predawn pick up and the company sent a text the night before confirming the pick up time from my hotel. It was over an hours drive out to the site of the geysers where the altitude was approximately 4,000m. The varied geysers were amazing and while standing beside bubbling boiling water and with many layers of clothing, warm hat and gloves, it was still extremely cold. We also made a stop at wetlands in crater lakes with an abundance of bird life including flamingos and even vicuñas ( relative of lamas) coming to have a drink. Such an amazing experience. Breakfast was set up on a table on another isolated stop out in the desert. We could make bread rolls with avocado, ham and cheese and tea/coffee and cake. We arrived back at San Pedro de Atacama about 11.30am after a totally unique experience Review of: El Tatio Geysers Tour from San Pedro de Atacama

review_text: Today, when we arrived at the vineyard, we had the worst experience ever in Santiago! We arrived 10 minutes early and when we entered we were not told that we had to go through the ticket office. We only found out when we arrived at the entrance to the wine store, where the tour begins. Then I had to run back to get the bracelets and this made the guide leave without waiting for us. They should have instructed the doorman to tell them to stop by the reception to pick up the bracelets. When we arrived the guide had already left and when we caught up he spoke Spanish! Did I hire the 9:50 time slot for the Portuguese language? Why do they offer this service if they don't comply?!? Unfortunate! I paid and didn't use the guide in Portuguese! The worst of all is that there were several guides speaking Portuguese with other groups! After the end of the tasting he took us to the bathroom next to the entrance to the basement where there are the wine barrels and where the Del diablo local wine presentation takes place! He entered and left some people behind, including us!! There were two other couples who went straight to the wine store thinking that the visit was over, but they still had to do it inside the devil's cellar! Terrible guide service, because when asked why he forgot us, he simply laughed! A disastrous experience, it ruined our trip! You can be sure that I will not recommend this winery to anyone! Another thing was about the children's kit that we paid for. No one told us where to get it and there were no different flavors to choose from. Children like traditional juice and not other flavors. They should reserve more traditional grape juices, knowing who paid. Anyway, a morning spoiled by your disorganization, guide who didn't speak the contracted language. Here in Brazil this is called lack of respect for the customer!

review_text: Chris was our driver. It was my husband and I along with 3 others. Personally I think our group had a great dynamic and that in itself made the tour fun. What I also appreciated was Chris's professionalism and knowledge - not just on the vineyards and the area, but Chile in general. We discussed everything from nature to economics covering history, mining, and energy as well. It was a great conversation and a lot of fun. I think next to the vineyard tour, the car-conversations were one of my favorite parts. Not because the vineyard were bad, but because the conversation was that good. For the tastings, we opted for the 3 tastings. The first tasting was two from Casablanca and two from another Valley that was partnered with that Vineyard. This was a treat as my Husband and I were not able to visit other valleys during our short stay. The second vineyard was Loma Larga and it had one of the best vineyard, winery, and tasting tours we have ever been on. A little background - I greatly enjoy visiting industrial and family breweries, wineries, and stills as I also work with fermentation and distillation. The knowledge on this tour was not only accurate it was presented in an easy to understand fashion. Even better - I learned a few more things I didn't know before. After Loma Larga we went to our third winery where we at lunch. We had the option to taste their wines (not included) but we all just ordered a glass instead. It was a generous pour and another great wine. Pinot Noirs from Chile are probably going to be my new favorite followed by their Carmenere and Malbec. The last tasting and vineard was a beautiful building high on the side of a hill. This one allowed us to taste a Late Harvest which we hadn't had the opportunity to try at the others. It was a great end to the day. You are able to buy wines at each vineyard which we did. I would recommend doing it this way as my husband and I noticed the prices were less at the vineyard than at the stores in Santiago. Supposedly the vineyard all export to somewhere in the United States so we are now on a hunt to find them here as well (Yes - they were that good). review_text: My wife and I were directed by our hotel staff to go to the Costerna Center on Christmas Eve, December 24, 2016. The hotel staff told us that the Costerna Center would be better and safer than some of the places in the center of Santiago. We wanted to get a video game for my daughter's boyfriend for Christmas. We took the Metro Line 1 from U. Catholica to Tobalaba station. When we got on the Metro we were treated to the graciousness of the Chilean people. I sat down next to an elderly man and he began chatting with me. He only spoke Spanish (and I did not speak any Spanish) and I replied in English. However, we had enough words in common to communicate on a very basic level. In addition, a young man sitting next to me saw the words "Costerna Center" printed on the top of my Metro map and, even though he only spoke Spanish, he indicated to me that he and his girlfriend were going to the same place. When we exited the Metro we followed the young man and his girlfriend and the led us around a block or so from the Metro to the entrance to Costerna Center which had an elevated walkway across a busy street. My wife attempted to chat with his girlfriend who asked my wife a question and when my wife answered the young girl burst into a good natured laughter. When we got to the point were they were going in a different direction, the young man pointed to the entrance of the Center. As we entered we realized that Costerna Center was a HUGE mall of 5 or 6 stories and very modern. It had every store that you might find in the United States and then some. We found our way to the information center and asked about the specific type of video we were looking for. We were directed to the fourth floor and we quickly found the video store. When we entered the video store, we were helped by a young man. I showed him the specific video type we were looking for and he proceeded to show me several different video games of that type. I selected one and he took me to the cash register to pay. I gave him my credit card when he rang up the purchase and the credit card receipt that I was to sign required a passport (which was locked in the safe in our hotel room). I showed him my driver's license instead and wrote that number on the receipt. That was adequate and our purchase was complete. This huge mall is so different from the many other places in Santiago were you shop for things. This mall was almost exactly the same as any huge mall in the United States, including the bathrooms. It felt very much like being home and it looked like you could find anything there. The mall was very crowded on Christmas Eve as everyone was apparently shopping for Christmas gifts. We returned on the Metro with the perfect gift.
