review_text: Just finished trekking the W circuit from east to west. Flew into El Calafate from Buenos Aires and used Always Glaciers to transport me directly to TDP, bypassing the need to go to Puerto Natales. TDP is VERY busy and reservations at the Refugio's are HIGHLY recommended. There are two companies that operate the Refugio's in the park: Fantastico Sur and Vertice Patagonia. Fantastico Sur operates Refugio's on the east side of the park and vertice on the west. You can book directly via their websites. Calling or emailing is terrible. You'll be lucky to get a response. You can either stay in their "lodges", camp using their tents and equipment or bring your own tent. Given the unpredictability of the weather, I'd recommend staying in a Refugio. If you're insistent on camping I recommend using their tents and sleeping bags and food so you don't have to carry it. You can book all of this directly on their websites. The weather is hard to predict. Google will say it's sunny but it's actually raining. I wouldn't rely on a weather forecast unless it was 24-36 hours in advance. So with that, it's best to be prepared for multiple days of rain. On a sunny day Patagonia is beautiful. But on rainy days it can be a nightmare if you're camping. It's best to over prepare for rain. Your tent should have a rain fly that goes all the way to the ground and it should be able to hold up against strong wind gusts. You'll want some flex in your guy lines to avoid anything from ripping. Most of the Refugio's have wood platforms for tents. They'll give you a hammer and some nails for stakes. But bring a few stakes to tie your rain fly down. Pack a quick dry towel to wipe the rain off your tent when you have to pack it away in the rain. When it rains, it rains for a while and unless it clears up, the sun won't ever have the chance to dry anything. And because you can't have fires in the park everything stays wet. So be prepared for this. Be sure to have a heavy weight rain cover for your back pack. Parts of the trail have low hanging branches that will catch your rain cover and tear it. Plastic bags will shred on this stuff. Pack your clothes, sleeping bags, tent and other items you want dry in plastic bags. Once it gets wet it will be very hard to dry in Patagonia. The Refugio's have stoves but they're overcrowded and it's impossible to find a spot to hang things inside in the common area. Drying out a sleeping bag? Forget about it. Make sure you have good boots with good gore tex. Some parts of the trail have sharp rocks and will tear your soles to pieces if you're wearing tennis shoes. Additionally, on rainy days many parts of the trails turn into streams and mud pools. So be prepared for getting dirty. Bring a large poncho big enough to cover yourself and your back pack. This is the safest way to ensure things stay dry. If not, bring a poncho at the minimum in addition to your waterproof coat. You'll want a dry coat once you get to camp. And if it rains multiple days back to back, nothing will dry and you'll wish you had a dry coat. Bring good water proof pants that are also breathable and can quickly be pulled over your boots and pants. The cheap pants don't breathe and you'll just sweat in them. You'll want water proof pants because the trails can be narrow and brushing up against the grass and bushes on the side will unload all of the rain water onto your pants. Bring hiking sticks. They'll help you keep balance and help you move faster through streams and mud pools. You can drink the water from the steams. Just be smart about where you're getting it. Food in the Refugio's isn't bad (except for the packed lunches). They do have wifi for a cost. If you're staying in the Refugio's, expect staying in an overly used hostel. Wash your hands regularly. Nola virus is there. Overall, Patagonia is beautiful on a good day. On rainy and cloudy days it can be miserable. No views. Just rain and chill. So be prepared to give yourself an extra day or two in areas where you want to really see the views. Otherwise, you can do the W in four days. Catching the catamaran is easy. Schedules are posted at all Refugio's. You buy tickets on the boat. You can hitch a ride a pudeto on one of the many local bus companies to Laguna Armaga or to Puerto Natales without having a ticket. Just bring Chilean pesos. Patagonia is a lot like the Tetons in Wyoming and the rolling mountain hills you would find in the Rockies. Add some Glaciers and worse weather and you'll be in Patagonia.

review_text: We primarily booked this tour so that we could tour Valparaiso and photograph the street art, and this is what happened on this tour - we first stopped at Veramonte winery, which was a nice stop to see their winery and sample two wines, then drove to Viña Del Mar and had a very very brief stop at the flower clock to take a photo, then went to the beach for a bit and then to lunch. Following that, the tour took us to Valparaiso and Pablo Neurda’s beautiful house on a hill overlooking the water. When that was finished, it was going to be time for the walking tour to see the street art. At that point, the guide asked who wanted to go on the tour and who did not, and because more people voted to not go on the walking tour, he skipped it altogether, even though a substantial number of guests still voted to go on the tour. It was extremely disappointing, especially since this was the primary reason we booked the tour, and the promotional photos showed photos of the street art, and it was listed in the itinerary. It was our first visit to Chile and I’m not sure that we will ever have the opportunity to make it out there again. The tour company offered us Santiago Hop-On-Hop-Off bus tickets as compensation for this issue (which we did not need or accept), but would not offer any type of refund or other option to make up for the incomplete tour. Also be aware that this tour does not take you see the sea lions or the Easter Island Moai in Viña Del Mar. Overall, if I were to book this tour again, I would choose a different tour company that delivers what it advertises. Review of: From Santiago: Valparaíso, Viña del Mar and Neruda Museum We deeply appreciate you sharing your experience with us, it motivates us even more to keep improving and deliver the best experience.

review_text: We visited the geysers via a tour, as the road up is a bit difficult and we didn't have our own vehicle (although we passed one brave soul biking and a few more trying to hitchhike!). All the tours leave super early in the morning, about 4:30 AM, because the geysers are most dramatic in the morning light, while the steam is still very intense. It was only 18,000 CLP per person, not terribly expensive (about 30 USD). However, since the geysers are at about 4,500 meters above sea level, it is COLD before the sun comes up (for us, 6 degrees celsius below zero), so wear warm clothes and bring gloves. But also bring a swim suit for bathing in the geyser-heated pool later! They geysers themselves are really cool to see. My girlfriend has been to Yellowstone and seen the big ones there, but even she got a kick out of watching these smaller ones shoot up out of the ground. Also, you can get much closer to these geysers than some in other places (but be careful not to get too close!). Just mind the altitude and the cold, but otherwise definitely worth a visit! We also saw some fauna, such as vicuña and flamingos, on our way back down to San Pedro.

review_text: If you think you’ve seen amazing landscapes, wait until you get to know the Atacama Altiplanes Lagoas. This is one of the most magical tours in the Chilean desert — and also one of the highest: you reach more than 4,000 meters altitude! The tour begins early, and the first stop is in Socaire, an Andean village where you can taste the typical local breakfast and already feel the coldness of altitude. From there, the road rises towards the protagonists of the day: the Lagoas Miscanti and Miñiques. The intense blue of the water contrasts with the snowy mountains and volcanoes in the background — it’s so surreal that it looks like a hand-painted landscape. These lagoons are within a protected reserve and are home to flamingos, vicunhas and other animals you can’t imagine seeing in a desert. And a curiosity: they formed thousands of years ago, after a volcanic eruption that blocked the flow of water between the valleys. Prepare for the cold wind, breathtaking views — literally — and a peace that only the silence of the desert can offer. Tip: go snug, bring water and don't forget the camera. Because this is the kind of place you never forget again.

review_text: Now let's face it..... Futalelufu is not on many peoples radar screen as a travel destination....by car from Bariliche it is a good 5 hrs including time to cross the border...fortunately the road trip from Bariloche is visually stunning , the roads are paved 85% of the way so the travel time passes quickly..... But given the rocks that were flying on the unpaved road if you are renting a car you should get insurance for covering at least any small scratches from flying stones.... The roads are relatively empty with seemingly safe drivers.... Another challenge that Futalelufu has is a shortage of high end lodgings...Uman Lodge (see my review) is the only place that I'm aware of .... BUT all of these shortcomings are worth it if you are an avid fisherman, lover of kayaking or river rafting of just hiking. I've travelled all over the world...the closest Futaleufu comes to visually....would be a remote part of Switzerland with snow capped mountains in the summer, beautiful expanses of pasture for milk cows and sheep and the ocassional lama..brisk clean air, almost no people AND what separates it from Switzerland is the magnificent Futalelufu river. A sizeable, powerful , turquoise colored, pristine river flowing through the valley ...absolutely stunning. During our stay in Futalelufu we went fishing, rafting and hiking. One guy in our party, an avid fisherman, claimed that it was one of his most memorable fishing experiences having caught 30+ trout in one day. The white water rafting..including class 5 Rapids...was over the top....see my review. For three relatively inexperienced rafters pushing the envelope.....we can all highly recommend the experience.....and lastly there is the hiking ... Down mountain sides, through fields of wild flowers and beautiful pastures .... all so pleasant. Lastly the town of Futalelufu can't be more than 5 blocks square.....it has a very nice park at the center off of which one can find "simple" restaurants , a church, B&Bs , etc. for one of the best views of the Futalelufu river venture up to Uman Lodge, order a glass of wine or coffee, Go sit out on their terrace and soak in the wonders of nature. Futaleufu and its river have clearly remained undiscovered due to its isolation and possibly the few upscale lodges that are located here ...but this is also an advantage for those seeking the very best that nature has to offer without being over run by tourists. If you plan to drive allow for four nights in Futaleufu ...your arrival night, then 3 days of activity...hiking, rafting and fishing and then returning to Bariliche..,and yes, there is a gas station in Futaleufu to fill your car up for your return trip. If you rent a car in Bariliche make sure you get the proper documents to cross the border into Chile ... Depending on the number of people the border crossing will take 30-45 mins ...but both in Chile and Argentina there were 4-5 people manning each border crossing.

review_text: The quality of the La Serena and Coquimbo City Tour provided by LST tours on behalf of Viator was not at all good. The guide, who gave her name as Giovanna, was badly organised, lacking in knowledge and certainly not the expert bi-lingual guide promised in the tour description. The offering we experienced,could in no way be described as a 'guided' tour. Giovanna offered no information or commentary of worth as we moved from place to place and instead acted more as a courier simply telling us what we would visit next and how long it would take to get there. Upon arrival at each of the stops her input was limited to 'it is beautiful, we have ? minutes here, be back at the meeting point by...! She spent most of the early part of the trip taking orders for lunch and gave no information of worth about local life commerce and culture and that which she did offer, she had to check for accuracy on her mobile phone! She offered no information at all about city square in La Serena and at the cultural museum when questioned about the Easter Island figure, she told us that it was a replica, before once again consulting her phone and going round to tell people that it was an original. Her time and group management were both very poor. We spent a very, very long time, well more than an hour, at the Cross of the Third Milenium, while waiting for a very slow lift to take people to the top. People would have actually accepted being told that there was not enough time for this. We then spent almost half an hour at the Lighthouse in La Serena, which was far too long in the poor weather and visibility today. Unfortunately that meant that when we arrived at La Recova Market were allowed only ten minutes! Finally upon arrival at the Japanese Garden, we were all asked to leave the bus and then we were immediately asked to get back on, as she had decided that because of time constraints we should go straight for lunch and return to the Japanese Garden later. Lunch did not start until almost 3 pm and we did not finish until 4 pm The lady clearly had limited skills as a guide and when I asked her whether we would be receiving a refund for the tour she seemed genuinely ignorant of the abysmally low standard of experience that she was responsible for! Based on everything described so far, a good third of the group asked for the tour to be concluded at this point and she agreed that the bus driver would return us to the ship - after which he would return to the restaurant and complete the tour for those who wished to continue. After agreeing this, she even had the temerity to request a group photo and ask that we all smile!! Whilst awaiting our return, things changed again and she asked everyone to get back on the bus and that the tour would continue in a shortened form once we had been off loaded - in the end, and as we left, barely a third of the group opted to stay on board. This was not a cheap excursion and as we booked through Viator we asked for a refund less the cost of the meal, which in itself was good quality, and frankly the only highlight of a wasted day. Picking up a taxi driver at the port gate would have been a less expensive and more informative option. Viator bounced the complaint on to LST who refused any form of refund, as we had chosen to leave the tour early In summary, the tour was not as described, the quality was not what we'd paid for and I would advise caution when booking this tour Review of: La Serena & Coquimbo City Tour - Short Cruise Excursion

It was fascinating to watch.

S&F took such fantastic care of us -they picked us up directly outside our apartment in a beautiful, new air conditioned van (very comfortable and clean!). Fran immediately welcomed us with warm hugs and an offer for fresh (and freshly washed ;)) fruit and bottled water for our drive out to Maipa. Our horseback ride through the Chilean Alps was idyllic; Seba was able to ride with us and provide translation into English when necessary (including a helpful description for why my horse was named 'Festejado'... ;)) Lunch was great, and coupled with a few surprises planned by Fran and Seba (I won't give away their surprise additions to these tours; I'll just say they're unique and lovely :)) F&S really do their part in making your time with them memorable and fun, I highly recommend any of their tours! review_text: When we found a special airfare to visit Santiago from Los Angeles, the pressure was on to put together a short but great trip with as many memories as possible. We compared tours listed online and emailed with many companies. We selected Thomas based on his fantastic email response time and his willingness to accommodate our requests rather than suggest a preset itinerary. My husband and I toured with Chile Private Tours for 2 days. The first day with Julio we went up into the mountains to see El Colorado and Montana (2 ski resorts). There had been quite a bit of snow and Julio knew so many places to take amazing pictures, patiently allowing us to "reshoot" to be sure we got the best shots. In the afternoon we went back down to a very special vineyard in the middle of Santiago. The family owned vineyard is a wonderful refuge tucked away behind big walls just inches from the freeway. We had a personalized tour of the entire grounds and a special tasting at the end. Julio spoke perfect english, passionately shared great history of Chile and South America, and most important helped us take lots of photos. A perfect trip to the mountains! On day two we lucked out and got Thomas all to ourselves. We began with the Loma Larga vineyard and one of the most special tastings ever, an entire hour focused on us - with reserve tastings and so much education. We were met as we got out of the car by the master sommelier Alejandra who shared almonds that she had just harvested and roasted. An extensive tour was ended with some of the most impressive wines we've ever had. Then off to Valparaiso and Vina del Mar. The pictures can't prepare you for the awesome sites - so much history and color. Allowing for our picky palates Thomas arranged a very special and delicious lunch. 10 hours flew by so quickly, we packed quite a bit into the day. Later that night we were so excited to receive a special treat from Thomas - an email with a suggested city-tour for our last day, including options for lunch and guidance of the best time to leave for our flight home that night. On both tour days we were picked up promptly on schedule, and delivered back to our hotel just in time for dinner. The tours are reasonably priced, well paced, full of photo ops, and you're on the tour they are flexible to accommodate last minute inspiration (translates to "Oh wow can we see that???). Both Julio and Thomas are brilliant historians and can answer all questions. Touring with Thomas and Chile Private Tours is the best decision we made on our trip, and in the end gave us most of the lifelong memories we take from our vacation. Seemed no end to the careful focus on little things they did to create special stories we'll be sharing for years. Call or email Thomas today and let him create a special trip for you. We'll be back to Chile again soon!! Thank you Thomas - we had a blast!

review_text: Do not miss the chance to explore this distant area if you are in San Pedro de Atacama. Many tours do not include the Piedras Rojas and those who do include it as a particular attraction, but in fact it is a beautiful area beyond the famous Miscanti and Miniques lagoons. The area is perfectably suitable for self driving, which is in my opinion the bust way to explore natural wonders.Follow the Chile 23 road and you will drive into wonderful areas.The Piedras Rojas is just an interesting rock formation inside the huge and astoundingly beautiful Salar de Talar. Driving even further, you shall find the Laguna Tuyaijto, which is as beautiful as Miscanti but far less visited, less crowded, and with no entrance fee. The road itself, and the mountain scenery, are also breathtaking One thing that must be taken in account is the risk of altitude sickness, for this area is above 4550m

Unfortunately clouds generally are low enough to hide the bbest parts of the range. The only solution is to take a trip of some length and hope that there is a sunny day or two. And investigate whether the rain and clouds situation is better or worse at different times of the year.

review_text: I have taken quite a few Hop on Hop off bus tours throughout the world. This was not one of the best. The second stop where you get off to go up the mountain to the statue of the Virgin Mary was the best. After that mostly just a lot of buildings to look at and history to listen to, not a lot of sights to see. Santiago takes a long time to drive around, it is a very sprawled city and the bus had to go very slow to give all of the history information. We purchased the Premium tour which included the ride up the mountain on the gondola, and down the funicular. It also included a walking tour. I would not recommend the walking tour. We got poor directions from the bus attendant, to find the walking tour, but eventually found it 2 blocks away from where the bus drops off. The walking tour only walked two blocks and it took an hour and a half. A lot of time sitting and waiting, some of which was to allow the guide to first do the tour in Spanish and then repeat in English. When we got back on the bus, we realized that the bus gave us the same information that our guide had, as we drove by these same two blocks. There is a beautiful cathedral in the old part of town, that is worth seeing, so get off at stop 5 and see the cathedral and wander around instead of the walking tour add on. We were told that the whole tour with stops to the Virgin Mary and walking tour would only take 3 hours; 7.5 hours later, we finally caught a cab back to our hotel. Review of: Tourist bus around Santiago for a day Dear SeattleGail, we regret the situation and we are sad to know that you did not fully enjoy your experience. We will take into account each of your appreciations in order to improve and continue providing a quality service to each of our visitors. We wish you a happy return home.

review_text: My husband and I had the good fortune to book multiple tours with I Love Chile Tours prior to our visit to Santiago in late January 2018. Fran and Seba met us at our hotel for the first tour--a Day in Valparaiso. Two others were on the tour. After a friendly greeting and the offer of fresh fruit and water, we headed to our destination city. We stopped at a lovely winery in the Casablanca Valley where we were offered a small wine tasting and a "comfort stop." We arrived in the charming and colorful maze that is Valparaiso, and Fran guided us on a walking tour that covered the harbor, many streets at sea level and then climbs up the populated hillsides. To reach the pinnacle we used a funicular and were able to have great views of the city, harbor and the tony neighborhood of Vena del Mar across the harbor. Fran gave a running commentary on the history and current changes taking place in the City. Outdoor art plays a very important part of the Chilean culture and no more than in Valparaiso--murals, attractive graffiti, and unfortunately...some ugly "tagging." We lunched in a local restaurant, and the fondness displayed by the owners toward Fran and Seba was typical of interactions they had with other native City natives. Because of Fran and Seba's excellent command of English, we were able to communicate all day long and ask whatever we wanted...including topics such as politics and religion. It was long day, a fun day, and an important part of our memories of I Love Chile Tours. We also took a walking tour of Santiago with their associate Clara and spent another day in Vena del Mar with Fran Seba. GREAT tours! Review of: Valparaiso Day Trip from Santiago - Private Tour for Small Groups

review_text: Jose was our Uncorked guide for our full day wine tours in Maipo and Colchagua valleys, and we were pleased with the vineyards he had selected. In the Maipo Valley, we visited Perez Cruz, a very large winery with an unusual architecture, including big arcs. The tasting room was small and we tried three different red wines. The second visit to William Fevre was led by an energetic and enthusiastic host. He had set up a table along the path leading to the winery with a vase of flowers, bottle of chardonnay, and two glasses. We proceeded to try wines from the tanks, two from barrels, and three reds with some cheese and crackers. (At the end of the day, Jose gave us the opened bottle from the tasting, which was a very nice touch.) The last “tasting” was at the restaurant at Haras de Pirque where we had a fixed lunch of shrimp with tomatoes, salmon with potatoes Anna and some sort of custard. The “pairing” was a glass of chardonnay and a glass of their red wine. The restaurant overlooked part of the vineyard. It was not really a tasting. Jose was our guide again into the Colchagua valley where we first stopped at the Lugarejo winery, owned by a History professor (PhD from UCDavis ...) and his wife. The winery is tiny but they are clearly passionate about their hobby, most of which is in a sort of garage with a single bottle bottling machine! We had a lovely time with Elina and tried three of their wines. She had a plate with olives and crackers. The second winery was Neyen where we could see vines growing up into the hills of the valley. A young lady walked us (and another tour group) into the vineyard and explained how the vine stems were made to root on either side of the “mother” vine for cloning. Then we tried three of their wines. The larger, second group also seemed to be an EcoChile or Uncorked group that had come for a day tour from Santiago. This was definitely a premium (or, as they tend to describe them in Chile, "iconic") wine, and very good. The last vineyard was Viu Manent where we first had lunch of grilled tenderloin (not too tender) with two wines. After the lunch, we went across the road to the tasting room to taste seven (!) different wines! At the very end of the day, Jose left us at the Hotel Santa Cruz in Santa Cruz. The wine tours were the best parts of our two-week visit to northern Chile.

review_text: Cerro Concepción is one of the prettiest places I have ever been, but it is also very quirky. The rickety old ascensor takes you up the hill into lots of interweaving, narrow streets splattered with graffiti, murals and colour everywhere you go. There are lovely restaurants with terraces to sit out on as well as lots of hotels and hostels. The market is one of the better ones I have seen in Chile, selling more authentic jewellery and crafts. The hill joins to Cerro Alegre which is great for having lunch or an ice-cream. Around every corner is a colourful surprise and you can happily spend all afternoon wandering through the alleys and streets!

review_text: We did the 10-day north tour. I loved it - we talk about it all the time, and I would kill to go back and do it all over again! From reading these other reviews, we were hesitant to book, but we took the plunge. I think Pachamama tours can be hit-and-miss. My experience was definitely a hit. I went with one of my best friends, and the only other people on our tour were another set of 20-something best friends and a recently married couple (there were 6 guests total). This made the tour really familial and intimate. We loved it, but I can see how it wouldn't have been the same if the people in our group weren't great. If you're looking for a tour in an official charter bus with tour guides in matching polos who maintain an arms-length relationship, this isn't for you. It's definitely more South American in style - remember, you're in Chile! The guides and driver were very kind to us, and chose to have dinner with us and hang out with us most nights. Our guide, Jorge, was extremely knowledgable, and was training another amazing guide, Paulina. The driver, Pedro, was one of the kindest people I've met - he buys food for the stray dogs along the 10-day route and tirelessly cares for them each time he completes the loop. We saw beautiful, remote places we would have never seen if we hadn't taken this tour. I really feel like I've seen most of the top half of Chile after doing this trip. Jorge really pushed us to get out of our comfort zones - riding horses on steep mountain paths, riding in little boats in the Pacific to see penguins, arguing about politics, etc. This was an incredible experience, and I wish I could do a tour this style in every country I visit.

review_text: I spent an hour or more walking around the Botanical Garden on the University of Austral De Chile. I visited the garden on a Saturday afternoon, just walking over the river bridge from Valdivia to the university campus, about a 15 minute walk. There were few people around, but the one person I asked directions from pointed me in the right direction (near the medical school and right off the river). Much of the garden is given over to pastoral expanses. It was a good place for a picnic. I visited in early spring and many flowering plants were bursting forth with their blooms. There was no admission fee. The one disappointment was how few identifying signs there were for the many plants found in the garden. It was not clear to me that any docent led tours were available so I left knowing not much more about the plants I saw than when I arrived but I still enjoyed the visit.

review_text: I did carretera austral backpacking and hitchhiking. It's amazing! And it's tough. Most part of the road is not paved. This brings very bad conditions. There is very few public transport (like 1-2 bus / day). And in high season (Jan-Feb) there are lots of backpackers. So, there's big competition in hitchhiking. It's like 5 hitchhikers for each car :) If you come by car, make sure you have a 4X4 or something nice and high. Not recommendable with a regular sedan car. There are 3 ferry crossings. For passengers, no advance planning needed. But for cars, there's limited space and in high-season they may tell you to come back in 2days! So, better buy your ferry ticket in advance online. Enjoy the nature!

review_text: This tour is great. Sure you have to leave San Pedro at 4am but set your alarm and bring a warm jacket and gloves. The ascent to the area of the geysers takes about 2 hours and is in darkness so just close your eyes and rest. Tour arrives at the geyser plain at about 6:45am and the temperature was -8 degrees C. The guide gave a good explanation in spanish and english of the geology and processes involved. The reason to be so early is that the extreme temperature differential at that hour creates more impressive clouds of steam. It is like walking on the crater of a volcano with multiple fissures erupting with boiling water. The emergence of sunrise through the plumes of steam create a spectacular sight. Sunrise also prompts time for a breakfast to be served with welcome hot coffee greeting the rising temperatures. After a good time to wander we move on to another close-by area that also features a pool of naturally heated water where it is possible to bathe for awhile. The trip back to San Pedro features spectacular mountain scenery and the multi-coloured peaks are amazing. There are a few stops for photo ops especially when the animals such as vicuna and llamas are present. The final stop is at a small settlement called Machuca for souvenir purchases, water and snack replenishment, restrooms or just photo ops.We were back in San Pedro at about 12:30pm. An early start, a bumpy bus ride but a superb experience. The guide from Touristour, Salvador, was both friendly and informative.

review_text: This trip was my first time in Chile and after researching I knew that I couldn't miss seeing Valparaíso and Viña del Mar for myself. I contacted Stamp's Tour and reserved seats for my group in advance by contacting them via email. Their response time was very quick and very clear. Stamp's was also flexible in that they were able to pick us up from our apartment since we were not staying in a hotel. After visiting the walking portion of our day tour we had lunch at a cozy spot in Viña del Mar. The meal was a great way to get to know the people we were on the tour with and the food was delicious. The cost for the meal was 21000 CLP plus tip. Our last spot was Viña Indómita, Casablanca & Maipo Vineyards. The vineyard is beautiful and wine tasting is optional but when in Chile, why not? The wines were amazing, the sample size generous and the price very reasonable. I would definitely recommend Stamp's Tour.

review_text: I travelled up the Funicular railway, stopping at the zoo on the way, and then walked down. The funicular railway is a fun experience, even if it is very short. There's not a lot to do at the very top of Cerro San Cristobel, but there are good views of the surrounding city, and a garden that is well maintained, and on the day I visited was warm and quiet despite the large number of visitors. There are a few food and souvenir shops (good if you are hot or hungry!). The zoo is not stunning but worth a visit nevertheless.

review_text: The tasting we arranged for CLP 20,000 per person consisted of 5 premium wines, three of them being from the Casa Marin label (thus under the supervision of María Luz Marín) whereas the remaining two were of the Litoral label (creations of her son, Felipe). I am mentioning the above because it is a tasting that while not in their webpage, can be arranged as this winery is flexible in that regards, which is a very good thing. Our guide was Fernanda, which sitting us in the wine bar thoroughly educated us on the different wines being served: a Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Riesling (rare thing in Chile), Pinot Noir and Syrah. Leaving aside the great quality of the wines, a positive thing of the tasting is that Fernanda is very knowledgeable of wine. She is an English teacher graduate (thus making an English tasting possible) and has also taken sommelier courses in Santiago. Hence, this was not a scripted tasting but rather a conversation on the different wines being tasted. Personally I think their Pinot Noir and Riesling are very interesting and full of life and expression, something that most of us as amateur consumers appreciate (in opposition to a somewhat complex wine filled with hints maybe too subtle, as their Syrah probably is). Although you can buy wine after, I am conflicted by the pricing of this vineyard as I think is a bit off market-price (on the higher end of course). Nevertheless, buying wine directly in the store is certainly cheaper than doing it in a supermarket or specialty store anywhere else. We did not do a tour but the grounds seemed pretty and with a feeling as if you were in somebody's home (actually, I think part of the building was María Luz's house). If doing the tasting, we suggest you to request the fire of the wine bar being lit, as it is a pretty cold and gloomy room which can use the extra light and heat.

review_text: With adventure travel comes the possibility of upsets and changes in plans. How an agency cares for their clients in such situations speaks volumes about their integrity. In our situation our trip had to be cancelled due to a severe low pressure system in the Antarctic peninsula region. Leading up to the cancellation it looked like there might be a possibility of getting in with an abbreviated schedule. They offered us that choice with a discount, complete cancellation or shifting to a future trip. When weather conditions did not improve the sent representatives to our hotel in Ushuaia who waited there for three hours awaiting our return from a day trip so they could speak with us and support us personally. They worked with us on options to get to Punta Arenas including air options, bus options and a cruise option through the fjords ... Which was due to depart in ninety minutes. We chose the cruise and the representatives handled calling to confirm availability and worked with a local agent to stay late so we could pay. In addition, they paid for one of our nights in PA AND sent us a transfer on our day of departure. There's nothing they could have done better in such a situation. Very well done!

review_text: We booked the 5 day/4 night W trek back in June via email. Carlos the owner was responsive and professional and answered all our questions. We paid through Pay Pal and waited for our trip to begin in December. Carlos picked us up from the bus station in Puerto Natales. His nephew was visiting so we met him and Victor who would be our guide for the trip. As we headed to our hotel, Carlos and Victor gave us a rundown of what to expect and what to pack. They pointed out some restaurants for us to try as we drove through town and then dropped us off at our hotel. The next day they arrived at the hotel promptly at 2pm. After a beautiful 2 hour drive through the country (mountains, lakes, guanacos), we arrive at the park and immediately see the iconic Towers. We bid farewell to Carlos and the 3 of us start our trek. Everything about the trek was wonderful, there was challenging terrain (moraine and boulders) and easy terrain (forest path). Poles helped a lot. The views were spectacular and ever changing and the weather held up for us for the most part - our last day was extremely windy. Definitely dress in layers, we ended up in short sleeve shorts many days. The Refugios were as expected - bunk beds for 6-8 people, hearty food and lots of Europeans and Aussie/NZ travelers hiking without guides and camping. Victor was a spectacular guide. Due to his frequent trips he knows many employees at the various refugios and he was always able to score us immediate seating at the restaurants, more food and special coffee. He totally took care of us and checked up on trail conditions and weather in advance and explained what to expect each day. He also told great stories and provided us with lots of chocolate. We could not have asked for a better guide. Do not hesitate to book with Extremo Chile - you will not be disappointed. Thank you Carlos and Victor!!

review_text: We visited Neyen on February 20th, it was our second day in Santa Cruz, and we had visited a few other wineries. We heard that this winery was great by our chauffer but unfortunately what we were promised, and paid for, was only half of what was actually given to us. We had the tour and wine tasting with Sophia and things seemed well (we were tipsy after having had other wine at this point in time) but we are disappointed in learning after we left that the experience was not what we expected to receive for the price we paid. We did not visit the cellar nor get any cheese with our wines (only one piece of chocolate) and the "tour" was very short and basically just showed us 2 vines close to the visitors center. This leaves us feeling sad that the cost of this experience, $33,000 CLP, was so expensive and we did not even get half of what was promised to us. To add insult to injury, upon trying to get into contact with their Visitor and Hospitality manager, Roxana, after sending 2 emails immediately after we realized this grave oversight, there was absolutely no response. Lastly, the 3 wines we tasted, only 1 was decent, the other two were too young, considering they are reds and definitely not worth the price that we were charged. Be very careful of this winery and make sure that you received all of the services that they charge you for!

review_text: We did a 3-day tour of Parque Lauca starting and ending in Arica and staying 2 nights in Putre. We had previously spent 4 days and nights in San Pedro de Atacama. The time spent at and above San Pedro’s 2400m probably helped acclimatize so that after a rather headachey first night we were fine at Putre’s 3500m and the highest point of the tour was 4600m. For us these 3 days were more enjoyable than the time spent in San Pedro because of the quietness, lack of other visitors to Parque Lauca and the richer wildlife. The infrastructure (toilets, changing facilities at hot springs, the tour company’s van, hotels, roads (miles and miles of washboard)) was poorer, but it is so much nicer it was well worth the hardship.

review_text: I went on a one day tour to Valparaiso and Viña Del Mar with Somos tours in October 2017 and it was a very bad experience. I wouldn’t recommend anyone to go with them. The short (TRDL) version is: we only had 1 guide leading a group of 30 so we were constantly running behind schedule and in the end didn’t have time at all to explore the hills of Valparaiso, instead we just rushed through the area in a bus! If you would like to walk the hills of Valparaiso and enjoy some time taking pictures of the colourful houses, DO NOT GO WITH THEM! There are lots of good tour operators out there, but despite all the reciews, Somos is definitely not one of them. Most people take such tours only once, you don’t want to take your chances with them. So here is what happened. For a large group of 30 people, we only had 1 guide. He is constantly looking for people during the tour and try to gather everyone. Most other groups I saw on the way are 10-20 people. We visited Viña Del Mar in the morning, after lunch and a museum in Valparaiso, it was already 3.30pm so we had to rush to the wharf for a boat ride at 4pm which means we had no time at all to walk the hills of Valparaiso, instead we just rushed through a couple of famous streets in the bus and couldn’t take any decent photos, which was supposed to be the main purpose of the tour! Also I was the only person in the group that doesn’t speak Spanish/Portuguese and the guide explained everything only in Spanish. I don’t blame him because if you have this many people to manage, you wouldn’t have time to do your explanations twice. The tour was so badly organised that I believe they just wanted to grab as much money as possible without considering the experiences of the customers. I enjoyed the tour so much. I highly recommend this tour.

Drove us through the coastal mountains to Santiago – great information, felt so comfortable. review_text: this is a very nice, short walk up a small hill overlooking much of Santiago. you will be rewarded with a panoramic view of the city and also the Andes to the north/east, assuming there's not much smog about. there are also a small garden, a catholic sanctuary, a small shop, and some limited dining facilities at the top. the elevation gain is only about 1000 feet (300 meters), and the grade is not steep. in parts the surface is a bit irregular, but most all people will have absolutely no trouble at all navigating it. to get to the trail, simply walk several hundred meters along the road that winds to the left (west) of the visitor information booth at the north end of Avenida Pio Nono - this road (Manuel Mackenna) will bring you to an obvious (though i don't think obviously sign-posted) trail veering up the hill a bit more steeply to your right. alternatively you can take the cable car if you're pressed for time or don't want to walk. just don't do what we did right before we walked to the top on a hot (high 90s F) late afternoon in January - polish off a whole pizza and guzzle a couple of (at the time) refreshing local beers right before we took this otherwise enjoyable stroll….

review_text: I was so excited to finally get the opportunity to visit Lapostelle in December with a group of girlfriends. My husband and I tried to go previously but were unable to as this is one of the few wineries in Chile that doesn't allow children. The building itself is spectacular - an architectural wonder, with a spiral staircase going underground and all of the wine making process happening via gravity (with the wine moving downward in the building with each stage). The cellar at the bottom looks like it is from a James Bond movie - all glass, with the entrance forming the tasting table, so you look down into the cellar as you taste the wines. The wines in the tasting were awesome and included a few wines I had not tried before. I've been to a lot of wineries in Colchagua Valley, Casablanca Valley, Maipo Valley and near the coast (Leyda Valley) and this was my favourite tasting tour. Highly recommend!

review_text: Our family, including two children with little prior horseback riding experience, enjoyed this horseback riding tour twice during our December holiday stay in Santiago. First tour was with Claudia and her sister, Francesca. Absolutely wonderful day, with on-time pickup at the hotel and a quick drive up to the Lo Barnechea area ranch house. The horses were traditional Chilean horses, acclimated to the mountain trails, matched to the kids' capabilities, and responsive to the individual riders. The trails themselves go up and down over a series of ridges and valleys, with spectacular views of the mountains and the city. Natural elements, both flora and fauna abound, with opportunities for photos literally everywhere. Claudia took all our photos for us, so that we could focus on enjoying the ride, and later sent us the photos for download via Google drive. We ended the day with a fantastic picnic lunch of veg, meats, cheeses, fruits, olives, and Chilean wine (Claudia even brought fresh lettuces from her garden for our wraps). Our second time 'round was just as spectacular, this time with Lorraine as our guide. Again, horses matched to capabilities, with a ride up and down through the mountain trails - different routes from the first, and ending with another wonderful picnic lunch. Highly recommend this tour, the guides are very knowledgeable and friendly, the arrieros (Chilean cowboys) take care of everything related to the horse, the views and food are spectacular, and the proximity to Santiago makes it so convenient! review_text: The tour was nice, but if I was to do it again, I would look for transfer only, as I don't believe it was worth the money. You'll visit the town of San Jose de Maipo and walk around main square full of souvenirs and crafts. You can also have lunch in one of the restaurants there. You'll also visit an independent, "chocolate house", where you can buy some treats (there's no tour of chocolate making process). Our van broke down, but the driver was great and organize replacement very quickly. The guide was also great, cracking jokes and making everyone enjoy the tour. To international tourists: Chile is expensive and not really worth a visit. Neighbouring Bolivia has so much more to offer and is far far cheaper! In Chile, there is a discrimination fee at ATMs; every time you're getting cash, you'll need to pay extra. It's a way of greedy banks here, saying "welcome" to foreigners. review_text: This was another gem, away from the big crowds of TdP. - no cost, no pretense, just beauty and about 10 miles beyond airport - very close to town. Just follow the road (9) north out Puerto Natales and watch for the sign on your left fork Laguna Sofia. We drove up fr a last morning, dawn walk, and wish that we had left more time for hiking much further. Parking is adjacent to a beautiful dark gravel beach, which is about a half mile long and a nice walk. On our return, we realized that there was a nice trail to the left along the edge of the lagoon under the bluff, and we only went out about 15 minutes on this. It looked as if we could have gone much further, but our flight beckoned. It should be noted that there is probably parking for 20-30 cars, and 4-5 groups were camping. Review of: Trekking Laguna Sofia

review_text: Anyone with even a passing interest in stargazing and/or astronomy should do this tour! It's purpose built to show people round which means the telescopes aren't industrial strength but it means the whole place is set up to show the public why Chile is the best place in the world to look at the stars. Our guide had great English and knowledge of astronomy and used a laser pen to point to stars and constellations and tell us about them. Then he fired up the main telescope and let us all see the moon, Jupiter and its moons and a star cluster magnified hundreds of times which was awesome. The guide even took each of our smartphones and took a close up photo of the moon which was a great keepsake. But for me just being outside in the dead of night in the middle of nowhere looking at the Milky Way on a crystal clear night was the highlight. The tour ended with a a fascinating presentation with a film showing us how small and insignificant we are in the universe! It was truly humbling. The only downside was the size of the group, about 20-30 people. We all struggled to fit in to the main telescope observatory and it meant looking at the telescope felt rushed so they could fit everyone in within the time. Overall though a really memorable experience learning lots of new things about the night sky.

review_text: We booked our 3 day Uyuni tour from Lithium in San Pedro in April 2018 and although we were skeptical at first (due to reading lots of reviews) but after our Hostel owner recommended them, we were sure they were the best choice - and we were not disappointed. The dinner on our first day (hostel in Villamar) was lacking, but the next dinner (salt hotel in Uyuni) was better. We would recommend going with Lithium Aventura for your Uyuni tour. review_text: We recently went on the Astronomy tour in San Pedro de Atacama given by the enthusiastic!!! Jorge Corante! This is definitely an exceptional tour, if only because Jorge is so energized and excited about astronomy. First he pointed out Venus, Saturn, and Jupiter in the sky, and then he gave us a brief history of astronomy which was followed by our looking through one of his many telescopes at Jupiter. We then took a break for “snacks” which were more than snacks – hot soup, beverages, cheeses, meats, etc. It was starting to get cool so we bundled into provided blankets. Jorge then proceeded to focus his many telescopes on stars, constellations, galaxies, double stars, and the like. We would follow his voice in the dark to view the findings. He could just not stop!!! Kid in a candy store!! We got back to the hotel around 1:30 am and fortunately, did not have an early start on Monday. We can definitely recommend this tour and Jorge.

When he brought us to the President's palace, he pointed to where the tanks rolled in, snipers were stationed, and even pointed out some bullet holes that were still present from the historic event that took place there in the 70's. review_text: Los Dominicos Village is very easy to get to on the Red Line Metro- it is a very short walk from the Station. It is a very pleasant little set up, with many more shops than I was expecting. You'll find a fantastic assortment of jewelry- most of it made with Chilean stones like Lapis Lapzuli and the Flower Stone. There are shops with handcrafted leather products, wood carving (watch the carver at work), items made from local copper, clothing, bags, pottery, childrens toys. There are a couple of little cafes. There are also a couple of pet shops and a LOT of caged birds. Whilst the cages looked well cleaned and maintained, there is definitely overcrowding happening and I couldn't help feel sorry for the animals. There are no activities, as such, to do in this village. It is a great local crafts shopping experience, where you can buy from the actual artisans, but that is all.

review_text: Great day tour from Punta Arenas to see Parque Pinguino Rey (King Penguin Park) with Turismo Fin del Mundo. Overall, very good tour with informative guide Paula and driver Antonio. The guide told us information along the way and made sure we knew the schedule, stop by stop. From 7:30 am to about 9:00 pm, it was a long day with quite a bit of unnecessary driving on a small, cramped bus with one ferry ride and a lunch stop in Porvenir before getting to the penguin park. The penguin park costs 17,000 pesos for foreigners (why charge more for foreigners?) to be paid with credit card because the cashier doesn't have change. Only one hour at the penguin park--lots of cute penguins! Instead of going back the way we came, which would have cut about two hours of driving time, we drove north, took another ferry, and drove back to Punta Arenas. Unclear why the long route to get home when it could have been shorter. Enjoyable day tour, though, particularly if you are a fan of seeing king penguins and some beautiful landscape at the south end of Chile.

review_text: Mirasol, is a Local beach located in Algarrobo, specifically in an area called Mirasol too. This area is also known by the locals as "Algarrobo Norte". This IS NOT A BEACH TO SWIM!!!. But, It's a beach where you can spend all day perfectly fine. You can have a nice pic nic (please if you do so, bring back your trash; let's all take a good care of our home). OR you can walk!. From this beach walking south, in aprox 5 kms you will find Downtown Algarrobo. A place where you can eat delicious sea food, enjoy a nice cold beer, or a hot coffe, depending on your mood, and walking through the different arts & crafs galleries - "ferias artesanales" in spanish (probably a useful word to learn if you go there, because it's a good reference point). It's a quiet, but very, very beautiful place. Locals are very welcoming and you can find hostals & hotels, or you can either rent an apartment, or a house... It's up to you. Now, if you aren't much of fan of crowded places, I would recommend to visit this place during the week, or weekends that aren't hollidays. It tents to get a little packed. Oh!... I forgot to mention the BIGGEST pool in the WORLD is here!!!... on your walk from Mirasol to Downtown, you can find it in San Alfonso del Mar. (You can't get in, it's a private condo, but you can take pictures from the beach, they all look pretty good). So, Connectivity. You can get to Algarrobo from Santiago, or Valparaíso. You can take a bus (aprox $6,000 CHILEAN pesos), or you can rent a car and go there. There are plenty of ways to get around in Algarrobo; Local busses, taxies (with a fixed fare-black ones- , and with fares that varies depending on the time...these are known as "colectivos", and are yellow). So, again, if you ever have the chance to run away from Santiago, or just feel in the mood to disconnect yourself and going to the beach, Algarrobo is BY FAR the place to go. Only an hour 15 mins away from Santiago (or 90 mins bus ride) and you can find peacefulness and amazing views.

A place where you can eat delicious sea food, enjoy a nice cold beer, or a hot coffe, depending on your mood, and walking through the different arts & crafs galleries - "ferias artesanales" in spanish (probably a useful word to learn if you go there, because it's a good reference point). It's a quiet, but very, very beautiful place. Locals are very welcoming and you can find hostals & hotels, or you can either rent an apartment, or a house... It's up to you. Now, if you aren't much of fan of crowded places, I would recommend to visit this place during the week, or weekends that aren't hollidays. It tents to get a little packed. Oh!... I forgot to mention the BIGGEST pool in the WORLD is here!!!... on your walk from Mirasol to Downtown, you can find it in San Alfonso del Mar. (You can't get in, it's a private condo, but you can take pictures from the beach, they all look pretty good). So, Connectivity. You can get to Algarrobo from Santiago, or Valparaíso. You can take a bus (aprox $6,000 CHILEAN pesos), or you can rent a car and go there. There are plenty of ways to get around in Algarrobo; Local busses, taxies (with a fixed fare-black ones- , and with fares that varies depending on the time...these are known as "colectivos", and are yellow). So, again, if you ever have the chance to run away from Santiago, or just feel in the mood to disconnect yourself and going to the beach, Algarrobo is BY FAR the place to go. Only an hour 15 mins away from Santiago (or 90 mins bus ride) and you can find peacefulness and amazing views.

review_text: We had a wonderful experience with Tours 4 Tips in Chile. A great way to see the city from a local's point of view and get to know more about the people than just the famous sights. Our first time was in Valparaiso with Camilo for a guide, he was excellent and very enthusiastic, great explanations and tips for more places to visit ourselves plus things to eat and try while in Chile. During the tour he also paid for our transport on the trolleybus and elevator plus we were offered free alfajores tasting and drinks at the end. All in all fantastic service for something that has not got a fixed price nor any obligations, but after such a great time there's no way you wouldn't tip! Also this time at the end the group got all together toasting with a terremoto (local drink), great atmosphere. After two great tours we decided to do also the third one offered, which is the Santiago Highlights at 3pm. This time I must say we were a little disappointed compared to the other two. I didn't feel there was anywhere near as much enthusiasm coming from the guide, nor that the itinerary itself was as interesting as the other two. Nor did it feel the guide had gone the extra mile to give us a great service, I mean it's not all about getting free drinks etc. But it's those little unexpected attentions that make for an even more special experience. My suggestion would be if you're going to do all three tours, start with Santiago highlights so it's just gonna get better.

review_text: On my trip to Santiago I was reviewing the various options for winery tours. Generally, unless you wanted to rent a car, the tours involved van transportation to and from the winery and ran in the range of 50,000 CLP and up. Then the tour itself only costs 6,000 CLP and you get to keep a souvenir wine glass. The tour is offered in both english and spanish by very knowledgeable guides. I've been on many brewery and winery tours where the guides are actors hired to put on a show and do not know a whole lot about the process or the product. My guide at the Cousino Macul winery, on the other hand, was a certified somellier who knew all the ins and outs of the production process. It was a fantastic tour around a beautiful facility.

review_text: The Resort is not very luxurious, the rooms are neither too large nor too sophisticated but are comfortable and quiet. The bathroom is tight and has no heated floor. Hotel offers all the essential services for skiing and it is possible to rent or buy equipment. The slopes are wide and well ⁇ ined. The lifting means (telecoms, gondola and others) are slow compared to Europe and the USA, which is good for those who need to rest between descents, but bad for those who want to enjoy the day to the fullest. I imagine that those who go skiing for the first time should be quite lost: the hotel does not offer a concierge or something like that to guide those who do not have experience and do not know Things to do or where to go to rent equipment or hire instructors. There are good ski instructors, even for beginner children and adults. It is not very cheap to hire them: $60 to $75 per hour, depending on how many hours you hire, but they offer good service. The restaurants of the hotel left a little to be desired, except the French, which is comfortable, has good service and good menu. The 2 bars (who doesn't like a drink after skiing?) do not meet the demand and often do not find a place to sit. The service also needs to be improved: it is too time-consuming, the attendants are not very cordial and do not realize when we call them. More than once we wait for the drinks until (20 or 25 minutes later) the drinks are delivered along with the food. It was not possible to transfer the bill in the room (I do not know if it is always so, but I had to pay at the bar every time), which forced us to go out to ski with a credit card to be able to go straight to the bar afterwards. The hotel is not very accessible: it has many stairs and those with locomotion problems will have difficulty to move around. Despite the downsides, I think it is a great place to stay when the goal is to ski in June/July/August.

review_text: We, my parents and I, contacted Ecotours Chile for services while staying 5 days in Santiago. Cristian Cosignani, the owner, recommended excursions and hotel accommodations for our stay. Lots of restaurants, small shoppings and a very safe neighborhood. We chose a half day city tour for the first day, and visited several points of interest. In the end, we visited a fantastic lapis lazuli store, and Cerro San Cristobal with its fantastic view. Beautiful and friendly Santiago. On the next day, we went on a full day tour to Valparaiso and Viña del Mar. We had lunch in a beautiful seafood restaurant , just like a castle in front of the sea, and celebrated my father´s 78th birthday. Gorgeous views and sceneries. Another day we went to the Maipo Valley and visited Concha y Toro winery. On our way, we visited a local place to eat empanadas and enjoy a glass of wine. Later, we enjoyed lunch in a local restaurant, with music and good food. Very good picks !!

review_text: Siempre Verde made our visit to Chiloe absolutely perfect. My wife and I traveled with our children (ages 5 and 8). Rather than rent a car, we contracted with Siempre Verde to pick us up and return us to the airport in Puerto Montt, as well as arrange for two days of tours. Jose was right on time when we arrived, and on the way to Castro (after crossing on the ferry to the island) we stopped for a delicious lunch in Ancud with beautiful views of the . In Castro we stayed in a palafito (recommended by Jose). He picked us up promptly at 10 am the following day, and we spent the middle part of the day hiking in the national park, followed by a delicious late lunch of empanadas and cazuela at a restaurant on the road back to Castro. On day 3, Jose again picked us up promptly and took us on a memorable tour of Isla Quinchao, followed by lunch on the wharf in Dalcahue. We spent some time in the feria artesanal and then let the kids play in a playground across the street from the city's main wooden church (currently under renovation). We then returned to Castro, where we toured the very beautiful cathedral in the main square, then we took a boat tour of the Castro fjord. After Jose dropped us back at the palafito, we dined in a seafood restaurant (Octavio's} right on the water (recommended by Jose). As Jose had forewarned us, the food was great, but the service was slow. However, since we were in no hurry whatsoever, this was not an issue. Jose's knowledge of the island's history, its flora and fauna (especially its birds) was extensive. He speaks English very well and has a very tender way with kids. Jose travels armed with binoculars, birding books and snacks, so whatever contingency arises, he's well-prepared. You would be hard pressed to find a better guide for your visit to Chiloe.

review_text: We did this trip before Perito Moreno glacier and overall liked it better. Reason is because of the different shapes and colours in the ice, rather than the rather cliff edge style of Moreno. But you can't get out and walk and there is no viewing from the land as you find at Moreno. Might be that whichever you see first, you prefer. Warnings about the walk to the boat are to be heeded, though. You can get a courtesy bus from the hotel if you book there, but you still have a couple of km on foot, first over a very bouncy suspension bridge over a wide and rapid river, then the shingle spit, which is well over 1km long. Going it is OK because the wind is behind you, but coming back you face a slog into a wind typically up to 100kph. That and walking on loose shingle is a bit of a test, but exhilarating. We took the path up the island to the viewpoint before starting back and that is lovely, but again, very windy. You can't go all the way round the island because path on the other side seems to be out.

review_text: If you have a bit of patience and want to save a lot of money! I followed the very good review of 'Corderio' from 16th June 2014'. His instructions were so so simple!! I'm not a big wine fan...infact I rarely drink it..but this tour was amazing as I learnt so much about the different varieties etc. I'm not there for the wine so it's a skewed review I suppose ? MY wife drinks wine and she wanted to go to at least one winery. We decided Undurraga over the other main stream ones. The day before, just book your tour with an English speaking guide : http://www.undurraga.cl/ It's just an email, very simple and quick reply. Getting there allow just over an hour to be safe...we JUST got there 5 min late and it was ok. -Take the train to Estación Central. You will need a Bip! card if you haven't gotten one. Easy to do at the station. The train network is really easy to figure out. -From there walk to the shopping centre and through the shopping centre towards San Borja which is the bus terminal station. It's about a 5 min walk in the really large mall. -Take the no. 75 bus to Talagante. However, ask the bus driver 'Undurraga?' and they will direct you to which no. 75 bus it is (there were 4 when we were there...they must take different routes). -From there about 30-40 min bus ride..try to sit at the front to tell the bus driver..I just had google maps open so I knew when it was coming up. -The bus stop is right outside Undurraga....couldn't be easier. Go in to reception and find your guide. -To come back is a bit of a drama...the bus stop is on the other side but the buses may be full and you may have to wait about 20 min until one comes that's empty. Most people get off after 15 min in so you'll get a seat afterwards. -Drops you off just outside that mall and you can make your way to the station or food court as we did to grab a bite to eat. So the bus costs 1000 Chilean peso's each way and the tour 8000 Chilean pesos...so compared to all those organised tours...you get the same out of this. You just pay for transport the other way. The guide was very informative, we only had 3 people in our tour so could ask a lot of questions. I was amazed at how he talked about the different types of grapes etc which ones do well and why. How they store and create the wines. There is some wine tasting at the end of 3 or 4 wines and you can purchase more at the gift shop. It's nice of them to give you the wine glasses in a nice box to take with you as a gift. By the way, there is no food available there, we were hoping to have lunch there so don't make that same mistake. No restaurant

review_text: La Arena Cove (Caleta La Arena) is located 45 kilometers south of Puerto Montt, Chile. The small town is near the entrance to the Reloncavi Estuary and although the population is small there are several restaurants and a tiny yellow church. Ferries link La Arena with Puelche Cove to continue on Route 7 to the town of Hornopirén. The trip takes about 40 minutes offering wonderful views to the wooded coast and this beautiful fjord. This is a section of Route 7, known as Carretera Austral (Southern Way) which runs about 1,240 kilometers through the Chilean Patagonia. This is a really wonderful place. Make sure to visit if you come to the Puerto Montt area, Los Lagos Region, Chile.

review_text: Santiago seems to be a city where Arts and Culture find ready patronage amongst its residents- and what better way to experience this than the Municipal Theatre of Santiago, which is well known for its historic lineage, having been built in the 19th century, before being almost completely destroyed in a fire, then an earthquake, and then again in a second fire, before being rebuilt and modernised in the 1970s. The theatre retains its old world charm, which in a way, is it’s main problem as well, with narrow passages between rows and tiny seats, even in the more expensive seating areas. But the over hanging box seats, the opulently designed roof, the statues in the hall, with wine being served... they all are an experience to cherish. Tickets are very reasonable- I managed to get the Second row seats for a concert (Amengual/Penderecki/Brahms, with Luis Alberto Latorre of the Chilean Symphony Orchestra on the Piano and conducted by Maximiano Valdes) for about 40 USD, a couple of days in advance. The theatre is easily accessible by metro - the nearest station, Santa Lucia, is about 7-8 mins walk. The acoustics are expectedly wonderful, and I would strongly recommend box seats for a better view. All in all, I had a very entertaining and memorable experience.

review_text: Rather than crossing the river as in the past, the new trail stays on the east side of the river the entire trip. To get around the sections where the river is against the east bank, the trail goes up through the forest in two short sections--these include some big steps, a few steep 2-m vertical sections of slippery sand and mud, and lots of roots. Overall the trail is very easy but farily long; we took 7 hours including some fairly long breaks. The unmarked trailhead is a few right of the restroom in the Ventisquiero Campground and the trail begins with a few stone steps. We enjoyed the views and seeing the raw landscape of the glacier, the icefield above, the trees (coihue_) killed by the 2008 eruption, and the many landslides caused by earthquakes. Recommended.

review_text: This was a very interesting experience - to ride local buses, see the local food market, see an old restored house in the city where the kitchen is and to participate in some cooking, as well as a generous meal with drinks. This was less participatory in some ways than other classes we have taken. The chef had to move through the market quickly to buy food, for example, and was a bit too busy to be 'touring the market' with us. Similarly, with the cooking, the chef did a good deal of the cooking without us seeing or participating, though we did a lot of preparatory chopping of vegetables etc. The dynamics of deciding what dishes to prepare were a bit complex - the guests participating had to come to a consensus among themselves, which was awkward at times. It might be better to have the chef indicate what was being cooked that day, taking into account some alternatives if some guests had food allergies etc. But at the end of the day, this was a very valuable window into Chilean cooking, food preferences and the like. review_text: My friends and I traveled to Chile for the new year spending the actual New Year in Vina before heading down to Puerto Arena. We caught a 1.30AM flight out of Santiago arriving in the Punta Arenas early in the AM. We had already reserved the 2.5 hour bus ride to Puerto Natales, and basically slept in the lobby with a bunch of other backpackers awaiting the first bus at 7AM. We bought our tickets ahead of time with and it was nice b'c you could pick your seat! We arrived at the bus deport on time and checked into our hostel for the night to prepare for the trek the next morning. It was nice to have the full day, to get equipment we were missing, check tents, get food, and make sure we had enough cash to pay for everything in the park (entrance fees, catamaran). We stayed at erratic rock, and also attended the information session they do every day at 3pm. Def informative and gives you a good background, esp if you hadn't already done your research. They recommended we buy our bus tickets to the park ahead of time, b'c in the crowded season they were selling out. If you miss the early bus (7.30AM it will mess with the rest of your schedule esp if you are doing west to east and also need to catch the catamaran). You can buy them online, or at some of the hostels. Day 1: We arrived at the entrance to the park along with what seemed to be about 50 other buses. It took about and hour and a half to buy entrance tickets, receive map and watch short video. B'c we were hiking west to eat, we had to take another 35-40 min bus ride to the catamaran site. We ended up missing the 11:00 clock catamaran b'c it was too full. We waited about and hour and half and were able to get on the next one. (Please note they don't always run and extra catamaran, but it was crowded so they decided to do so. Otherwise we would have had to wait until 2pm) . You pay the entrance to the catamaran on the boat. When you arrive an Paine Grande you would have option to stay there at the Refugio or continue hiking with your pack. We had reservations to camp at Grey and so we continued up the path. There is a ranger at that station checking your reservations. We had them, so it wasn't an issue, but I think it all depends on the ranger and how you approach the situation. They are def attempting to limit the ppl on the trails though. The hike is supposed to take 3.5 hour, took us about 5 (11KM). We had some ppl with injuries and the weather was not in our favor day 1. We finally arrived at Grey, and being we were one of the last larger groups there, we had to set up camp in the middle of open field. Tip- take your time on trails, but get up early and make it to campsites early. Day 2: We slept in a bit and headed out on the trail around 11.30AM. (There are some trails to go up and get a close view of Glacier Grey, if you have time some of the pictures I saw were incredible). Going back it took about 4 hours with stops for us to arrive back at Refugio Grey. We took a short break there as they have a place to purchase food and a beer if you like. We parted ways with some of our friends that had injuries. They took the last catamaran back to wait for us at Camp Central. The rest of the group continued on the trek to Camp Italiano. It was about another 7.5 KM and 2 1/2 hrs but much easier than the hike to and from Camp Grey. The scenery is beautiful and even taking our time we were able to make it in just short of 3 hours. Camp Italiano is a very primitive camping site. There is no running water, electricity, or amenities other than a place to put your tent. They have a small shelter where you can cook and a river right next to the campsite for water source. It is def chilly in the campsite as you are so close to water and hidden under a bed of trees, and the ground can be a bit wet. If you can fit a tarp in your tent bag, its a good thing to have. Again we arrived late and there wasn't much space. We ended up behind the latrines, and yes it smelled! If you arrive at camp early enough you can take a short hike over to Domo Frances and get hot food and possibly sneak in a shower! Day 2: We got up early as we took an hour hike up to see Glacier Frances. The hike is uphill the whole way, but with out the packs not too bad. We got back and started off on what was to be the longest day, hiking to Camp Central to meet the rest of our group. It would have been about 16 1/2 KM and about 7 hours with no stops. Unfortunately we didn't make it. We stopped at Cuernos (2 1/2 hrs) to get a bite to eat and a beer. We enjoyed it so much we spent a little too much time there and the 4 1/2 hours we had ahead of us seemed to be too much. Fortunately for us, the front desk was very helpful, and they quickly changed our reservations from Central to Cuernos for the night! Hot showers, food and a shelter to cook in was a great treat after Italiano. We camped on the floor vs a platform as those were all taken, however it ended up working in our favor. There was a terrible wind storm out there and ppl who had no barrier to their tents (aka trees/ forest) and were sitting on platform got their tents shredded to pieces. Many ppl ended up sleeping in the cooking area that night and were left without a tent. Day4: We got up early and started our 4 1/2 hour hike to central. The scenery was stunning and although there were some steep hills, the majority of the hike wasn't too bad. We made it in about 5 hours and set up camp with out friends who were patiently awaiting our arrival. We treated ourselves to a delicious meal at the hotel and some drinks! We then decided to relax for a couple of hours before we started our night hike to the Torres. (Originally we would have spent 1 night in Central, then hiked up to the Torres campsite with our packs to see the sunrise and be only an hour away. However b'c of our stop at Cuernos, we chose instead to stay another night at central, leave our packs and hike up at night to get to Torres by sunrise). We started our hike around 10.30 to ensure we had more than enough time to get up there. The hike takes about 4.5hrs, but in the pitch black dark, you never know! Leaving our bags behind ended up being a blessing as much of the trail is straight up hill. We brought some food layers and our sleeping bag, which was much lighter. The trail is marked fairly well, although we did loose it a couple of times and had to backtrack. Just make sure you are always looking for the trail markers, esp at night. Once we finally reached the Torres and our body temperatures cooled down, it was freezing! Sleeping bag was a savoir up there waiting for the sun to rise. In the end it was all worth it! Breathtaking! We then hiked the 4.5 hrs back to Central. We arrived to camp around 10 AM, 12 hours later! It was enough time to shower, eat and get on the 2'oclock bus out of the park. Overall it was a fantastic experience and can def test your limits at times. Just go with an open mind and realize things don't have to go exactly as planned and still be a great experience. Direct Message me if you have any further questions!

Many ppl ended up sleeping in the cooking area that night and were left without a tent. Day4: We got up early and started our 4 1/2 hour hike to central. The scenery was stunning and although there were some steep hills, the majority of the hike wasn't too bad. We made it in about 5 hours and set up camp with out friends who were patiently awaiting our arrival. We treated ourselves to a delicious meal at the hotel and some drinks! We then decided to relax for a couple of hours before we started our night hike to the Torres. (Originally we would have spent 1 night in Central, then hiked up to the Torres campsite with our packs to see the sunrise and be only an hour away. However b'c of our stop at Cuernos, we chose instead to stay another night at central, leave our packs and hike up at night to get to Torres by sunrise). We started our hike around 10.30 to ensure we had more than enough time to get up there. The hike takes about 4.5hrs, but in the pitch black dark, you never know! Leaving our bags behind ended up being a blessing as much of the trail is straight up hill. We brought some food layers and our sleeping bag, which was much lighter. The trail is marked fairly well, although we did loose it a couple of times and had to backtrack. Just make sure you are always looking for the trail markers, esp at night. Once we finally reached the Torres and our body temperatures cooled down, it was freezing! Sleeping bag was a savoir up there waiting for the sun to rise. In the end it was all worth it! Breathtaking! We then hiked the 4.5 hrs back to Central. We arrived to camp around 10 AM, 12 hours later! It was enough time to shower, eat and get on the 2'oclock bus out of the park. Overall it was a fantastic experience and can def test your limits at times. Just go with an open mind and realize things don't have to go exactly as planned and still be a great experience.
