review_text: I do not recommend this trip. We arrived at the company office at 6:00 AM as requested. People arrived until 8:00 when we finally departed on our bus to a location 45 minutes out of town, where we entered our small catamaran to travel the 45 minutes to Isla Magdalena, ostensibly to see penguins in their "natural" habitat. The small island was comprised of a roped path around the island where we observed hundreds of penguins cowering in their holes, probably as frightened from our presence as from the blowing wind and rain. After 45 minutes of admittedly interesting observation of these molting, dung covered creatures, we returned to our boat for a twenty minute failed effort to reach another island to observe sea lions (wind and waves too rough), and a 40 minute ride back to the shore, where we caught our bus back to town. So...if you want to ride in a bus and boat for three hours to see a few penguins for 45 minutes, hop aboard. Otherwise, save your money for a trip to Antarctica, or take your grandchild to see "frozen" again.

review_text: We did the tour to the lagoon with no hike. Communication prior to the tour was poor leaving questions unanswered or mis-information. Pick up of all passengers at various hotels was quick and efficent. Two bano stops on route and a stop at San Jose Plaza de Armas. A few photo stops on route. Our guide Andres was excellent and highly informative. Our driver was respectful and polite. Once at the lagoon at 12 we were given 1 hour to do as we pleased. A box lunch with wine, juice or water was provided. We took our lunch to the edge of the lagoon. Dress warm as it is cool there with plenty of wind. If you wish to walk to the water wear hiking boots. Long drive for 1 hour of lagoon scenery but this is an individual choice. review_text: I visited the lakes in August, 2014 and the scenery there was great. Though they are located high at 4200 meters high, I took a pill for altitude sickness before I went there and I was fine. The guide told us drinking water also helps as it contains oxygen. I went with the travel agency called Vive Atacama, with the very friendly driver Freddy and and the guide Jimena, who loves nature and is really passionate in her work. She gave detailed introduction about the places in the minibus before we got there, and left us some quiet time to enjoy the view. On the way there the guide spotted a fox. Some vicugnas were drinking water by the lake. It is a serene place and I really want to stay there longer.

review_text: I was first a bit sceptical as the winery seemed very close to the city center of Santiago. But I am glad we still went. The Cousiño winery has a great history to tell and was founded when Santiago was still a bit smaller. Nowadays they own another vineyard outside the city. Our tour was in English and our guide even spoke some German. He was very knowledgeable and did a great job on explaining the history of the vineyard as well as talking about the process of making wine in the past and in our time. At the end you get to taste some wine and we could even take the wine glass with the Cousiño emblem home, a great gift. It's easy to reach. For us it was a 40 minute metro ride and then a 3 minute UBER/taxi ride (or you take a bus it you walk 30 minutes). We totally recommend it!

review_text: We decided to self-drive and left our hotel at 4:45am with the sunrise scheduled for 6:38am. The drive is mostly straightforward and can be done with a regular sedan, even though there are a couple of fairly steep climbs. There are a couple of forks and all but one have visible signs that direct you to El Tatio. At the fork to Baños de Puritama, however the sign is not visible from the angle you are coming and most drivers will follow the road along to the right. That is wrong and a long detour! My advice is to download a map for this area in google maps and use it offline. Be aware that you are going from 2400m above sea level to 4200m. The lower air pressure at 4200m will exhaust you quicker than in San Pedro de Atacama. We did the drive in late November and it was around freezing at El Tatio before sunrise, while it was 45 F in San Pedro de Atacama. We arrived at 6:15am and the geyser field was only visible a few minutes before we arrived. We actually saw the sun about 25min after the official sunrise, because it had to get above the mountains that encircle the geyser basin. Most tour buses appeared to arrive at around 6:50am. Interestingly, the geysers fume output appeared to triple or quadruple for maybe 15min starting shortly before the sun peeked over the mountains. After those 15min, the output was back to how it was when we arrived before sunrise. I have been to Yellowstone and the geysers in Iceland, and I can say that El Tatio is different - the geysers are constantly fuming or erupting (hot water is spilled maybe 1ft to max. 2ft high) and not erupting on some schedule - and I think it is definitely worth seeing them. If you don't want to get up super early, then don't hesitate to go there later in the day. After sunrise, the temperature quickly rose to above 50F, which is much more bearable but still cool. Admission was 20,000 Pesos per person. There is also a warm pool where you can swim. The pool is fed by 2 small hot springs which heat the water to only luke warm temperatures. So, don't expect a nice warm or hot pool. Some changing cabins are near the pool. Long story short: I consider El Tatio a must-see.

review_text: We met our guide in the lobby of our hotel in the morning and proceeded north, out of Santiago and into the countryside of some of Chile's prime agricultural land. It was interesting to have a glimpse of how the growers work the fields (we're interested in that sort of thing). Our first stop was in a town called Llay Llay; a native phrase meaning "Big Wind." We visited the Quintessence Alpaca farm where we saw Alpacas and the process from wool to garments. Next, we drove over to the coast to see penguins. This would have been extremely interesting if we hadn't just completed a cruise to Antarctica and the Falkland Islands, where we observed penguins mere feet away. Still, it was fun to see a different kind of penguin, and it was especially fascinating to see the Pacific coastline. We couldn't help thinking how much like California the coast looked. We walked along a trail by the rocky shore for a bit and took in some scenery. Finally, we had reservations at a seaside restaurant for lunch. Our seating was outside where we could see divers harvesting clams as we had lunch. Below, we marked this tour as for couples because TripAdvisor only allows one box to be checked, but the truth is, this tour was suited for everyone, in pretty much every combination. The restaurant was a bit sophisticated for very young children (we didn't see any Happy Meals and Mac & Cheese on the menu), but still doable. review_text: “The story of Chico Mineiro and his faithful leader Edgar: After a day of hard work and intense cold, go down the Chico Mineiro and Edgar mountains. The van is full of adventurous tourists, but Chico and Edgar face the mountain range’s biggest challenge “The tourist who bought his driver’s license and rented a car”. Facing the eyes of the beast, in the steep and narrow passage that would lead them towards the happy destiny, Chico and Edgar have the growing fear that that tourist imbued with perverse intentions, will not cooperate by crashing along the narrow road and climbing the snow, which precedes the fall to the endless precipice, tries to pass through the van and continue towards his dark fado. Chico goes off the van while Edgar struggles behind the wheel, the battle will be intense, and this becomes evident when the driver slides with the car over the ice that covers the road and the passage is closed. Chico, imbued with heavenly powers, holds Van with his hands and avoids the fatal collision, but not for long because as if he challenged fate, the perverse tourist speeds and gets trapped between the van and the precipice! The traffic accumulates, and the two vehicles block the road, NONE BACK AND NONE UP, there are two options left: push the tourist's car slope down, or Edgar miraculously drag the van through the opposite snow wall and get rid of the demonic car. Here the adventurous tourists come down from the Van, and against all the hypotheses of fate they push the car, not towards the precipice, but towards the road, liberating the Van from its deadly enemy. The price paid for this courageous effort was an enormous scar left in Van's bakery. ⁇ Eyewitnesses saw the moment a police officer pulled out his pen and noted the data of the unregulated driver, muting the same. Chico Miner and Edgar were finally free to guide their troupe to a new adventure! After all, it was just another day of work in the Mountains. Legend has it that the driver of the car is still in the mountains, trying to climb the 56 curves.” Thank you for the adventure friends! Who is wondering if it is worth renting a car to climb the mountains, not worth it! Agenda with Chico miner and Edgar!

review_text: We went with Politur agency in Pucon, with guides Guido (Swiss) and Juanito (Chilean). They were very professional and a perfect combination of pushing us to get to the top while allowing us the occasional rest. Most equipment was provided - you just have to bring your lunch, sunglasses and sunscreen. We had a beautiful, clear day, but it was very windy, which prevented us from taking the chairlift. This added a significant amount of time to the hike - it was seven hours hiking up and two hours sliding down on either small plastic discs or your butt - depending on the steepness of the slope. Our group was small, just four climbers and two guides. We would highly recommend this trip, it provides you with a great sense of accomplishment. And they give you a beer back at the shop when you're done to celebrate. Cost was about 42,000 CLP per person

review_text: This is a fairly small museum, run by the local university. It has 2 parts, one mostly detailing the culture of the different tribes that populated this area throughout history, showing well preserved objects such as ceramics and tools. There is a decent amount of information, but only in Spanish. The objects are well presented. In the second part the focus is on the mummification proces and tools used, as well as the mummies themselves (some are naturally mummified, others went clearly through an elaborate process). In this culture, even fetuses en new born were mummified, unlike in ancient Egypt, where only the very rich could afford mummification after dead.

review_text: We were in Antofagasta for work and had an extra free day. We heard about “Hand of the Desert” and thought that we should see it since there seemed nothing much to do here. We were lucky to find Ruhiscos Travel. Maglio from Ruhiscos was our tour guide. He picked us up from our hotel in a comfortable van, and dropped us back at the end of the tour. We bought a half-day tour to see Hand of the Desert, but the tour included visits to the other top 3 popular tourist attractions of Antofagasta which are the Tropic of Capricorn monument, La Portada, and the National Historical Monument Huanchaca. At each place, Maglio provided detailed, interesting commentary. We impressed with a big hand sculpture popping up in the middle of the desert, a must-see site for visitors. But we also liked our visit to La Portada, the sea rock formation in the ocean. We also learned a lot about the history of Antofagasta and Chile at the Huanchaca museum. This tour covered high spots in Antofagasta and let us see the other side of Antofagasta besides the beautiful ocean. Maglio can provide tours in both Spanish and English. We highly recommended Ruhiscos for your Antofagasta tour.

review_text: My friend and I did the Santiago wine tasting in Barrio Italia at the start of our trip and the Colchagua Valley Wine Tour at the end of the trip. Both were wonderful. The Santiago wine tasting was at the Uncorked Wine House in Barrio Italia. We tasted 5 wines and had some lovely cheeses, bread, and nuts to accompany the wine. Jose led the tasting and was very friendly and knowledgeable. You can buy the wines there if you find one you like so you don't have to find a wine store in Santiago. The tasting lasted about 90 minutes. The Colchagua Valley Wine Tour was a full day. We left our hotel just before 8 am and returned around 7 pm. We visited three wineries. My friend and I loved Clos de Apalta and Neyen - the hosts and scenery were were terrific. Viu Manet was a bit more commercial and felt less personal for the tastings but the restaurant there served a fantastic lunch. This is actually my second experience with Uncorked - I did a cooking class with the company last year. Because I enjoyed that experience so much, I didn't hesitate to book these wine experiences with them. I was not disappointed! Review of: Best Wine Tasting in Santiago

review_text: I was here just last night and I still can't stop thinking how awesome it was. Was originally booked to go to mamalluca observatory but after a cancellation by the office and reading the reviews I figured I would not have enjoyed it anyway.. Mamalluca tours consist of at least 50 people, the guides are just that, tour guides - they are not astronomers. You spend more time watching videos than observing.. A lot of kids and a lot of queuing. A very weak telescope as well that won't allow you to see anything interesting.. HOWEVER, the observatorio del pangue on the other hand consists of small groups of only 10 people. The guides are true astronomers that have a huge depth of knowledge and explain everything so well.. Its a very cosy environment and you feel welcomed to ask questions and converse. Most importantly, you spend the entire time observing the stars and then looking at beautiful nebula's, a super nova, far distant galaxies and the remnants of an exploded star (supernova).. My wife and I opted for the English tour and our astronomer Eric spoke perfect English.. He made sure everyone got to see every object through the telescope spending a good few minutes on each object. There was no rushing you could spend as long as you wanted looking through the (big) powerful telescope.. Our group was only 5 people and everyone was so friendly. On this rare occasion because of the cloud cover on the previous night it was moved over to tonight. The group was originally around 12 people and they split it up into two groups. That's how seriously these guys take the importance of your experience. And on this rare occasion we were allowed to use the telescope that wasnt for the tourists because of the group being split into two. A bit more powerful but manually operated..Eric showed us how to move it around and use it which was super easy and honestly it made the experience for me even better.. If you're serious about seeing the beautiful night sky, want a tour that is not rushed, want to be able to see the most beautiful things the cosmos has to offer, want the most polite, friendly and knowledgeable astronomers to teach and show you the cosmos then this is the tour for you.. It costs more than mamalluca but it is worth so much more and it's true value for money.. To everyone at the observatory and Eric, thank you so much for such a magical experience.

review_text: We booked with Chile Nativo and I was nervous about it in the beginning as I couldn't find much information on them prior to booking. After doing the 5-day W Trek in Patagonia with them, I highly recommend them and understand why there's not too much info on them. Chile Nativo has been around for over 10 (maybe even 15) years. It started off as a small operator and I think they've grown their presence and team more in the last year or so. We actually got connected to Chile Nativo through Swoop Patagonia, which has a bigger marketing presence and are basically third party sales agents. Swoop Patagonia is based in the UK and I guess have their own operations or other vendors they use as well depending on what tour package you do. Anyway we booked this trip back in May 2018 to do the W trek in early Nov. We had an amazing time and were well taken cared of. Communication prior to the trip was generally pretty good, though sometimes I had to follow up with them first if I hadn't heard from them as the trip approached or if someone didn't get back to me on something. But overall they were very responsive. We were a larger group than normal (10 guests) so we had two guides, Pelin and Fernando. Both were super amazing at their job. They made us feel very comfortable, answered all our questions, were very patient with us during the trek, and looked after all our needs. Felt like friends as well as teachers. One of the reasons why we booked so early is because we didn't want to be stuck tenting outside at the refugios or deal with the refugio bookings which sound like it's getting more complicated! Anyway while my group of 4 had beds at every refugio, there were a couple of guests who booked closer to Nov. who had to sleep in tents outside due to no more room. Luckily one of the nights we also got to switch refugios from the one most people dreaded (Domo Frances) to Los Cuernos, as they had room and could take us. So, you never know what you might get. We were also super lucky with the weather! I really braced myself for awful rain and windy Patagonia weather but we had three straight days of sun and no wind, which is rare! On the fourth day it was pretty windy and drizzly but still not too bad. The hike from east to west was good, as we got the hardest part of the hike over and done with on the first day (Blue Towers) and we were going without the sun in our eyes for the most part. The food provided by Chile Nativo on the first day was SO GOOD too. The rest of the packed lunches are provided by the refugios and some were better than others. We made all the hikes in good time and got to relax after a long day. I really don't know how the guides have the energy to do back to back trekking hikes (one of them started all over again right when we got back to Puerto Natales!) but they were lovely and had great energy and if they were ever tired or irritated they never showed it. You can tell they really love what they do. I would highly recommend booking with them; they really try to address all your concerns and find alternative suggestions if something doesn't pan out due to the weather (some side activities got canceled). The refugios we stayed at included Torres Central, Los Cuernos (but it was supposed to be Domo Frances, which I'm glad we did not stay at based on reviews!), Paine Grande, and Grey. We'll let Pelin and Fernando know of your kind words. Chile Nativo is actually 17 years old, but it did start as a small tour operator with few trips per season, and started to grow in presence over the last 5 years approximately. =) Hope to welcome you or any friend of yours into Patagonia in the future. Kind regards, Chile Nativo Team

review_text: I've been in this city many times,and always has something new to show me. Constitución is 5 hours by bus from Santiago, you can find a bus in the bus terminal in Santiago (Universidad de santiago metro station) . The price of the ticket is around 10.000 CLP TO 16.000 CLP one way depending on the bus agency. This small city in the coast of the Maule Region has many enchantments, it has nice beaches cover by black and thick sand, the waves are nice so here you will find some surf and body activities. This city has a nature national monument which is La piedra de la Iglesia , and also has another famous stone named as Arco de los enamorados. Cerro Mutrún is a popular spot for the locals, here some parties are done in summer , and also is famous because there were a tribute in honor to some deceased people who died in the earthquake of 2010.In this place you must have a camera , there is an excelent view ! Some other attractions are kayaking through the Maule river, visit the market in the harbor which is really popular because the fresh fish.To get to the market you travel trough the costanera which also has a spectacular view of the ocean. If you decide to go to the other side and to discover the green areas you have the way to putú , this path is cover by green fields and forest. Also there is a road beside the maule river ,which also is full of green and here you pass by the Puente ferroviario Bancos de Arena( built by Eiffel). I also want to recommend a place which owns of a relative, Aqua perfect gym is located going to Putú and is an excellent place to enjoy with the family and friends, has pools, games,music, barbecue spots, and they sell snacks. You can get to the place by bus or by car. The weather is cold mostly all year, it has lot of wind , summer is nice weather but at night is cold. The principal square has a lot of night life for everybody, kids,youth and adults , in summer there is always a little amusement park ,other games a handicraft market. Also the shore is cover by many pubs and discotheques.

review_text: Coquimbo’s Cruz Del Tercer Milenio, Third Millenium Cross, was built to commemorate the birth of Christ over 2000 years ago and was blessed by the Pope John Paul II. Construction began in 1999 and was completed in 2021. The cross is made of concrete and is 272-feet high and 131-feet wide and sits on the El Vigia Hill. Besides being taller than Rio de Jannero’s Christ the Redeemer statue, it is one of the largest crosses in the world. Designed by architect Gabriel Guarda, the base has three pillars that form a tripod, a reference to the Holy Trinity. There is a 2,000-step staircase or use an elevator to have a remarkable 360 ° panoramic view of all Coquimbo, its bay, and the Pacific Ocean.

We drank the Pisco sour and two wines, a white and a red, while we were cooking and eating. I would highly recommend the class.

review_text: Just got off the bus from the panoramic trip. Lucked out with a wonderful guide, Viviana. She could work as a simultaneous translator at the UN! review_text: This tour was one of the highlights of our trip to Chile! It was my wife and I as well as our two sons, ages 14 & 11, as well as my son’s friend, also age 14. The waves were predicted to be too rough on day we originally had scheduled our tour. He was very flexible and seemed to get joy from us having a nice experience:-) Transportation was solid to/from our Airbnb in Valparaiso. The boat was just big enough for our group of 5 plus our tour guide. It was so cool to see penguins for the first time in their natural environment! Our boat captain was Juan, who seemed very experienced. After our boat ride, we walked around areas where we saw cool plants, some of which we had never seen before as we are from the US. Though not deserted, we were surprised that our tour areas were not overcrowded with tourists, which was nice. On the way back, we stopped at a place where we had the best empanadas I’ve ever had! Highly recommended! Tip: we had two members of our party who sometimes get seasick. If this is you, I recommend taking some of the seasickness medication medication before you get on the boat. We are only on the boat about a 30 minutes. Review of: Penguins Watching Navigation Cachagua Island&Lunch From VALPARAIS Hello Ivan and family. We are very happy that the entire excursion was excellent considering that we had to make changes for navigation due to the natural conditions that we cannot handle in our company, and you were able to be available when we saw better conditions and above all for safety, which is the most important thing on these excursions. We are grateful for your reservation and we will continue to improve our services. regards

review_text: Salar de Uyuni Even though the service at the agency itself was excellent, there are a couple of issues that I'd like to publicly address. First, I was added to the whatsapp group with information regarding pick-up and Bolivian customs very late and so I did not receive the messages in the chat. The other people showed me because they all had filled out the custom form online already (in the end there was no problem at the border, but still!). Second, the agency is one of the more expensive ones and for Salar de Uyuni, they cooperate with Sajama Expediciones from Bolivia (which did an excellent job btw) and they openly communicate that. However, other agencies cooperate with that agency as well and they offer way cheaper tours. I paid 235.000 CLP while others in my group only paid 160.000 CLP (even with a private room!). Most of the money you pay stays with Horizonte Atacama. They only pay 150.000 CLP to the Bolivian agency. The only thing they do is that a driver brings you to the Bolivian border and provides you breakfast at the Chilean border. This is not only rip-off against the Bolivian agency, especially the guides/drives, because they have 3 days of work and get paid very poorly. But also, it is a rip-off against customers. Hence, I recommend asking with which Bolivian agency they cooperate and rather look at their reviews when making a decision.

review_text: This tour was really enjoyable with some stunning scenery, within a short drive of Santiago. Javier the guide was great - very enthusiastic and excellent bilingual (English and Spanish) commentary, explaining the geography/geology of the area really well in particular. I saw that some other reviews complained about walking, but there wasn't really that much. The bus stopped at a viewpoint on the way up for photos, then at the edge of the reservoir for around 40 minutes, and we were given the option to walk further around to the end if we wanted to...this was a flat path (no incline!) and an easy stroll (worth it for views too). I had been out really late the night before (beware of the very friendly Chilean people and their generous measures of Pisco!!) but found the trip to be pretty laid back/easy going, as did one of my fellow passengers who had been similarly way-laid the night before by the infamous "terremoto" drink! :-) Meanwhile, Javier and the other guides set up a snack table with juice and small plates of cheese/nibbles. The scenery was lovely - quite windy at the other end of the reservoir so maybe bring a light jacket with you (and some sunscreen!) As it is in the mountains and part of a national park, the main draw of the tour is the scenery (no shops or anything else, as you would expect!). There is a stop in a small town on the way up, but the main point there is to pick up any extra snacks you want as lunch is around 3pm on the way back (and for the guide to register with the tourism office there). I thought the lunch was pretty good - we were given a discounted price of 16,000 pesos for an all you could eat buffet (including a glass of wine/beer or soft drink and a coffee/tea). Again, this was optional so you could take a packed lunch if you wanted to skip it. The food was really tasty though (and not having had breakfast due to aforementioned late night, I think I got my money's worth!). There was a glass of wine included in the tour too (we had it at the lunch location as you're not allowed to drink in public/at the reservoir). Other details - I got picked up from my hotel pretty much on the dot at 8.15am. This is a shuttle service and they take you out to the main Turistik loading bay at the big Parque Arauco shopping mall to the north east of the city centre. You then join the main bus for your tour...there were lots of other tours leaving around the same time, but each bus has a sign in its window with the name of each tour so you can look out for yours there, and there were also lots of guides with clipboards to show people which bus to take. You then get driven up to the Maipo Canyon, with a stop in the little town for snacks, followed by a stop for toilets (at the place where you will have lunch later), then it is on to the reservoir (as mentioned above). If I remember, we left the reservoir around 2pm(?), and got back to the lunch spot around 3pm. I was dropped back at my hotel by 5pm ish (roughly!) It also looked like there were good places to do other outdoor activities if you have more time to spend in the area and are into these things (e.g. rafting/kayaking/skydiving/bungee jumping). So if you want an easy way to get out of Santiago for a day and see some of the Andes scenery, then this is a pretty good way to do it. review_text: I did the 5 day W trek. There are different bus companies that pick up from Puerto Natales and take you to the park. First you have to register yourself and get a pass and pay the national park fees. Then you have the option of either taking a bus to the accommodation or walk there. I took the bus (costs about 6000 Chilean Pesos) to the Las Torres Central and checked in. I did the hike to Base Las Torres taking nothing but my camera and bottle of water. It was the most difficult hike due to the steepness. It was cloudy so we couldn't see much of the three towers. On Day two, it was raining and cloudy but it was a pleasant walk to Cuernos. It took a bit longer for me since I was really sore from my hike on day one. I did some leg exercises and recovered fast for Day 3. On Day 3, the highlight of the day it was sunny and we got to see the real beauty of the national park and I got really excited and started sprinting on the track. It got a bit steep towards the end. I got to the lookout near camp Britanico and the lookout was amazing. Not be fooled, there are two lookouts on this point. One is pretty flat where you can have your lunch and admire the mountains. The second one (about 30 mins walk) is a bit further but a better lookout. On Day 4, it was cloudy again and I walked from Cuernos to Lake Refugio Grey, was another struggle due to sore legs and steepness but made it :). On Day 5, it was cloudy but it was a short walk (about 3 hrs) to Paine Grande. I rested there on that day. Later that day the it got sunny and again the beauty of the park was revealed. I took my camera and rushed outside and took as many photos as I can. On Day 6, it was sunny and waited for the boat (tickets can only be purchased on the boat) back to Pudeto to catch the bus back to Puerto Natales. During the boat ride, what I would say is the most photographed picture appears before your eyes. Overall, it was a really good hike and I encourage people to spend extra time to appreciate the beauty of the park rather than joining a one-day tour. FYI, please take appropriate clothing, the weather in the park changes very often and it gets very windy. Take enough cash with you, national park fees and boat fees can be paid in cash only (USD or Chilean Pesos). Book your Refugios very early in advance. These get booked very fast especially during peak season and your meals as well. There are no powerpoints in the hostels, there are only one area in each Refugio where there are limited powerpoints and they are normally full with phone chargers. Please be considerate of others and decide whether you want to charge your phone or camera battery. BTW There is no phone signal in the park :)

review_text: My husband and I made a five-day detour during our Chile trip to sample wines, hike and horseback ride in Colchagua Valley. We stayed at Lapostolle, which is not only an incredible winery, but also has a small boutique Relais & Chateau hotel on its premises. If you were staying at this property for three days or less, there would really be very little reason to leave. They have fantastic wines to sample, every type of Grand Marnier ever produced, since the owners also own Grand Marnier, hiking trails, horseback riding, beautiful pools for swimming, and perfect casitas from which to relax with a glass of wine, read a book and take in the incredible scenery of this picturesque valley with the surrounding mountains. When you do venture out to tour some of the numerous surrounding wineries, there will be no shortage from which to choose. Our favorites, besides Lapostolle, were Montgras, Neyen and Montes. If you are into the finer wines, be sure to request a special tasting of their top wines. Most of the vineyards do offer this for a bit higher price, and it is well worth the freight. Otherwise, you might be stuck tasting the more pedestrian wines that you find in the discount stores back in the states. Huge difference in quality. The last thing I would suggest is to hire a driver for the day if you are going tasting from winery to winery. Some of the roads are not marked well, and it is a pleasure to be able to imbibe and have someone else take care of that task. The hotels can recommend bilingual drivers if you need them.

review_text: Review for spa one and only I visited Santiago for two weeks and one of the absolute highlights of the trip was Spa One & Only. The environment is soothing and peaceful, the spa is beautifully designed, everyone who works there is friendly and accommodating, and the treatments I received were fantastic. I booked my appointment a few weeks before I arrived and somehow (totally my fault) I saved the appointment in my calendar for the wrong date and didn’t realize until the day before when I got an appointment reminder. At that point I was double booked and had no way to cancel my conflicting plans. Originally when I contacted the spa about my dilemma, I was told they were booked the next day (the day I thought my appointment was) but they went above and beyond to shift things around to get me in. Instead of seeing one therapist for the various things I booked, they split my sessions between two which I didn’t mind at all. It actually ended up being a blessing in disguise because I got to experience two separate therapists who were both incredible! I started with a 60-minute aromatherapy relaxation massage with Victoria and honestly I went in thinking it would be a “fluff” massage (that’s what I call it when the therapist just lightly glides over you and goes through a set routine rather than tuning into your body and finding/working on actual problem areas). I have some pretty serious back pain due to previous injuries and usually anything under 90 minutes doesn’t cut it since I need some pretty intensive work. Let me tell you that this was anything but a fluff massage. From the start, Victoria’s pressure and technique were perfect…and she somehow managed to work on more areas in 60 minutes than some people do in 90. She definitely moved quickly in order to do as much as she did but I didn’t leave feeling like she neglected or rushed through a single area. I can only imagine that a longer massage with her would be even more amazing but I was thrilled with the experience I had with her. Next up was a 90-minute Holistic Energy Clearing Ritual with Daniela. I originally booked the Holistic Experience with her which was 2.5 hours so initially I was bummed at missing out on the full experience…but that was before my actual session…and trust me, I didn’t leave feeling like I missed out on anything. The entire session with Daniela was so incredibly beautiful that I’m finding it hard to put into words. I’m an energy healer myself but I rarely take the time to get treatments from other healers and this was much needed on so many levels. I had a few specific areas where I was looking to release energy/emotions and that definitely happened during the session. Daniela spoke throughout the entire session and gave the most beautiful explanations along with guided meditations and breathwork. The session also included reiki, crystal healing, singing bowls, smoke cleansing, and beautiful songs. One big surprise is that a massage was also included and I had no idea so that was an extremely pleasant surprise. The session ended with a short reading from an oracle deck and the cards were so spot on for everything I was going through. Another nice touch is that she opened a window during the session and I could hear the birds singing the entire time which added to the overall soothing experience. I thoroughly enjoyed both of my sessions with Victoria and Daniela and highly recommend both therapists. Whether you live locally or are on vacation and looking for a reason to pamper yourself, do yourself a favor and book yourself one (or hopefully more) sessions at Spa One & Only. If you’re not a Spanish speaker (which I unfortunately am not) you’ll definitely need a translation app to book your appointment through WhatsApp and be prepared to have it handy for checking in/out. Both therapists claimed their English was terrible but I disagree completely. We had no problems with communication at all. Daniela especially speaks phenomenal English and I was astounded at how deep she got with the topics she spoke about during the session, especially for her claiming to not know English well. I left the spa feeling so much lighter and stress-free. I haven’t felt that level of peace in a long time and wish I could transport myself back right now.

review_text: I highly recommend the w-trek and hiking it from west to east so the wind will be predominantly at your back. If you hike east to west, your first day is a brutal 4 hour ascent, not the way I'd want to start! Each day is very manageable on its own, but by the end of day 5 we were exhausted. I would not do this trek without a neck warmer to block wind from your face and ears (I couldn't keep a cap on my head or scrunch in my hair since winds were ferocious), a water bladder so your hands are free and you can stay hydrated while moving instead of a water bottle, and trekking poles to save your knees! It barely rained in November, but a waterproof cover for your pack is a good idea just in case. Be sure to have a small pack (for your water, lunch, etc) that you can take with you when you hike up to Brittanico as you can leave your large pack at Italia. We stayed in the Refugios each night which are clean and comfortable. However, be aware of your belongings! I had a Patagonia fleece jacket stolen off the hook outside my shower at Chileno. I'm pretty sure it was the girl cleaning the washroom at the time as she would not make eye contact with me after this incident, yet was super friendly upon my arrival. I don't like making such an unkind assumption, but I really do not believe any hiker wants to add more weight to their pack and staff are paid very poorly. In the end she likely needs the jacket more than me, so I hope she's the one who has it. Other women told me they had things stolen as well when they were showering. We had all meals provided by the Refugios, the bagged lunches are plentiful. Each refugio has a bar to relax in during the evenings and reminisce with other hikers about the day's adventure. Patagonia unites diverse people from around the globe while being surrounded by the most stunning scenery. This was an amazing experience. We booked through Experience Chile as trying to reserve Refugios online wasn't working for me and this was a last minute trip so time was not on my side. Charles was my contact and was so so helpful! He even gave me his personal mobile number to contact him during our visit in case anything went wrong. He booked other tours for us, transportation, accommodations, and was very responsive from beginning to end. This is a must hike for anyone who enjoys the outdoors. I also recommend flying to Calama, renting a car (Chile appears to only have manual cars which was an unfortunate surprise to other visitors we met), and drive to stay in San Pedro de Atacama. The desert is so different than Patagonia! The Valle de Luna is a must visit, as well as driving to El Tatio to view the geothermal field with more than 80 active geysers! Review of: W Trek Torres del Paine

review_text: My friend and I booked several excursions with Chile Off Track which we all loved! Tessa took us on the Pomaire tour which we loved. It is touristy as that is what the town lives off, but it still remains authentic as it is really rural. We were able to get some nice souvenirs like a nice Alpaca poncho, some lapis lazuli jewellery and a nice sombrero! We had a nice hearty lunch with a BBQ on the table, serving different cuts of meat of course served with some spectacular Chilean wine!! Later in the evening Tessa took us to the Observatory. We were really overtaken by this beauty of this place. The owner spent a fortune in arming this private toy and only opens a couple a times a week for the normal public. The young astronomer was very knowledgeable and his English was flawless! The evening ended with some nice tapas and wine after which Tessa drove us back to our hotel. The next day, Tessa picked us up to drive even further into the Andes on the Snow Mountain and Wine Tour. Getting at our destination at Valle Nevado, we had a cup of coffee while the condors were circling above the hotel. Apparently the staff throw some scrapings in the morning so they come and get some food…amazing birds!!! The view!!! We loved it! We had another good lunch in Providencia with more good Chilean wine and finished the day with a tasting at Cousiño Macul. There was a huge group of Brazilians that came in at the same moment, but luckily Tessa arranged a private English speaking tour for us.

review_text: It's a pretty unique experience! Don't expect a cruise-ship experience. This is a ferry. As ferries go, this is a pretty basic ferry. We've been in much nicer ferries in many parts of the world.... We chose a Triple A cabin. This included 2 single bunk-beds (which were comfortable), private bathroom in the cabin, a fully openable outside porthole (with no outside deck), a wardrobe, desk and bench. It was quite austere - basically painted metal walls, with utilitarian furnishings. The bathroom was essentially a wet room with exposed shower, and flickering fluorescent light, which did give it that unique "horror-movie" atmosphere. (Watch Das Boot, and expect a little bit better!) I could not have imagined sharing cabins or bathrooms with strangers on this trip. The rooms are very small. I overheard someone, while standing on deck in the cold rain, say of their cabin, "It's like a prison cell." But, with the Triple A private cabins, it's a better experience. Ours was right next to the Officer's Mess, so there was some noise, plus this is working ship - so expect to hear industrial-type noises. The ship itself, and the decks are well-maintained. The bar area for presentations is bright, and comfortable. But then.... we get to the dining room.... Picture a 1970s hospital or school cafeteria. Long metal tables, cavernous fluorescent lit, bare room, and food that borders on gruel. Our first breakfast set the tone, when the cooks ladled a spoonful of runny, thin porridge onto our tray. Little did we know at that time, we were actually having a treat, with 5-6 raisins in our portion for this time! (Bring your own snacks to supplement the bland meals.) The common areas can be quite noisy as they tend to have TVs running, in Spanish. The truck drivers all hang out here. There is no wifi, no safe in room. Lectures were given daily in Spanish and English on the geography, culture, flora and fauna of the region. The guide was enthusiastic and had a great sense of humour. Potentially, this trip could have amazing views, and is a worthwhile way of seeing this area of Chile. The weather on our trip was rather poor, but there were glimpses of huge mountains and waterfalls, whales and seals. Thank you for taking the time to comment about your experience with Navimag ;)

There were tour buses and cars coming the other way so we knew we were on the right track. Stop to buy your ticket then and use the bathroom then drive some more. A pleasant hike but nothing compared to those in Torres del Paine so set your expectations accordingly.

review_text: My husband and I just completed the W trek with Ricci and team about a week ago, and had an incredible experience overall. We were picked up from the bus in Puerto Natales and then taken to the beautiful Garden Domes, where we had upgraded to the private ecodome (highly recommend). After some tea and snacks, we went to our group dinner and briefing with Ricci at El Brisket. Food was amazing! Ricci gave some helpful advice about the trek and offered some wisdom to help ensure we'd have the best time. Then we went back to the Garden Domes, and we managed to get a nice soak in the hot tub with the most breathtaking views before we were off on our adventure. The next morning we stored our luggage and had a delicious breakfast before leaving for the park via private transportation. We absolutely loved the guide Andy that trekked with us on the first day, and from there the path was extremely easy to self navigate the rest of the way. We enjoyed our refugio experience overall - there was one miscommunication with Domo Frances, where we were supposed to stay in the dorm but instead had camping, but it turned out to be super fun and Ricci made it right by refunding us some money, since camping was less expensive. The only reason I am not giving a 5 star rating is that communication between Ricci/team and guests could be improved upon. We returned from our trek at about 10pm with the expectation that we were going to a pizza party with our group and some other groups that had completed the trek that day, only to find out that they had overbooked the Garden Domes that evening and most of the group did not have a place to stay. Some people were panicking out about this, which caused a tizzy - this is understandable, especially after a 5 day hike, a long journey back to Puerto Natales, and how late it was. Ricci made it right immediately by booking all of us in the nicest hotel in town, but the whole situation could have been avoided had his team given us a heads up about this a day or two in advance so we'd know what to expect upon arrival. My husband and I gave Ricci this feedback directly and he was very receptive, but I do believe in writing honest reviews so think it's important to share our whole experience. We initially chose Chiletours due to pricing, as they were much less expensive than other tour operators that we researched, and they ended up really surpassing our expectations. Overall, Ricci/team took excellent care of us and I would absolutely recommend Chiletours to anyone that wants to do the W trek and not have to deal with the logistical hassles that come with booking (ie booking refugios individually, transport to and from Puerto Natales, etc.). We travel a ton, and this was one of our favorite trips yet! Review of: Full-Day Torres del Paine Mountains Advanced Hike

In addition to these inconveniences, it should be considered that the tour ends at the Central Market. Even though the tour initially indicates that anyone who wants to return to the hotel should notify them in advance, this option was not given as the guide and company would go on another tour later, making it necessary to request an Uber or taxi to return from the Central Market.

review_text: I was on the same ship's tour as Elisabeth. After making the effort to be on the first tender, we had to wait over an hour for the rest of the tour group to arrive. In the next two and a half hours, travelling in an old, uncomfortable bus, we saw fishing boats in Puerto Aysen, a small waterfall and a bridge over the Simpson River. No time limit was given at each stop and much time was wasted standing around talking. One other couple on the tour had come from the same area in England as Jackie and she was distracted all day by these people. I took very few photos as I was expecting to see what had been promised in the published itinerary and waiting to visit the National Park and see three waterfalls and the stunning Simpson River Valley that had been described. At 2pm we arrived at the farm for lunch - one pisco sour, one bottle of wine per table of four, bread, lamb and salad. Extra lamb was offered but there was still one half of lamb on the spit when we left at 3pm after the dancing display, to be back at the ship by 4pm. It was a very expensive day for what was provided for US$130 paid in advance, with extra costs through PayPal. A friend who did the ship tour to Coyhaique and Scenic Simpson Valley said that the highlight was driving through the Andes and into the town of Coyhaique. Other friends paid US30 each for a van with five people, picked up at the meeting place near the port. They left promptly and had a great day visiting the National Park, Virgin waterfall, Indian head, seeing condors, travelling through the Simpson Valley into Coyhaique and spending time at a handicraft market and buying lunch. I contacted Ann Hedderman after this tour and voiced my disappointment but the only excuse given for not being given an extensive tour of the Simpson River Valley was time constraints. My advice is to do your research if you want to experience the natural beauty of the Simpson River Valley and travel into Coyhaique, rather than just a cultural experience with lunch. review_text: This is a good trip to do on your first day in the Atacama and most tours take in Piedras Rojas and the Chaxa (Flamingo) Lagoon as well as these two lakes. It's a long day but it does let you acclimatize gradually to altitude as you slowly drive up to these lakes and then descend back to San Pedro. The tour also departs 2 hours later than the 5 AM departure to El Tatio Geyser and is not as cold so it is easier on your system. Still a wind breaker is good to have. The light is incredibly bright and the blue sky and water and yellow flowers are highly photogenic. There are also vicunas to be seen but there are better viewings in the wetland area below El Tatio Geysers. This is a worthwhile trip, but if you can only do one tour, I would recommend El Tatio instead.

review_text: As a couple on a budget, this was a great way to see Valparaiso and find out more about its history. Our guide, Alvaro was really polite and full of knowledge. The tour was easy to walk, and we even took an ascensor up one of the hills at our guide's expense (thank you, Alvaro!). This city seems a little on the rough side, but the art and culture make up for it, which is what gives Valparaiso its character. There is art everywhere, with each piece having its own unique meaning. During the tour you will not only see the art, but you will also stop to taste a complimentary pisco sour and have a chance to try one of 80+ types of empanadas (for purchase, but you are not obligated). At the end, it will be explained that tips are appreciated, but not required. Just used your own discretion and tip what you think the tour was worth. One side suggestion: after the tour, catch the local "O" or "612" bus at the bus stop next to the port for an inexpensive way to catch the beautiful views that overlook Valparaiso!

review_text: Two friends and I used an outfitter called Antu (they were awesome) to climb Villarrica in May 2017. We have no proper climbing experience but are all in good physical shape. This is *not* a walk in the park. It took six hours to the summit, then we spent a short time at the top, and the way down was probably two or three hours. We chose an outfitter the afternoon before, when we got fitted for all of our climbing gear and outerwear. I wore a long sleeve tshirt/heavy sweater/down jacket on top, a base layer/cotton pants on my legs; two layers of gloves; one layer of wool sock. They provided everything else. (Also, you bring your own food and water.) The climb up is steep, often icy, sometimes perilous. You have to concentrate on every step for probably three-fourths of the way. There were six climbers in our group (with three guides from Antu), and two of them had to slow down while the other four continued on. I was exhausted that evening. The experience, though grueling and often nerve-racking, was totally worth it. Our stay at the summit was probably only 10 minutes, but that was enough. There were crazy strong winds up there blowing us around, the crater gives off clouds of sulfur gas, and it must have been 0 degrees (f). Three highlights: Views along the way were spectacular (we paused many times to admire the views and take pictures). There's a solid river of magma towards the top from a previous event that's frozen over. Assuming it's not too icy, on the way down, we sledded instead of walking.

review_text: I have been working in the area since 2005 and visited Laguna Cejar several times year ago. It's a beatiful system of a few lakes, worth a visit of max an hour. Yesterday, I returned there with my family after a long time, to watch the sunset, to find you have to pay in the afternoon 15,000 CLP (23 US$) EACH PERSON just for access. 10,000 CLP in the morning. This doesn't make sense!!! There is no maintenance for the place, nothing installed, no services - nada! Just a natural resource like many others. The lakes are a gem in the desert, sure, but about 30 minutes drive South you will find a much more interesting Laguna Chaxa, with flamingos, good explanation. Access costs 2,500 CLP per person. Plenty of explanations, a really nice walk. I am sure is the most beautiful place in the Salar. It's a shame that a natural beauty like this is banned - de facto - to families (we were 4 people: 60,000 for a max 1 hour visit???). What if such an exorbitant fee would be required to access all the beautiful natural beauties all around the world? And don't trust to the popular story that the moneys go to the indigenous population: they just go in the pocket of a few families in the area. I think the municipality of San Pedro should immediately stop this shameful exploitation of a natural beauty like that. But San Pedro changed so much in the years. The surrounding area is really wonderful, but totally uncontrolled exploitation of tourism transformed the village and some of the natural resource in a mean bazar. What a pity... In 3 words: DON'T GO THERE ANYMORE!!!

review_text: As we were pushed for time so used a travel company highly recommended to us by friends called Imagine Latin America, who were able to tailor and a programme covering the best attractions the Atacama Desert had to offer. Based in San Pedro de Atacama, La Casa de Don Tomas, a very comfortable and friendly hotel - all our internal flights and pick-ups were taken care of by local operators booked by our travel company, which took all the stress out of paying for guides, entry fees and coaches. On the first afternoon we were taken on the fascinating Valley of Mars (also known as death valley) tour ending up at the a huge sand dune to watch the sunset over the Andes, unforgettable. Day two included two excursions, the morning was taken up with an Archaeological tour of a pre-Columbian village from around 2.800 b,c. In the afternoon we visit to the largest and driest salt lakes in the world which is home to various species of flamingos. Another spectacular sunset with the backdrop of the Andes, changing colour as the light danced and faded. On day three an early start 4.00 AM was required to experience a full tour to the El Tatio Geysers and Machuca. Arriving early allowed for an amazing view of the sunrise over the Geysers and raised the temperature from a very chilly minus 20! After breakfast at the Geysers we took a bath at the hot thermal pools located a stones through away and outdoors! On the way back we stopped of at small traditional village for lunch. Be aware the altitude is very noticeable on this trip and alcohol is not recommended before you travel. The fourth day was free and we hoped to book a star gazing tour form one of the many tour companies located in San Pedro de Atacama, however this was the one evening it was cloudy so alas this was not possible. it was some consolation we had experienced many clear evenings - the local guide on the previous trip to the Geysers gave us an impromptu star tour! We flew to Santiago the next day but had an amazing trip and toughly enjoyed our visit I would highly recommend .

review_text: Literature Nobel Prize winner Pablo Neruda's very interesting house, great location by the sea. Of the three Neruda's houses, this one is the most interesting to visit. The electronic audio guide explains every room of the house in different languages that explains interesting facts, objects and stories about the poets life and personal life. I highly recommend this visit. Beautiful place.

review_text: We are a super fit adventurous Australian family of 3. Our son is 12- but your outdoor, adventurous, nature loving very fit and able 12 year old. My husband and I have a high and constant level of fitness. We have just finished this trek today ( sept 19)...... This trek to the top point- the 360% Mirador is not for the half fit or low active people at all. The first 1 to 1.5 hours ( if u r fit) is Brutal and straight up hill- there is no let up, it is relentless and on an old unused road. Once you reach the Refugio your walk into the Forrest growth but it is still very much up hill walking. Currently the snow starts to become visible after about 20/30 minutes and then you arrive at the first lake. From here on the snow starts to increase and within 20 mins of walking past the lake u r walking in full snow.... The snow is at times on the flat ankle deep but the terrain is flat. Once you pass the frozen lakes you start the long climb to the mirador and at times currently this is and can be snow to knee deep depending on your choice of where u place your feet. We wore gortex trekking shoes, gators and had walking poles and were ever thankful for them all. The climb of course get thicker and thicker with snow.. This is tough- it's not something anyone should take without being well equipped and have enough food and water. The view once you get thru the snow and finish the relentless uphill will forever be simply a 360 degrees view that words don't and can't describe. This trek is brilliant if u have the fitness level to take it to the top. Our son was brilliant and made it with complete ease and enjoyment . We stayed for 1 hour at the top to have lunch and lap up the view. The slide/ walk down the snow was at times even tougher- this is where u need to have your wits about u as u r fatigued. So take care . But with 1 hour at the top we returned to our car in 6.45. This was and will forever be one of the best treks we have done... The snow factor truly made it a snow drenched wonder land of wow wow wow..

The actual tour then started early in the morning in the middle of Santiago, we were picked up at the hotel before we went by car at 3000m above sea level. Overall we were almost 9 hours on our feet with several breaks and sufficient food. Vicente had prepared a perfect packed lunch for us, for the sandwiches we still have to say thank you, they were just perfect. Hot coffee at the summit and a cool surprise at the end of the tour. Yes and there is not much to say about nature, you have to experience it yourself. Indescribably beautiful this day and above all perfectly organized by Vicente and Pumaadventures! We will come back and want to experience many more tours together with Vicente! review_text: The Atacama is breathtaking; I love deserts and have been to many, and was very excited for a 5 day camping trip around this area. I am definitely glad I went, but I wish I had known a lot of things beforehand, so that I would be prepared for what it was, not what I expected it to be from my research. I'm going to share those things with you, so you don't have that tough acceptance period, where you grapple with the fact that your carefully planned itinerary is blown up due to closures, and you're in for a very different trip than you'd imagined. We'll start with closures. I'd carefully researched the things to see in the Atacama, and crafted an itinerary that would allow me to see the ones most important to me, and minimize driving. When I picked up my truck with a rooftop tent, they handed me the daily closure report. Half the places on the list were closed, including the places I'd planned to hit those first few days. The lesson here is just to not get SUPER attached to visiting specific things. There is a lot of beauty to be found in that desert, but if weather and road conditions aren't on your side, you just might not be able to see certain ones. Go in with a flexible travel plan if possible. It is pretty hard to come by reliable and current information on where you can and cannot camp in the area. That's pretty standard for this kind of travel, and is part of the adventure - the great unknown/surprises! But that said, finding a spot to camp each night ended up being a huge source of stress, as it seemed that many places it was not allowed, some places it was allowed but very unsafe (risk of rain stranding you, temps way below zero/snow, lightning storms), and then there's a lot of grey area. The point of camping in a desert, for me, is to be away from other people, and away from the town/light pollution. The only places that I was told it was acceptable and safe to camp were places that were close to town and sure to be full of other campers. Now, I didn't camp in any of those places, and did manage to find cool secluded spaces - but it was stressful, time consuming, and just hard damn work. I'm not sure if where I spent each of the nights was technically allowed (they were not any of the spots I was specifically told were NOT ok to camp in) and that added to the stress as well. I don't really want to get into trouble in a foreign country, as a rule. Crowds! You will rarely to never be at a laguna or other attraction alone. That might be what you'd expect, but add about 50 people to whatever you were expecting. I understand other people want to do exactly what I'm doing - totally fair - just saying, know that there are buses arriving full of people to almost every location. You can't get close to most of the attractions. Most of the lagunas and salt flats I checked out were surrounded by markers keeping you well away from them. Totally understandable - preserving the environment. It just wasn't in line with the photos I'd seen online before my trip, with people getting to sit alongside these gorgeous lakes and enjoying them up close. It is more like being in a museum, and being herded down a hallway with a bunch of other people, looking at the art behind ropes as you pass. Still beautiful - but be prepared for the art museum, not the nature hike. There are a few exceptions to this - but the vast majority of places are as described above. Weather. This is totally my fault. I read driest desert in the world, and a dark sky area great for stargazing and astral-photography. I should have looked closer at a breakdown of specific months. I did look at temps (usual desert stuff, be prepared for hot days and freezing nights), but didn't realize how much rain I'd see during my time there (almost daily), and how cloudy the nights would be (saw the sky clearly less than 50% of my total nights there). It was just a bummer. Apparently from January to March is the "winter" where occasional showers are to be expected. Plan accordingly, research your dates, don't make assumptions :) San Pedro de Atacama - loved this quirky little town at first, it's like stepping into an old western! But once I had a vehicle in my possession, and needing to find food supplies and gas, I came to think of it as my own personal hell. Navigating the town in a vehicle SUCKS, and you can't park anywhere. You're basically forced to park on the outskirts of town and walk in, leaving your rental and all of your gear and hoping it doesn't get broken into. You can only get really super basic supplies - there is not really what I would think of as a real market or grocery store in the town. There IS a great little produce market that popped up on the eastern side of town center - in a dusty lot near the intersection of the B 245 and Licanbur/R23. You can find ice at the liquor store on Licanbur, and basic stuff like water and TP, a little produce and chips/chocolate bars/hot dogs at the "grocery store" a block from that. Gas. Oy. There is one gas station in the entire area. None of the other little towns have one, it is SUPER weird. The Copec station in SPdA is hard to find - it's down a dusty alley that is a minefield of ginormous potholes, and is marked only by a small sign reading "combustibles". As soon as you turn in, you are in a line. That's how you know you're in the right place. There is always a queue for gas. It's not too long of a wait usually though. You'll notice I still gave this place a 5/5 - because it IS awesome. I just want other people to maybe see this, and know what I'd wished I'd known. I managed to let go of my expectations pretty quickly, and enjoy this for what it was, but my travel companion had a much harder time with this. She was more excited for this part of our trip than even myself (we were traveling through Bolivia and Chile), and she would probably rate it a 1 or 2 now. If she could have seen a review like this ahead of time, she may have opted not to go, to go at a different time, or would have arrived with a more realistic picture of the whole thing - and had a better time for it.

review_text: We bought a full-day trip to vulcano Pili. Due to road opening times, we had to convert it to a 1.5-day trip (additional fees). We left the hotel at 4pm to go to the base camp. The guide decided to start walking at 2am. We started to walk in the scree (the whole mountain is a scree) in the night with a very cold wind. The guide was walking very slow and stopping each 10-15 steps. We asked him about this; he answered : "I must breath!". As he was not following the best climbing line, we started to climb our own path, before him. After 2.5 hours of walking in the night, we reached the middle of the ascension. In the second part the wind was forcing and we were upset with seeing the guide climbing like a snail and waiting for him (we had to wait in order to know the rough direction to take in the night). We also remarked that at this "speed" we would have reached the summit before the sun. We decided to stop this awful situation and get back to the hotel. When we were back at the base camp, the sun was gently rising and the wind had gone; this could be the good time to start the tour, as initially booked (walk starting at 6am). Back in San Pedro, we went to Vulcano Chile at 10am (opening schedule) which opened at 10:45. It was not possible to discuss any partial refund. The guide told us that we woke up at 2am in order to avoid avalanches. We think he did not mind that there was no snow at all in the region! 600 USD for that is a shame! que tu no puedas subir un volcan , no quiere decir que los guias no sepan! ellos organizan y hacen cambios si es necesario de acuerdo a lo que saben y conocen Hemos hecho aqui miles de expediciones , pero nadie puede garantizarte que subas ! o no xq depende de ti , de tus condiciones , no de la hora , ni de otros agentes

review_text: I think overall if I could choose again I might not do the tour and just do a one day tour of the salt flats. We booked a couple of days in advance in the store which was an easy process. We wanted to know specifically what guide we were going to have and he said Omar. We then agreed as the reviews with him were great and we were nervous about getting a good guide as we would be with them in the desert for 3 days! Day one overview: Minibus was due to pick us up at 6:30, arrived at 07:05 but have come to realise that this is generally expected. Guy in the van initially spoke Spanish and then English. Then I think he got bored and only spoke in Spanish. When we got to the border he gave all the important information about passports and documentation in Spanish. When we asked what he said he rolled his eyes and gave the very shortened version. When we got past the border and were assigned to the drivers and guides, our driver was called Joel and our guide Izequiel. I then began to panic and I didn’t know anything about this guide. I asked the guy that had taken us to the border where Omar was. He then pretended to not speak English and said ‘I don’t understand sorry’. Another passenger translated into Spanish to him and he then said ‘who’s Omar’ and then quickly walked off. He then started whispering to the guide and then left. So basically we were stuck and had to go on the tour. Our new guide then said ‘just to warn you guys I’ve had no sleep for over a week so I’m really tired and we are going to have to take it slow today’. Really really bad first impression. We then got in the jeep and there were no seatbelts! Even worse impression as we were completely stuck. The next 3 days were a mixture of highs and lows. Positives of 3 days: Joel the driver was really safe. The majority of the time Izequiel was really nice and had great English. The accommodation was basic but clean and quiet (no one else was in either accommodation each night). We even had a double room the first night without paying extra. We covered all sights and even finished late the last day as we were given loads of time. Negatives: No seatbelts The food was honestly disgusting. We had the vegetarian and mostly had cold undercooked potatoes and egg. One lunch consisted of tinned sweet corn, bad feta and avocado?? My boyfriend was vomiting a lot the first night. As we werent sure if it was a bug or altitude in the morning I asked if we could try the emergency oxygen ... he said it was empty? We were then given random pills that were really old which he wasn’t completely sure what it would do. We were then taken to the doctors which was closed. Luckily he wasn’t that ill so we said not to bother and to continue with the tour. Note: It’s luck as to whether you will get along with your group. We were put with three immature, selfish girls. On the first day we made a huge effort to make conversation, they would answer short answers and never ask a question back. By the second day we just gave up and didn’t talk anymore. They didn’t respect the wildlife despite explanations from our guide and were late for everything. This didn’t effect my rating but just a warning it’s not always happy families :) To be honest there isn’t much choice in Atacama for good tour services but if you are sure you want to do the tour have a look around and bare in mind you won’t necessarily get the guide you want.

review_text: A very good trip with TurisTour which included the Domeyko Mountains named after a Polish surveyor, Yerbas Buenos with ancient rock art ( petroglyphs), Rainbow Valley & finally the very small village of Rio Grande with their terrace farming. Throughout the trip you have great vistas & climbing the rock to see the petroglyphs was interesting and fun. As you cross Matancilla which is green due to the river and actually has trees - you enter Rainbow valley -stunning. The various colours of the rocka are due to the composition of the minerals - we stayed about an hour and the camera was on click overdrive.We also saw vicuna & llama which was an added bonus. Finally what made the trip so great was that we were only six -" Totti " our Argentinian guide was fantastic as she kept up a running steam of information, switching from Spanish to English without skipping a beat.We also had a delightful Chilean family onboard -a great morning out.We saw nobody else on our trip -just us & the landscape.

Everything was well organized and ready for us the next day. Out of a big selection we chose 5 dishes of our choice. Together with our chef Inés we bought all ingredients fresh at the local market. She explained everything in detail and it was really easy to follow her instructions. She made us understand to not only "cook" as it is written in the recipes... but to give more attention to the smell and taste and also to the consistency of each dish while preparing the menu. In the end we had a very delicious and fresh meal including a starter and a dessert. Also included in the price for the cooking class was a selection of different wines from a very nice wine yard not far away from Valparaiso. We have been lucky cause we even went to this wine yard, called Emiliana, in the morning together with Rafael. We had a tour around with a guide who explained us the different sorts of their wine and each single step of their wine production. And in the end we also tasted a selection of their wines. So if you have the chance I recommend to do a combined tour of a visit to the wine yard and the cooking class. It's really worth it! Thanks to Inés and Rafael! review_text: I can't say enough about the great team at Summit Chile, the trekking group I went with on a hike up Villarica Volcano a few days ago. A few great things in particular about Summit Chile: 1. They were very easy to work with -- the information they provided was very clear, and they lived up to everything they indicated. Where other guides were taking groups of 20+ people up the volcano, Summit Chile only takes a handful of people in each group, and has a ratio of no more than 3 guests per guide (our group consisted of 5 of us clients and 2 guides). 3. I highly recommend Summit Chile and hope to be back later this year to do another volcano summit with them!

review_text: First of all - there's free transportation to Viu Monnet and Lapostolle from Santa Cruz hotel. You need to book in advance at the agency inside the hotel, one day ahead was enough (in April). We spent 2 days in Santa Cruz and wanted to visit 3 wineries (and save some money) so this is what we've done- First day - visited a small winery called OWM. Was fantastic, the owners shared with us their experience in creating a new winery. For us this was the best tour of the three. Second day - we took the free transportation at 09:45 from Santa Cruz hotel. Got to Lapostolle which was very beautiful and impressive. The tour was good and revealed how premium wines are made. From there the free transport took us to Viu Monnet (but you might need to get back to town to switch transport depending on the driver). We ate at the restaurant which is very beautiful. The tour was fine. Really gives you the opportunity to see a high scale traditional winery. This way we got to see different kinds of wineries in this valley and managed to save some transportation money.

review_text: After reading about the clear skies in the Atacama we had planned a family holiday to Chile to do some stargazing. I found Atacama Desert Stargazing after a good bit of web research and they did not disappoint. Jorge was easy to get ahold of, very flexible and made it generally easy to book, even when we had to reschedule after a missed international connection. As we are neophytes we booked the SAT1 course and it was a great experience. We were picked up at our hotel and driven about 20 minutes out of town. The evening began with a lecture on the history of astronomy and a discussion of telescopes and optics. We then spent the next several hours viewing 17 different astronomical objects (stars, globular clusters, nebulae and planets) through five or six different telescopes. The group only included nine people so we each had ample viewing time. Jorge also provided a full menu and an open bar as part of the evening. We would absolutely do this again and highly recommend the experience. Jorge is both highly enthusiastic, and while he is not a professional astronomer, he clearly knows a great deal about astronomy.

review_text: We schedule all our Atacama tours with We Love Chile (8 scheduled, 7 carried out). From the beginning they were very attentive and helpful, answering questions, showing flexibility and helping us organize our trip in the best way. Overall, we really liked the tours, both the guides, the food offered and the general structure. They have good service via Whatsapp and the staff at the agency located in San Pedro is also very attentive, especially Felipe, who helped us several times. Negative points: - Twice we caught drivers who were racing a lot, and we are talking about dirt roads and often driving in mountains. We found it dangerous and reported it to the organization. - They always inform you of a pickup time at the hotel, which has an interval of 30 to 40 minutes so that you are available. This was a bit uncomfortable because we had to wait on the street without knowing when exactly they were going to pass by. This often happened in the middle of the night. - Most of the tours we took were outsourced by them to another local agency, and this was never informed during the hiring process. In fact, they always made it seem like everything was operated directly by them. They weren't bad, but it made us feel like we were paying extra for the We Love Chile structure and not getting exactly that. - We pay part of the package in advance and with a discount. However, by hiring directly from the agency in San Pedro, the cost of the tours was cheaper. So it's not worth booking in advance, I didn't feel there was any risk of us running out of space on the tour. - Super positive point: When we arrived in Atacama, we decided to cancel the trip up Cerro Toco (already booked) as we believed we wouldn't be able to climb the altitude. They canceled it promptly, without imposing any difficulties on us and refunded our money. Excellent experience. Oi We Lover! Ficamos felizes que, no geral, a experiência tenha sido positiva, especialmente no que diz respeito à flexibilidade e ao suporte da equipe. Agradecemos os pontos de melhoria que você compartilhou, pois são super importantes para continuarmos aprimorando nossos serviços. Esperamos ter a oportunidade de receber vocês novamente e proporcionar uma experiência ainda melhor! ❤️

The clouds, very low that morning, cut us off from cities downstream, which intensified the Impression of greatness that the Milky Way brought above our heads. review_text: Iso100 and Miguel Fuetealba and his friends, Nico and Pau have given me an outstanding and perfect visit to Torres del Paine National Park, its wildlife and nature. The views are out of this world and Miguel did his outmost to show me the nature that he obviously loves so much and ... knows so well. I had gone there to be able to take a few photographs of the puma and the condor, the most iconic wildlife in the park, but I ended up with literally 1000's of photos of both. It blew my mind how Miguel and his team could spot puma's from what seemed like km's away and could with precision determine where they would be after some time. I had, thanks to them, close encounters with the Puma and succeeded puma and condor, and all other wildlife there during the 5 days I did spend with them. We layed flat on our stomach to photograph armadillo in a meadow, and they took me to far-away places to try to spot and photograph waterbirds. Miguel is always in a good mood and "delightfully loco" but he took care of me with coffee and tea and maté ... picked me up by car at 06:00h in the morning after a 2 hour drive from Puerto Natales and dropped me back of at the Estancia where I stayed at 06:00h in the evening. He is a wonderful person and a joy to be with, he is an expert guide and goes to great lengths to show his world, his Patagonia. I can only hope that we will meet again, by preference in his backyard, Patagonia.
