review_text: We drove part of Ruta 9 on the way North from Punta Arenas to Otway Sound. The road was paved and except for semi trucks traffic was at a minimum so the going was good until turning onto the long, long gravel road to Otway! After exiting the city we passed through some rather monotonous flat areas of farmland and rugged barren terrain. It would be much prettier if you drive south hugging the Strait of Magellan to road’s end at Fuerte Bulnes - part of it is also gravel. If a comfortable drive is your aim then take advantage of this highway because all others seem to be meant for four wheel drives - it didn't deter the mini buses from overtaking us though! Music would have been great as our rental car didn’t pick up any radio stations so bear that in mind in this remote area of Patagonia - also top up the tank before heading out. Enjoy your experience!

review_text: I booked a trip for our family of five, all adults, to Pumalin online through Alsur Expeditions, based in Puerto Varas. Gerardo and his team were first rate, and very accommodating to our needs. We booked well in advance, since we were combining this with a trip to Antarctica. This was good and bad. The bad: South American airlines are notorious for changing flights, and since we had scheduled only 36 hours to get from Ushuaia to Chaiten, there were some anxious times rearranging schedules because of flight changes. We were aware of the recommendation to add a lay day to the schedule, but ours was complicated with meeting the rest of our family in Santiago and a lay day wouldn't work. I used Despegar to book flights, and despite some interpretation issues, this worked well. The good part was that I was familiar with the procedures for rearranging plans. This proved helpful when we encountered an air traffic control strike in Santiago. Our flight to Puerto Montt, connecting to Chaiten got cancelled and we missed the Chaiten flight. An overnight bus, which was surprisingly comfortable, got us to Puerto Montt a day late. And on that day, a Sunday, there were no scheduled flights to Chaiten. We were in contact with Gerardo from Alsur through all this and he stayed on top of everything, including arranging a private charter to Chaiten. The Chaiten carrier, Pehuen, gave us nothing back for our missed flight, which I understand is standard practice. Just a word of caution on that point. As I kept repeating to our family, that's the nature of adventure travel. An English speaking guide from Alsur, Colin, accompanied us to Chaiten where we met a native gentleman, Alex, who drove us around the park and surrounding areas. Distances between trails and other features are far, and there is little public transportation. After getting to the cabins, which were unique and very charming, we had time for a hike to the catarats, double waterfalls each hundreds of feet high. The vegetation was lush, as this is a temperate rainforest. Both guides were very knowledgeable in local flora and fauna, and were a pleasure to be with. Dinner at the restaurant was a very cozy and an almost family like experience. Colin knew the managers well and pitched in to help out in the kitchen. The cabins were special. Rustic yet comfortable. We noticed that the door openings and ceilings were low. The doors were less than 72 inches and I could touch the loft over the ground floor. We later learned that this was an intentional feature to give the feel of old European cabins, built when our species was smaller. The were also Frank Lloyd Wright touches like a tree encompassed by a patio and a brook running underneath our cabin. It was a great place to cool beverages. The next day, as predicted by both our guides, the weather turned to rain. We enjoyed an ample breakfast and as a bonus our daughter, an amateur barista, had brought coffee from Santiago. With assistance from the kitchen, she treated us to wonderful fresh coffee. Not that the restaurant coffee was bad, it's just tough to beat fresh dripped brew. Later Alex picked us up and we hiked the sendero to Volcan Chaiten and nearly made it to the vista before turning around. We were socked in by the front, but it was still a presentation of erie beauty and other-worldiness. We all had good rain gear, but after several hours of steady rain, we were soaked. The perfect antidote for that condition was a drive to the local hot springs and a restorative dip. On the ride to the hot springs, Alex drove us past his old home, which had been destroyed in 2008 by the eruption of Volcan Chaiten. Volcanic ash covered it up to the window sills. Then to his new home a few blocks away, where he got towels for all of us, saving a long trip back to the cabins. Resilience is a strong characteristic of the area. The hot springs were convenient, encompassed by a concrete basin. An hour there and we were renewed. Back to the cabins to fire up the wonderful gas stoves and rig some clothes lines. Then a delightful dinner at the restaurant. We were the only Americans there, and although there were visitors of Chilean and many other nationalities, that was pretty much true for our entire visit to Pumalin. We missed the lost day in Pumalin, especially since it would have been sunny. I think the 3 days we had scheduled would have been about right for trekking. Alternatively, some extensive backpacking in the park would be a wonderful experience. The last day we had a 10 am ferry departure, which gave us time for more breakfast, and fresh brewed coffee. The managers were very accommodating and with Collins familiarity we felt warmly welcomed. The ferry ride was longer than normal, as a loading ramp in a nearby inlet that would have shortened the route was being repaired. Ah, adventure travel. The ferry was crowded with workers heading back to families in Puerto Montt for the Christmas holiday. It was overcast and the seas were up, conditions that have their own special attributes. It is a rugged and sparsely populated coast and we wondered how the isolated cabin dwellers spotting the hills managed. Alsur had arranged for a van to pick us up coming off the ferry in Hornopiren. It was clean, well maintained and very comfortable, as was Alex' van in Pumalin. Collin suggested a stop at some hot springs not far from the ferry landing, and we all agreed it would be welcomed. The hot springs were called Pichi-?, the local prefix meaning little or diminutive. Not sure of the rest of the name. The tubs were freshly rebuilt after a flood that had destroyed the old ones. They were naturally bedded pools demarcated by wooden staves There were many basins and a large changing hut. Collin talked with the manager while we were tubbing and told us later that the very large (some many square miles) surrounding property had recently been bought by an American from California, to be maintained in conservation. Part of the agreement was to allow the hot springs to be operated but no other development is to be permitted. We were quickly learning that frequenting hot springs is a lovely local past-time in this geo-thermally active region. Another ferry took us in the van on a short but thrilling ride over to Puerto Arena where Collin recommended stopping at a locally famous empanada cafe, a boliche de las empanadas. It is on the east side of the road about 200-300 yards from the ferry landing. Fantastic seafood empanadas in a rustic but clean setting. It even had a classic Chilean wood stove in the dining area. Then onto Puerto Varas and more adventures. Pumalin is a special place. It is currently immaculately maintained by a staff of volunteers who keep many of trails as neat as a country club, without affecting the feeling of being in the wilderness. There is much local pride in keeping this area place in it's natural state. A recent proposal to string power lines across it was fought and defeated. In the next few years, the current private status will yield to a National Park status as it passes from private to national ownership. It will be interesting to see if the same devotion to maintaining the wilderness feel will be maintained.

review_text: We have been travelling for 6 weeks around South America and this is by far the best thing we have done so far. A couple of points to be aware of. The website link on trip advisor doesn't seem to work but you can find the website at the same web address just using .com instead of .cl. We arranged this at really short notice but it wasn't easy to get in touch by phone as we think the numbers are mobile numbers and they are not often in range, keep persevering or email them. We sent an email the day before the trip and got a response in the evening with the trip sorted for the next day. We were after a full day trip but the morning session was booked so they arranged one for us with a 2pm pick up from Puerto Natales so assumed we were doing a half day trip but ended up doing a full day with a drop off at 9pm. Definitely worth it. The transfer cost 20,000 CLP (for the two of us) which is £20 there and back which is good value. The trip was 60,000 CLP each which was great value. If it's raining stick with it as you never know. When we got there it was throwing it down and looked like it was going to rain all day. The rain stopped in 30 mins and we finished in bright blue sunshine. Okay now the trip. Our guide Cristian was absolutely fantastic, really helpful, really knowledgeable, spoke great English which helped and was generally just a great guy. We can't thank him enough for making it a memorable trip. The ranch is in a really beautiful valley that most people wouldn't know existed as they generally fly past it heading to Torres del Paine. You can stay down at the ranch and do a multitude if other activities and if we had known this, it was something we would have done (you would probably want to have a car if you were going to do this) The trip was amazing, the views were some of the best we have seen even compared to going into the park which is probably due to the fact that you are just there on your own and also the sunlight that we had at the time. You head out of the valley up on to a ridge with great views along the way. On the ridge we had condors flying just above our heads. They are huge.... On the trip we saw parakeets (bizarre) and eagles. We stopped for lunch, bread, meat cheese, coffee,tea and there were snacks I.e. Cereal bars and fruit and nut mix. The horses were great, we did some trotting (optional) and there was potential for galloping In summary this is a great trip and is worth doing.

review_text: Last Sunday, December 28th, I was part of the al day wine tour of Colchagua valley. I like wine, but am by no means an expert. The day started early (7:30am) and we arrived at the first vineyard around 10:30am after picking up all the people and driving South. Over the day, we visited Apalta, Laura Hartwig, and Viu Manent. Along the way, our guide Jose gave us some Chile wine history during the drive down, and each vineyard tour added there own personal pieces. All wine tastings were included in the tour price, as was lunch which we had a Viu Manent. The restaurant was great, with each person being ale to order off the menu, rather than having a set lunch for everyone. The pace of the tour was good, with time at each winery to taste and purchase wine. Laura Hartwig was a highlight for me. I found the wine there to be some of the best I tasted. I would recommend the tour to any of my friends traveling to the region, but see this being a great tour for anyone wanting to explore and get to know more about Chilean wine. review_text: I did The W from West to East. I stayed at Refugio Gray, Camping Paine Grande, Domo Frances, and Refugio Torre Central. I did the full-day Ice/Glacier Hike and the half-day Glacier Paddle Tours with Bigfoot Patagonia while at Refugio Gray. Both were incredible experiences. I believe that hiking The W from West to East is the better direction because the winds, in general, blow off the glaciers and through the park from West to East. I could not imagine hiking with a backpack, on the roller coaster terrain, with a head wind of 20 - 80 miles per hour. The facilities in the west half of the park(run by Vertice Patagonia) are generally nicer(and the food is better) than the facilities in the East side of the park(run by Fantastico Sur). The weather, as everyone will tell you, is unpredictable. In one 24 hour period I went from trying to stave off dehydration and heat exhaustion to worrying about thermal exposure and hypothermia. If you are interested in hiking The W don't do it as your first backpacking trip and come well prepared.

review_text: Overall Impressions - Chile Off Track would not be my first choice when booking a tour in Chile. I spoke with various western branded hotels during this situation and none of them had heard of this company. - If you are looking for someone to coordinate your activities for a smaller-type group, Chile Off Track may give you a better experience. - As the organizer, I will say that I did not have issues working with the management and I hope that this becomes a learning lesson for them. - In regards to the tour operators, I was very excited to work with Tessa and left unbelievably disappointed in her service and behavior. - They handled our complaint very poorly, and it has resulted in many upset students and a lot of time spent after the end of the trip. Key issues: 1. They were the wrong fit for our group: -- We were a group of 23 international graduate students and two faculty who hired Chile Off Track for our fun weekend events in between two weeks of our studies. -- Chile Off Track is a small operation that although emphasizes personalized tours, are really more a point to point tour company. I imagine they are great for tourists who need help arranging and coordinating fun activities in a foreign place. -- Chile Off Track is knowledgeable about the different sites in Chile and accommodating to your group needs. They will work with your group to get you the activities you want at a reasonable price. -- Although I had had a call with our tour guide, Tessa, prior to the trip to highlight that we wanted a tour that focused on the history/information of the places we were visiting it was clear that this isn’t their forte, and if it is, it wasn’t indicated in their performance. 2. Terrible attitude of the tour guides -- We got off on the wrong foot due to our large group being ~20 minutes tardy but despite a number of attempts to assuage the situation, the tour operators did not act professionally. I had several talks with our guides Tessa and Juana, regarding their tone of voice and their abrasive attitude towards the students. After three separate attempts early on asking them to change their behavior they continued to talk down to the students, scold students who needed to use the bathroom, etc. -- Considering that we had faculty and a clear tour leader, and I had discussed with them on the objective of the day – to learn about the history of Valparaiso, it would have been very easy to start over and enjoy the remainder of the day. -- The tour guide unprofessionalism is the biggest issue that I have with the tour because there were a number of chances to rectify the situation. There was no need for it to escalate. This was an unfortunate situation that should have been turned around considering that we were paying clients who were alerting them to the fact that we were not getting the service we were looking for. 3. Behavior of management towards the customer complaint -- We filed an official complaint with the company after the first tour. The way the company handled the situation after the trip has been very unprofessional. Regardless of the size of the company, when you have a disgruntled customer it is important to understand what went wrong. -- Instead, the mangement chose to take sides and aggressive actions such as recording the telephone conversation with us without letting us know it was being recorded. -- I do believe that because they are a relatively small company their first response might be to get defensive, and when you feel that way you often react without thinking. Also, we held the conversation relatively near the date of the tour, I believe that emotions were high on both sides, which usually leads to less productive conversations. -- In the end, I currently have a number of upset students who paid for a less than fulfilling tour not to mention all the time that I have had to dedicate to resolving a situation that could have been easily rectified. Overall, Chile Off Track wasn't the tour company for us and may be better suited for your needs. I would strongly recommend stating your travel objectives and getting a clear breakdown of your trip should you work with them. I do beleive that they gave us a fair price and had the tour day been managed differently, we would have had a different outcome. Some individuals of this group have behaved in such unpleasant way that these 2 days are marked as black pages in our 6 year history. They arrived late for every tour which caused logistical problems in the planning of the tours, delayed the tours while we were on a walking trip, did not assemble when the guides were giving information, in summary: it felt for our guides as if they were managing a group of young children rather than adults. As management, we proactively sent an email after the first day suggesting a feedback conversation with 1 representative to help us to understand what had happened. In the mean time we offered the group a drink on the house for the next day in response upon their request for Chile Off Track to pay lunch for 25 people as they were not content with the tour. Unfortunately they declined the gesture of a drink. On both days we had our 2 desperate guides numerous times on the phone asking for help to manage the situation as they have never been treated in such a disrespectful way by any of our clients. With a member of the Faculty Management Team we have decided to waive the participation costs of the 2 last minute passengers (417 USD in total) on the first day not to cause any more dissatisfaction. The member of the Management Team has also admitted to our guides that this behaviour of the group has been a pattern throughout their trip. With already having received the feedback from our guides we entered the feedback conversation with the representative. After having heard his feedback we shared with him that we have received the same comments from our guides about the group’s behaviour. We explained to him that we have been working for a number of years with these 2 expert guides in particular and that we have **never** received a negative comment. We told him we would check back with our guides again and meanwhile contact the Faculty Management to find a possible solution. The representative told us he was not interested in feedback about his group’s behaviour and that he could perfectly manage his group. He gave way his true intentions of the “feedback” conversation and claimed a partial refund of the tour, otherwise he threatened to post negative comments about our “little tour company”. Meanwhile we have contacted Faculty Management and addressed the misbehaviour of this group of students, to explain how they have used the Faculty’s name to enforce discounts and finally to threaten a small company with negative reviews on TripAdvisor. In the mean time we have reached the agreement that only one person would write a review representing their group in order to stop the stream of libel by the other students, which for us seems fair. We have worked very hard in the last 6 years to establish the boutique brand of Chile Off Track and as an owner I find it very disappointing that the tours with this group has not worked out the way we both would have wished for. Chile Off Track is a Boutique Tour Company that organizes semi private tours for the sophisticated traveller. Most of our clients stay in boutique hotels or bigger 4 /5 * Hotels and we work closely together with their international concierges. We have been awarded 4 years in a row the Certificate of Excellence on TripAdvisor and have received 156 reviews, of which 143 are 5* reviews. Most of our clients have enjoyed higher education and are well mannered which contributes to a pleasant trip experience.

There is no information on the making or bottling of the wine. This is more the history of the vineyard. After, there is a flight of wines to try with bread and cheese. The sommelier was very informative and friendly. We were not in the least bit rushed. There is a restaurant on site, but we didn't visit it. If you have to stay stay in Santiago, this is a good tour.( If you have an entire day, get a driver and go to Santa Rita winery and book lunch.)

Not on your Bucket List...you might consider putting it there after the Road Awakening.

review_text: Torres del Paine National Park is being loved to death and the concessions (like Fantastico Sur and others who run the refugios) control seem to outweigh park management and habitat concerns. This is a truly magnificent and biologically important area and I can understand everyone’s desire to experience this place. Despite researching the park, reading reviews and travel guides we still weren’t prepared for how very very crowded the W-trek was. The sheer volume of people and supplies brought in to the refugios made for constant traffic. We visited at the end of the main tourist season in mid-March. Torres was our final week in Patagonia after spending a week hiking at El Chalten and the another in the Bariloche region. We started our W-trek at Refugio Paine Grande, staying 2 nights, then hiked eastward, staying 2 nights a Domos Frances and 2 nights at Refugio Chilano. We hiked to Glacier Grey the first day and back to Refugio Paine Grande for the night. On all trails we were constantly jostling with other trekkers, passing them, some passing us, other going the opposite direction. The weather started out rainy so major portions of the trails were muddy or had running water to wade through that people tried to skirt thus widening the trails. Between the trail conditions and the people, it was hard to get into a “hiking rhythm” and immerse yourself in the beauty of the landscape and the place. This was NOT a wilderness experience. The only day that was relatively free of people was when we took the “short cut” (atajo) trail from Domos Frances to Refugio Chilano. We weren’t able to hike the French Valley (Valle del Frances) during our stay at Domos because it was closed due to rainy weather with possibility of erosion and landslides. review_text: At the end of March, my husband and I booked a daytrip from Santiago to Aconcagua National Park with Andes Wind. Guide Christian picked us up at 07h15 in our hotel, to which we returned around 19h15. We paid in Euro’s (€100 p.p.). There were 2 other couples on the trip, making the total of participants 6. This was a comfortable size of the group, for both the drive in the van and for the walk. The drive to Argentina is scenic and doable (3h each way). Christian was of great help by getting us swiftly through border-control. The walk itself was short (5 km) and easy (indicated paths), but very beautiful. It was impressive to see the highest mountain of the Americas, and the vistas on the surrounding landscape are simply stunning. Due to this, we even consider this walk as one of our best, after having hiked for 3 weeks around Chile (Atacama, Easter Island, Patagonia). Personally, I would prefer to hike longer and this may be requested if you are travelling in a group. However, this means that you will be back in Santiago much later (+ 2,5h). On our way back we stopped at a classic ski-resort and a small food market (with fresh fruit and vegetables). Make sure you bring your passport (incl. Chilean border paper), sunscreen, warm clothes and wind jacket, and enough water with you on this trip. To conclude, we recommend this beautiful and easy-going daytrip if you are looking for an activity (after having spent already 1-2 days) in Santiago. It is fun to go to Argentina. It is something you would not easily undertake and arrange yourself (with the hassle of car hire, self-drive, border control etc.). Very much worth it! Thanks for your description and opinon. Going with small groups is the best way to enjoy places like this.

review_text: Our group of 13 took part in a 2 day trip out into the hills. Although I think that they don't normally run it during the winter period, Ellen & Harry were happy to move things around to offer an adventure that worked for us. Everything was really smooth from the start; Tito the driver picked us up from downtown Santiago to take us out to the ranch with no problems. After a delicious welcome lunch we saddled up (complete with hats and ponchos) and headed into the hills on the horses. The animals are all great, very sure-footed and easy to control, even for complete novices. A fantastic dinner, home-made pevre and pisco sours, and the BBQ was genuinely some of the best food that we'd had during our 3 weeks in Chile. Rigo, Victor and the rest of the arrerios are all excellent with the horses and you feel like you're in safe hands throughout - they even tolerated our (fairly dubious) fireside singing with a smile! A great bunch of guys and very professional. If you're after something like an authentic Chilean horse-riding experience, this will definitely not disappoint. I'd recommend this to anyone who'd like a bit of adventure or just to escape from the bustle of Santiago for a day. Great stuff and many thanks again to Ellen & Harry for making this such a special trip! Thank you. THis was a big experience for us too as we don't often take such a big group and we have never camped out in August (midwinter) before so it was a learning experience for us. So glad it all worked out!

review_text: What a lovely surprise in the middle of urban, industrial Santiago! We took the metro and walked a few blocks to the winery, where we were greeted by Andrea, who then took us on a bilingual (English and Portuguese) tour of the historical winery. There were about a dozen people in our group, half Brazilians and half Americans who turned out to be Cuban and Argentine. I particularly enjoyed that the tastings occurred at different points throughout the tour: A white in the restored dining/meeting room, a red in the upstairs storage and processing room (now an events area) and another two reds in the Bordeaux and Bourgogne-style cellars. This winery has a lot of history and is one of the oldest and most traditional in Chile. It was a great place for our first winery tour, as they tend to get more modern (in every sense) as you go into the valleys. Plus we got a half-bottle of Santa Carolina Reserva Carmenere each as a thank you gift! At 24,000 pesos total, accessible by metro and with a take home wine, this was great value and a wonderful experience.

review_text: We were a bit unlucky with the snow conditions and only half the resort was open which limited the amount of skiing we could do however it is obvious that this would be an excellent short stay (maybe 3 /4 days) resort if everything was open. The restaurants are expensive by chilean standards but I guess this is what you expect 3,000m up a mountain. Ski hire and lift passes are expensive so if you have the time, rent your kit down the mountain on the outskirts of Santiago. There are a few things you need to appreciate before booking here 1) It is 3,000m at the base of the resort and even though we'd been at 2,000m plus for the previous week, we still struggled with the lack of oxygen. 2) The road up to the resort is not for the faint hearted. There are 40 switch back turns (that's not counting loads of 90 degree bends) before you turn off to Valle Nevado. There are then about 17 more up to the resort. 3) the road is one way up on weekend mornings and one way down on weekend afternoons. This means that if you have a morning flight to catch on Saturday, you will have to leave the resort on Friday night as you can't get down the mountain until 2pm on Saturday afternoon and transfer companies will not pick you up as the driver has to come up in the morning and then wait until he can take you down. 4) bring everything you need from Santiago if you are staying in a appartment as the shop in the resort stocks nothing - no beer,no wine,no fresh veg,no fruit or meat. 5) even though it is high do not assume great snow. The Andes are a pretty dry mountain range so early season can be marginal Overall good resort but not to North American or European standards but you'll have fun for a couple of days if the snow conditions deliver

review_text: During a visit from my niece and her friend to Chile I booked a cooking class and tour with Boris from Chilean Flavours. Boris came very highly recommended by friends in Santiago so this was the perfect opportunity to go! We were collected from our hostel by Boris in the morning. We explored and wandered around this colourful port city listening to Boris's insightful stories and interesting history of Valparaiso. We discussed menu options on route and then shopped local markets for ingredients to create the dishes we had chosen from Boris's very own cook book. Back at Boris's home we enjoyed every minute of the afternoon. Boris's love for Chile and its cuisine is infectious and we all laughed, cooked, ate and even danced together. This experience was educational and fun for all. Our children, 9 & 11 loved the day and were involved in the preparation and cooking just as much as we were. While we made Piscos, they made their own special Pineapple drink, for which they say was the yummiest drink ever! My niece and her friend, both in their 20's had one of the best days in the 5 weeks of their South American travels! In summary, Chilean flavours is for all ages and I strongly recommend Boris to anyone visiting Valparaiso. All amazing!!!

review_text: We had a mixed experience with Ciclo Austral during our 30-day cycling trip through Patagonia along the Carretera Austral. We initially rented gravel bikes for the first half of the trip and switched to mountain bikes due to changing road conditions. Our experience started off on a rocky note. When we arrived in Puerto Montt to pick up our bikes, the mechanic, Rodrigo, was behind schedule and had to rush through the final bike preparations. Despite being assured that this was for our benefit, we quickly encountered issues: in the first 5 days, we had 5 mechanical failures (4 flat tires and a broken spoke). The spare tubes provided were even double patched, and the tire quality was bad. Additionally, the bikes weren’t supplied with chain oil, which proved essential given the rough road conditions(dusty muddy and rainy) . Thankfully, some fellow cyclists helped us with their own spare tubes. After providing feedback, Ciclo Austral responded promptly and gave us new mountain bikes, checked all our equipment, and provided more spare tubes. This made the second part of our trip much smoother and more enjoyable. The company also offers a helpful app for trip planning, though it could benefit from more detailed maps and bug fixes (particularly missing part from Lago Yelcho to La Junta). Overall, while our experience started off poorly, Ciclo Austral made improvements and provided a great second half of the trip. We would recommend the company, but we strongly suggest double-checking the condition of the equipment, especially gravel bikes, and requesting extra spare materials to avoid any issues while cycling through remote Patagonia.

review_text: If you are comfortable hiking for 4-6 hours, then you can (and should) climb Volcan Villarrica (mispelled above). This is essentially a hike with crampons on--nothing technical about it and very straightforward. The views are incredible the entire way up and you get to summit one of the only volcanoes with an active lava pit (thanks Wikipedia). Also, the way down was the most fun descent I've ever had on a hike/climb. You basically slide down the entire way on your butt, which takes 30-60 minutes depending on the time of year. Awesome. Outdoor enthusiasts: do not miss this Tips: 1) Bring a balaclava to cover your mouth in case the winds shift and blow volcanic gas in your direction. It's safe (so I've heard) to inhale this for short periods of time, but it's also pretty unpleasant. 2) You need a clear day to make the summit, so give yourself a few days of wiggle room in case you get a string of bad weather. 3) Pack lots of high-calorie snacks (in addition to lunch).

review_text: We did the W trek in December 2016. While we were planning (a few months beforehand) we couldn’t find all that much information on the trek so here are my experiences, which I hope will be helpful. I think that West to East is the best way to do the trek, it starts more relaxed and you end with the highlight of Torres del Paine Lookout on your last day. I also think the hike is a bit easier as you don’t have to do the really big uphill from Los Torres to Chileno if you are coming from the West. However, whichever way you do it, it will be great. Our Route Day One: PUERTO NATALES- PUDETO -REFUGIO GREY. We took an early morning bus from Puerto Natales to Pudeto. The bus will stop at the park entrance so you can pay your entrance fee. Our first night booked was at Refugio Grey. Initially we thought we’d be able to get a boat there and also get up close with the glacier. Hotel Grey apparently does offer this service but we found out after we’d booked that it was really expensive and not that accessible to get this boat by regular bus. So instead we took the 11am boat from Pudeto to Paine Grande and walked to Refugio Grey. This took about 4 hours, with lots of stops for photos. We arrived at Refugio Grey at about 4.30. We left our bags and went to the mirador close to check out Glacier Grey. We did a short walk around the mirador then headed back to the refugio for the evening. Day Two: REFUGIO GREY TO REFUGIO PAINE GRANDE. We walked north up to the suspension bridge to get better views of Glacier Grey than came back to Refugio Grey to get our packs and begin our return to Refugio Paine Grande (where we had landed on the boat from Pudeto the day before). It didn’t take as long to get back as we weren’t constantly stopping for photos. The hike back took about 3 hours. We also did a 2 hour walk down towards Mirador Pehoe that afternoon. Day Three: REFUGIO PAINE GRANDE TO REFUGIO CUERNOS. We were expecting this to be a big day- we were going to go from Paine Grande up to the Camp Britannico mirador then head back down to spend the night at Refugio Cuernos. However it was pouring with rain that day. Figuring that the view would be terrible, we decided to make a beeline for Cuernos and see if we could go on to Refugio Los Torres but Refugio Los Torres was full so we couldn’t change our plans. Cuernos is probably the least comfortable refugio we stayed at. It was much smaller, very full with minimal bathroom facilities. The refugio had 2 working toilets (that flushed 50% of the time) for about 60 women, which was not fun. Day Four: REFUGIO CUERNOS- TORRES DEL PAINE LOOKOUT-REFUGIO LOS TORRES. This hike was about 30km, but it was a great day. We walked first to Refugio El Chileno and left our heavy packs there. With little day packs we walked up to Torres Del Paine lookout. The hike is a challenge and very steep in parts, but we were there within 2 hours. We spent about an hour at the lookout as it is simply stunning (lots of photos to take and you need some time to take it all in). We were back at Refugio Chileno by about 3pm that afternoon and began the descent to Los Torres. It was at this point that we realised how lucky we had been not to be making the hiking from Refugio Los Torres up to the Torres Del Paine lookout, as it was really steep! Since we had come from Cuernos that morning, we basically avoided about 2 hours of steep uphill walking. Day Five: Bus out to Puerto Natales. From Refugio Los Torrens there is a bus that will take you directly back to Puerto Natales. You can book on the day, no problem. We went directly on to Punta Arenas. We could not get on a bus immediately from Puerto Natales to Punta Arenas as many were full, so had to wait a few hours at the bus station, but there are several companies that make the trip and buses are regular so there is no need to book in advance. Other useful information: We stayed in refugios (hostels) during our stay, though many people chose to camp. The W trek requires you to book all your accommodation in advance, which means there is very little room for error. The refugios and camp sites tend to fill up (they were definitely busy in December) so don’t count on being able to change your bookings once you’re there. We tried to change one of our bookings due to bad weather and simply couldn’t. I’m sure that it would depend on your luck, but when planning, think about your days carefully and what your plan will be if the weather’s bad. If you want to be safe, it makes sense to take it slow and give yourself a buffer if you run into some rainy days. There are 2 companies that run/own the camp sites and the refugios. Fantastico Sur is the better of the 2, but don’t expect too much from either. They have a captured market, so there is little incentive to provide good service or facilities. Also, you’re there to hike in the wilderness, not hang out at the hostel, so it won’t dampen your trip too much. Another point to note is that if you don’t pre-book your meals, there is a chance you won’t eat much. We wrongly assumed that refugios had restaurants/cafes that you could order food from once you arrived. At Refugio Grey and Cuernos there were no meals for those who didn’t pre-order. You could buy a big empanada for $20 at Cuernos, but it felt like money poorly spent compared to the set dinner. At the bigger Refugios like Paine Grande and Los Torrens there were more snack options.

Go, go, go!

Overall it was a magical experience, not only because the Atacama desert is one of the best places in the world to see the stars but because of Jorge. His tour is a must-do.

review_text: This stunning National Park is divided into three parts, which include Osorno, Petrohué and Peuilla. As a one-day visitor from the cruise port of Puerto Montt the choice as to which area to explore was a difficult one. We decided on the Lake Llanquihue circuit drive that took us in the opposite direction away from the emerald coloured Lago Todos Los Santos and the Saltos de Petrohué waterfall - the latter two are the most popular and touristy places to visit in the National Park. After Fruitillar and Puerto Octay the drive again ran parallel to the lake, then veered onto a separate road that climbed steadily so that we got a closer look at one slope of Osorno Volcano. This was paved so a little better than one rough area on our drive but there were some road works that held us up at one point. What we experienced on the ‘other’ side of the mountain was less traffic, fewer people and some extraordinary views of snow-capped Osorno amongst natural forest and some of the cleanest air imaginable! No notable stopping areas or services here but the lack of traffic meant we could pull over safely to take photos and absorb the backdrop of the volcano against a blue sky. It’s a pity we only had one day, as this park deserves several days to appreciate the serenity, the wilderness and the overall picture postcard magnificence. Hiking is an option but you need to plan for this and the ski area also has a road that gets you even closer to Osorno. Two other notable volcanoes Tronador and Puntiagudo also have commanding peaks within the park. Best of all though the park is free – except for Petrohué. We loved it here! Enjoy your experience!

review_text: The Valparaiso Heritage and Interpretation Center in the Villa Victoria is a family operation run by Kenneth and Victoria Pugh. They have spent more than a year lovingly restoring one of the few houses to have survived the 1906 earthquake and, as a family in period costume, interpret Valparaiso history. They do it in the best way, through stories and a nice multimedia presentation. Before and after our tour Victoria treated us to coffee and tea. They even have Internet. This is an excellent way to get to know and understand Valparaiso. After the tour we sat down with a map of Valparaiso and they gave me a much better idea of how to get around than the people at the tourist information bureau. After the tour we were able to set out on our own to find some of the places they talked about and gain a much better understanding of where we were and why it was important. I strongly recommend this house as an introduction to Valparaiso. Thanks for your valuable comment that has been followed by many visitors, using Villa Victoria as an introduction to Valparaiso. We love to host our guests, as is our place. We are proud of our history and we are most happy when the experience us useful for our visitors.

review_text: We took this tour January 2016 with 8 couples. Our tour started with a pick-up at the cruise port in Valparaiso and was to end in Santiago at our hotels. There were problems right from the start. Our van had no room for luggage – the driver had to take out seats to fit in the suitcases, and they ended up piled up to the roof of the van. Our tour of Valparaiso was fine and our guide was great. Lunch, which was to be a quick stop as we ordered in advance, took over one hour. And the service at the restaurant was awful. Once we left Valparaiso, the guide and driver argued with each other as to how to get to the winery. After several stops, one of which found us hitting a big pothole, which sent the luggage flying, we finally arrived to taste some wines. It only got worse as we headed to Santiago. Neither the driver nor the guide had a map or GPS of Santiago and we were staying at 4 different hotels. Arguments continued between the driver and the guide, neither one of them seemed able to follow directions or a map given to them at one of the hotels. After driving around for well over an hour, we finally got to all the hotels. Thank you for letting us know your opinion of your experience here. I am so sorry that you felt that you had a bad experience. Please allow me to inform certain things that occurred that day. The day before your tour, the original driver got sick and a replacement driver had to come. He did make a mistake not to bring the van configured to the specific amount of people in his service that day. I told him to take out a row of seats, which was how it should have arrived in the first place. He also had his own ideas as to how to get to the different places and our guide had a very hard time giving him instructions. I, personally am not satisfied with this replacement driver either and I have made sure that he will not be driving a van for us again. Sadly, his poor work soils everybody else´s efforts. Regarding lunch, since it´s high season, it´s sometimes hard to find places to eat (that are reservable and reliable) that are not full and have quick service, specially since in Chile, lunch is considered the main meal of the day. The good places tend to offer full sit down lunches which usually take a good while, and those who are in a hurry go to the fast food places, which, adding all of the people interested, end up taking a good while as well. I hope that you liked our local empanadas though. I have talked to the manager of the restaurant regarding service. We´re at the moment evaluating if we continue with this restaurant under new procedures or incorporate another option for a quick lunch service. Please believe me that I´m personally very sorry that your overall experience was less than desired. We´re not used to having our clients feel like they had a bad experience and it really makes us very sad and worried. You can bet that we´re doing everything that we can about it. Thank you once more for taking your time explaining everything. I hope that your overall trip to South America was great! All my best, Cristián Blanco

review_text: The Lapostolle winery is located in a privileged microclimate in Clos Apalta, a subsection of Colchagua. Surrounded on three sides by mountains, it receives the right amount of rain when it counts and gets the cool Pacific breeze at the right time. Adjacent to the winery is a B&B, which is small, luxurioous and extremely well-appointed. the food is delicious and the hotel is centrally located, within easy reach of most Colchagua wineries. Our visit to Clos Apalta was somewhat mixed. The palce is beautiful and the winery is modern, scrupulously clean, light and spacious. Our guide outdid himself to show us the winery and explain the history and the winemaking process. We then descended to the tasting room, which is in the middle of the cellar, at the lowest level. While the palce is beautiful, it is very cold and lighting is dim at best. Therefore, tasting wine is not ideal, especially reds that need to show color and transparency. We had tasted Clos Apalta before and it is an excellent wine. Tasting it on site, you wouldn't know it. The surroundings are wrong for a satisfying wine tasting. They should move it up to the sculpture garden at the top or the adjacent multipurpose hall.

review_text: It will be almost impossible for me to describe in words the amazing experience i had with the aguaventura team!!!! My dream was to climb the volcano with snowboard on my back and to surf all the way down. At the last hour of climbing Manuel suggested to take my board so I could climb easier to the top. We reached the top of the volcano the view was breath taking so as the smoke from the volcano we put the mask and we could breath easily. And then started the fun part we surf and ski from the top to the bottom the guide with ski and me with a snowboard waxed properly by the guys at aguaventura. review_text: We entered the park through the Lenca entrance. It was a bit rough since it's a dirt road to get to the park entrance. You park on the road leading up to the park. You walk next to a rive most of the way, passing one waterfall and several Alerce trees that are quite tall and old. Lots of plant life and trees to learn about while hearing the peaceful sound of the lake. If you are adventurous and want to do the Laguna Chaiquene & Triángulo (9.5 km/5.5 mi), you have to arrive before 11 am, and reach Chaiquene before 1 pm, otherwise you will be denied that second hike, but you can still go to the first lake. Other notes: -Foreigners pay 6000 CLP, in cash. -There are no trash bins, so take your trash. -There is only 1 full bathroom around the 2.5 km mark after the start, so be ready. -There are some parts where you have to ascend without rails nor bars to hang on to. -Go earlier the better to avoid crows (and go to the second lake) -You can't fully swim in either lakes, but you can submerge on it.

review_text: I closed a package with Deyd for the Atacama Desert and the Salar de Uyuni. The guide Esteban was incredible, he gave all the emotional support that a mountain climb requires. I was positively surprised by the crossing to Uyuni, many people talked about the troubles they went through and honestly I have nothing but praise! Even though I booked the package with a shared room, they put us in a private room for the 3 nights of accommodation. The guide Grover was always very attentive, the food was excellent and to top it off with a flourish we arrived at sunset on the mirrored Salar, it was beautiful! review_text: Experienced guide and highly knowledgeable amateur astronomer Jorge Corante has created a truly incredible experience for visitors to San Pedro de Atacama. Exceeded expectations. I left with a greatly increased knowledge of the history and technology of astronomy, the southern night sky, and star maps. After the lecture Jorge set up scope after scope to look at planets, notable stars of various colors, and star clusters. I felt giddy running from scope to scope to peer into the eyepiece. For me, the most interesting was pointing a telescope at what looked like a cloud and finding that it was in fact a cluster of individual stars. It reminded me of many experiences looking through microscopes and more generally of the stomach-dropping excitement that comes with looking at something familiar through a new lens. In addition to passing along his knowledge, Jorge is a warm and inviting host with infectious enthusiasm. I can't recommend this tour enough.

review_text: We did the tour on 1st May and well, where do I begin? We had read that the Atacama was THE place to do stargazing, and though at first we thought it was one of the more expensive things to do, we didn't hesitate to book as the reviews on Jorge were so good. We were not disappointed! He really was worth every bit spent. In fact, due to various reasons, we actually got a Special Astronomical Tour instead of the one we booked, so had even more time (pickup was around 7pm and we didn't finish until after midnight). As is said in another review - don't eat too much beforehand. He says snacks on his website but it's actually an incredibly good spread of food, including some hot soup. Jorge was incredible. He oozed enthusiasm and so much knowledge, and taught us almost anything and everything about the night sky, the history of astronomy and of course plenty of time to observe things through his many telescopes. We even got a few photos taken of us against a starry night sky and emailed through later. We were equipped with blankets, and he does have some great stand-up heaters, but be warned it still gets quite cold - wear a lot of layers!! If you're in the Atacama, we would strongly recommend doing this. It's one of those once-in-a-lifetime opportunities, and if you choose Jorge we guarantee you won't be disappointed. Thanks for a great evening Jorge!

review_text: If you can get a spot on this tour, don't even bother with the other options at the larger observatories. Mamalluca may have a more impressive setup, but del Pangue has the charm, intimacy, and personal investment from the 3 guys running it that make it what it is. These guys are amateur astronomers, but for as knowledgeable as they are of their equipment and subject matter, "amateur" is a misnomer. Between them they can cover tours in English, Spanish, and French. Tour sizes are limited to 5-10 people so you have plenty of time to look at a lot of features in the sky, and while I was there they ran an early tour leaving town around dusk, and late tour a couple hours later. On the occasion I went there were 2 groups of about 7 as they were making up from a cloudy evening the previous night, but with two telescopes on the grounds we didn't even see the other group once we got situated. They have two telescopes, one computer tracking and one that has to moved manually. The latter has the larger mirror and what I was stationed at for the evening. Moving it is extremely easy, but the guides will assist you if you're a bit skittish about it. And even when you're not looking through the eyepiece, just stand off to the side and look up. The views of the night sky there are the most amazing I've ever seen.

review_text: The most beautiful trail race I´ve ever been to. We did the course in 10 hours or so in the context of the "Navarino Trail Race". This wild course is quite dramatic and absolutely enjoyable. You really feel like you are coming back in time to a prehistoric age. Such are the untouched landscapes you experience in this course, which is quite technical. In this 50K trail, different surfaces challenge you: Dirt narrow trails, steep ravines, water crossings, turba (uproar), coastering, small and huge slippery rocks, deep mud, slopes of stones (expect a huge steep slope near Km30 mark or so). All, passing through different landscapes and more than 30 lakes and lagoons. The water of Navarino is said to be the world´s purest. The turba complex system is responsible to filter huge amounts of water as interconnecting so many rivers and lakes. Definitely the most pristine and beautiful place to experience true nature. Bring your GPS along with the course. Otherwise, download a KML, KMZ or GPX file to use with Maps.me or Google Maps.

review_text: La Vega Central houses over 500 fruits, vegetables, meat, and goods stores, and offers a variety of Chilean cuisine. Today, thousands of people pass daily through La Vega’s 60,000 square meters of stalls. In the 19th Century, the area was known as “La Vega del Mapocho” (Mapocho market) and the land was delimited and designated for produce consumption; the construction of La Vega Central started in 1895, with the installation of warehouses made of solid material inaugurated in 1916. Under moonlight, farmers and vendors from around the countryside drive truckloads of fresh fruit and vegetables to this massive fruit and vegetable market. In this place, shop ownersgather to pick the best products to sell in their stalls. They arrive at La Vega between 4 and 5 AM to get the best of the day’s produce, and end around 6 PM, when shops begin to close. Nowadays La Vega Central is a must and has now achieved iconic status in Chile’s capital. I invite you to visit this awesome 100 years old historical site and enjoy its messy, colourful and plenty of history background. Julio Peraldi Cultural and tour guide

review_text: It’s hard to know where to begin this review — there are far too many elements that went into the experience. So perhaps the best place to start is simply to say that the trip was extraordinary in every way. And in no particular order, to then articulate what made it so special. If it’s possible, set aside the fact that the environment, scenery & wildlife in Antarctica are all so entirely unique that it’s impossible not to be awed by its rare & stark beauty. So turn to the ship. In our case, the Hebridean Sky. She’s lovely. Perfectly appointed. Large enough to feel roomy, small enough to feel intimate. We had a suite with a veranda. We never closed our curtains, and relished the constant gorgeous view we were able to enjoy. Next, consider the staff. First of all, the ratio of staff to passengers was beyond luxurious. I believe we had under 70 passengers and about 75 on staff. Nothing was overlooked, delayed, forgotten. Ever member of the staff was dedicated to the safety & happiness of every passenger. And yet, it all lacked pretension. Our trip was simply filled with happy people, passengers & staff alike. It would be impossible to single out any one staff member for one basic reason: each one was brimming with personality & expertise. I can count on one hand the number of trips we’ve ever taken where we could actually say this. Everyone we dealt with was professional; knowledgeable, & filled with good humor. For any of them that may be reading this, THANK YOU for making our trip unforgettable. We didn’t interact much with the captain & bridge crew, but we know they negotiated the waters with skill. We always felt safe, even when the seas turned turbulent. Every day, nimble planning allowed 2 zodiac excursions to fascinating landings. The zodiac rides were as fun as the destinations themselves. The food on the ship wasn’t merely plentiful — it was also first rate. Breakfast, lunch, dinner, hot drinks upon arrival after an excursion, cocktails & appetizers at the early evening daily recap & update sessions. And then, the fellow passengers. An international collection of highly social well traveled people that were friendly & fun to talk & be with. We’d heard from others that any trip to Antarctica can be great. But the company you travel with can either elevate the experience — or not. We honestly cant think of one negative to report. Everything about our trip with Antarctica 21 was superb. Dear HuntleyNewYork First of all, thank you very much on behalf of the whole Antarctica21 team for taking the time and detailing every single aspect of your trip that made it so special. You're right, Antarctica itself is already a fantastic place to visit, and just being there is great, but I'm happy to hear that we were able to elevate that experience for you. It is a great motivation for us to read reviews like yours, thank you so much again for writing it.

review_text: The libreria del desierto is adjacent to the house of the owner, Diego, that together with Valentina and Sofia (their lovely 3-years daughter) lives there. The house and bookstore are no less than an architectural masterpieces, built one year ago in Solor, four km from San Pedro de Atacama. At night, when everything around is dark and the lights inside the house are lit up, the house looks like a starship that has just landed in the desert after having travelled through the amazing star-filled sky above. Outside, both the house and the bookstore are made of eco-friendly adobe. Diego has a degree in Philosophy and is not only the owner of the bookstore, but also a writer and editor. The bookstore is the only one within the radius of 100 KM. It might seem like a big (crazy :-) ) bet to open such a business in the desert, but Diego certainly won that bet, as I saw several customers during our six days stay in SPA. You can find the following topics in the bookstore: anthropology, archeology, ethnology, philosophy, history of Chile, kid's books, maps, etc etc Valentina and Diego will offer you a tea while you are choosing the best book for you. The view of the vulcano Licancabur and Juriques from the bookstore is magical, especially at sunset when they are colored in red

review_text: Great hiking options in this park. Not extensive loops, but enough to keep you busy for a couple of days, even without a boat to take you across the lake. Park at the free parking area, which is right past a paid parking area and closer to the trail. There are three directions visually, and no clear sign pointing to this 12 km trail. The one to the east goes to the lake (a nice place to cool off post-hike), and the middle one goes into a fenced area that looks like a picnic site. Go through the picnic area to a trail, and 500m in there is a sign for "Sendero Paso Desolacion 12km" with a good trail map and altitude guide. 4.3 km to the first junction, through flat, sandy terrain. When you get to a pair of deep arroyo / washes, you are almost there. The junction offers little in the way of places to stop for a lunch (though we did anyhow) but instead gives you the choice of a shorter hike down to alerce tree stands and the lake, or on up to the pass. 1.9 km further, with the latter half up steep sand, is a great look-out. Be careful, as the path divides and there seem to be multiple paths. Generally keep to the lake side of any path splits, though they all go the same general place, the saddle above you is visually obvious as a destination. That saddle is about 1 km further, and for those that are time constrained is a decent end-point. You'll see a waterfall to the east, and great views. At this point the steepness levels off to a gentle climb, as well as the sand giving way to packed sand / rock. Keep going to the end if you can! Why is this marked "Hard" in guidebooks? Here's our take: - Hot, exposed terrain. If it is sunny, bring hats and sunscreen, and plenty of water. - Walking on sand. We are experienced hikers, with plenty of altitude and distance experience. Yet a 400m altitude climb up a sand dune was TOUGH. Don't underestimate this calf-burner. - No exit points. This is what you came for, right? "Desolation". Yet we crossed path with someone who had sprained their ankle who was really suffering. We gave supplies to assist, and when we checked in the next day, it took them OVER 7 hours to do the last 5 km. It's not dangerous terrain, just really slow going if you get in a pinch. (If this was helpful, please hit the "thanks" button.)

review_text: This company deserves more than 5 stars. We waited till the last minute to arrange transportation from Santiago, Chile to our cruise port at San Antonio, which was about 80 mi. Our cruise left Sat. afternoon and since we had already booked a hotel in San Antonio for Fri night we were looking for possibly a wine tour or something to do on Fri. along the way down. He arranged for a personalized tour with our driver, Santiago, who drove my husband and me to 2 wineries (Undurraga & Chocolan) arranging for an hr long tour at Undurraga. He drove us to a small village (Pomaire) where we watched them make pottery and had a great lunch. We made an unexpected stop along Rt 78 at a strawberry farm where we were given some sweet, sweet strawberries to enjoy. review_text: Located in the Las Condes area of Santiago, this is one of the nicest urban parks we have visited. Everything was clean and well manicured. During our visit we saw many locals taking an exercise class, joggers passing by, and people just lounging on the well-maintained lawns. Along the park there were sculptures, an event center (Centro Parque), a couple of children's entertainment venues (Kidzania and Selva Viva) a skateboard area, exercise machines, a climbing playground, a dog park area, an artistic bridge over the boulevard Av. Manquehue, and even a playground for very young children across the street from a kindergarten school. We also appreciated the many signs asking people to clean up after their dogs and to help keep the park clean. This spacious park was a relaxing end to our three-week trip to Chile.

If you’re looking for a truly professional and supportive expedition crew, look no further 😉

review_text: We booked with another agency but were grouped with others on this tour. This trip is highly recommended, however, as we didnt speak Spaish we would have struggled without one of the other members in the car who spoke both English and Spaish. The driver/guide didnt speak a word of English although we were told he would. Towards the end of the trip however we were starting to get to grips with it and actually managed to understand some of it! Bonus. The trip itself was great, so many things to see and do, various coloured lagoons, thermal spas, guisers, flamingos, llamas, and a canyon that looked like an anaconda. This is all before we got to the main attraction which was the salt flats! We were up for sunrise on the saltflats and the pictures will never do it justice. We took a walk around an island of cacti, whilst our guide made us breakfast on the saltflats and then spent 40 minutes takig stupid pictures of each other danching out of pringle cans!!! We stayed in basic accommodation with shared bathrooms but it is possible to pay more and have private rooms and bathrooms. However we met some really nice people and enjoyed sharing a room with them. The food is basic but very filling and we had 2 hungry men at our table. On the last evening we stayed in a salt hotel/hostel, had wine and llama steak, which was actually quite tasty. All in all this was a fun packed, informative (thanks to our resident interpreter) and worth while trip. We would and have recommended it to anyone that has asked.

review_text: Based on what I learned during my winery tour, this winery is all about returning to more natural methods of wine-making. They are also diversifying into fruit-flavoured alcohols and balsamic vinegar as well. The buildings are very attractive and relaxing, especially the patio seating area outside the boutique. The wine cellar itself is beautifully set up, and you could see the care that had gone into making the clay pots and even the adobe walls. The cellar is naturally ventilated through spacing in the wooden roof of the building. The wines we tasted were mostly blends, and quite lovely. But the pure Carignan wine was both the most interesting and enjoyable. Our winery guide was quite knowledgeable and pleasant, making the visit a pleasure overall.

review_text: I've just done the 9-day Full Circuit trek. Fabulous. Wonderful, Amazing. Torres Del Paine is such a globally renowned destination that giving it five stars is the easy part; you know it will be stunning before you even arrive. Perhaps the best additional advice I can give is to recommend you carefully plan the season for your visit. We trekked in the first week of November; i.e. the shoulder (beginning) of the summer season, and I would thoroughly recommend that period. It's a bit colder, of course, but there were relatively few trekkers on the trail and we were extremely fortunate to have fine weather for (almost) the entire week, which is of course almost unheard of in Torres Del Paine. Having visited the refugios, I can well imagine that the big crowds that arrive in the summer season (December-February) would significantly detract from the experience, and personally couldn't think of anything worse than having to endure them both at the campsites and on the trail. Go early in the season or right at the end (March-April) - it will make for a far more enjoyable visit.

review_text: We stopped at this place after a long tour in the area, and after chasing it for a while (it was a bit difficult to find as the number was unknown!). Respect to many other places we have seen in the area the place is sort of peculiar. Not one of those run-down, decadent and careless places very common here, and neither one of those supposedly international restaurant that fill the area. This is something chilean but with some personality: typical menu, ok, but well done, well prepared, served with care. And here it is: the difference is really in the service. All the many young waiters that served us were extremely friendly, nice, attentive, and try to serve as quickly and honestly. The pork ribs were really good with the "arroz arabe". And so was the tabla montaña. The place has a pretty strange arrangment, quite typical here but with a personal twist. Not really cheap, but it is so much better than the typical other area that it's ok. Nice people, nice place, nice food. Last but not least: good music from Manuel Garcia, a chilean singer, as a background (the waiter told us that he played here and is a regular customer). As we cannot withstand Reggaeton, so common here, we would be back just for this reason! :) Bravi! Continuate così! (= keep going like that).

review_text: A great hike - strenuous and beautiful. There is one main trail (i don't think there are options). It's basically in the shape of a P. It's 12km long and takes about 5 hours return. You start at the bottom of the P... hike to the middle of it (all under the sight of the Volcano Osorno which is gorgeous). The first part of the hike is desolate. And the hike is appropriately called desolation! Remember this is all at the base of a volcano. When you get to the P you keep going straight where you are going to make your loop (up the straight part of the P). Then you turn right and down to the lake - where eventually you make your way to a hidden lake) to rest. It's quiet and gorgeous. Lovely! Then of course you can either walk back around or if you prefer (and it's summer) walk the beach back (which is not part of the P) but would look more like an upside down U if you were hiking it. Now, two tips. And these are IMPORTANT! 1- there is free parking right behind the paid parking lot. Don't waste 5,000 pesos paying for paid parking. 2- and most most most importantly - bring a hat or a fly swatter or something that you can use to bat away the terribly large and annoying flies that exist in this park. If you hit them they actually leave you - but if you don't they will stay with you the whole hike. I got good at batting them away so wasn't overly annoyed once I figured out the secret. The secret is to stop once a fly circles you. Just wait and you'll see the pattern he flies in around and around you. Then bat him away with your hat/swatter. When you do - he leaves. I saw others who didn't know how to get rid of them and they were sooo upset. I mean one guy was screaming get them away from me! It was quite funny. But after 5 hours of them... it does get rather annoying.

review_text: What a delightful day we spent exploring Santiago and soaking in the history of this vibrant and artistic city founded over five hundred years ago. All of this was made possible with the good humor, quick wit and vast knowledge imparted to us by Thomas Poussard, tour guide extraordinaire. My friend and I were heading towards Valparaiso for a cruise to French Polynesia and we spent the day and night in Santiago to get a taste of Chile. We only wished we had made more time for this wonderful city. Thomas and his friend and fellow guide Claudia picked us up at our hotel and we spent the next six hours seeing the historic downtown (the entire city is historic), visiting the Bellavista area and the ecclectic house of famous poet Pablo Neruda and the cathedral. My favorite part of the day was visiting an incredible wine bar with flights of Chilean wine. The owner had ingenious markings for the bathrooms using drawings of a wine opener to indicate male, female and handicapped differences! Truly fun. If you find yourself going to Chile call Thomas first, tell him what you want to see and he will magically make your Chilean dreams come true. Well worth the price for a private tour at your pace.

review_text: We emailed in advance of our trip to see if there were possibilities of scheduling an ice hiking trip given the season hadn't exactly started yet (we ice-hiked on Sep 23), and fortunately we were able to slot it in as weather conditions were favorable. We were also the 2nd trip of the season! Pedro was our main guide, and was thankful that he spoke very good english given that we spoke very little Spanish. He was very knowledgeable and made us feel safe the entire trip, and was extremely careful and attentive given it was our first ice-hiking experience. It was definitely worth every penny, and we had some awesome photos and videos to go with this experience! I would highly recommend them. The guides also gave great advice on our W trek, and even helped us lug a small ice glacier on our boat ride back because Mark's knee was twitchy. We felt really thankful for that - we were able to hike the rest of our W trek having taken their advice seriously. We had a lot of fun skipping stones, taking GoPro videos and talking about outdoor adventures together. Also, one small note, we did this one day 2 of our W trek, hiking West to East - best decision ever since somehow hiking 1 day behind everyone else that probably flew in to Punta Arenas and rode into Puerto Natales the same day meant we hiked a lot of the remaining route in solitude! Awesome!

review_text: I booked the Pacific Coast tour as a solo trip on January 3rd. I highly recommend Albatross Birding. The birding was excellent. Fernando Diaz, the owner, was my guide, and he is an exceptionally talented birder and a gracious and professional guide. In addition, he is involved in and knowledgeable about many aspects of environmental conservation, outreach, and ornithology in Chile and South America, so we had some great conversations about birding, conservation, etc. Honestly, much of the day felt like being back home, birding with my semi-professional birding friends...except that Fernando was patient with my constant, "what bird is singing that song?" questions. He took lots and lots of time to try to coax out a calling Black Rail (ultimately without luck) and a Striped-back Bittern (with luck!) I appreciated the professional commitment he made to ensuring we saw as many species as possible. He also quickly understood my interest in learning more about natural history, species behavior, etc., rather than just ticking off species, so for me the day was a rich and full birding experience. review_text: The easiest way to get to La Sebastiana is by taxi, but you would miss all the charm of the Ascensores (funiculars) which make visiting Valpo (as Valparaíso is affectionately known) a truly unique experience. The closest of the Ascensores to La Sebastiana is the Espiritu Santo (which is under repair now in January 2018), but you can also take the Reina Victoria Ascensor (closest to the Bellavista subway station) and walk to the San Luis Church, where you will take a micro (bus) that will drop you off on the corner of Calle Ricardo de Ferrari. There are three Casas de Pablo Neruda in Chile and in La Sebastiana you will learn how Pablo Neruda was a Master in enjoying life to the fullest. After visiting his house, you may want to take a stroll around the streets of Valpo and appreciate several houses and walls that are painted in many different colours and styles. These are called "Museo a Cielo Abierto" ("Open Air Museum"). You will also find a couple of places where you can stop for a quick meal, as you walk all the way down, back to the hustle and bustle that awaits you in the city below. The amazingly beautiful streets of the upper hills of Valparaíso remind us of Montmartre (it is the same "feeling", as many artists prefer to live and work there) but the way these charming colours contrast with the port of Valpo below is unique.

review_text: I write this from the viewpoint of a couple who have taken courses at UC Davis in enology and viticulture but still consider themselves amateurs. When we come back in the spring we will tour with him again. Review of: Best Wine Tasting in Santiago

review_text: THE tour to book! Whether you are a wildlife fanatic, or not even so much; you will love this tour. The enthousiasm with which tourguide Zita shares her love for Whales, Guanacas, Desert Foxes, Sea Lions and a lot more beautiful creatures living in the area has a very infectuous effect on the entire group. If you didnt love animals before; you will after this tour. Plus, they give so much info on every aspect of these animals, you will feel like an expert yourself! The day starts off early, since it is a 2 hour ride to where the boat tour starts. But you can step out of bed into the car without breakfast; because everything is taken care off by Zita. During this ride Zita will tell you already so much about the environment and the animals living there, time will fly. Halfway there is a breakfast break in the middle of the desert. Be aware; it will be the most elaborate breakfast you will have on your entire holiday; so dont eat too much before!:) Once you arrive at the small town/harbour you are welcomed by the local guardians of nature (CONAF). You also meet their local partners who offer the boat and are the experts on where to spot the whales and other animals. review_text: This mine tour was recommended by a couple of Chileans we met on the trip, and it certainly was worthwhile. Started in 1884, the coal mine was closed in 1976, and I don't think much has changed! The tour itself is in Spanish -- the guides are ex-miners -- so we missed out on quite a bit I know, but it was still a worthwhile experience. You are fitted with a lighted miner's helmet and battery pack, taken down in a cage-basket elevator, then walk through the mine (a little further down) and finally up and out. This is obviously not for the claustrophobic -- at times we were practically on our knees getting through some of the passages -- and it could be difficult for tall people; I'm 5'8" and I had to walk stooped over much of the time. Still a unique experience and a fascinating look into the conditions in which people had to work.
