review_text: We traveled to Atacama in December 2024 and did all the tours with Ayllu. The differential of the company in fact are the meals offered on the tours that are very good. However, the amounts charged are quite high and the services offered should be better in order for the price to be fair. Our first days of tours went smoothly, all walking according to the schedule, which is the minimum. More to the middle of our trip we made a tour with a guide from the agency, who had already accompanied us earlier. The trip to the Altiplanas and Rojas stones lagoons leaves early and the guide in addition to driving super badly (having given light exits from the road a few times), was all the way drinking coffee and energetic, chocolate and asking for music so that it did not give him sleep at the wheel. In addition to speaking energetically at all times and being "on 220v". We followed the tour and, in addition to the strange behavior of the guide, the stove used to be part of the breakfast leaked gas, we were in a closed car and the incident was noticed by us, which left me quite tense (the worst is that this was not the only situation in which the gas from the stove leaked into the car, it occurred again beyond this). I feel that we did not enjoy this tour as much as expected with the constant tension caused by the wrong direction of the guide and their signals that you could sleep at the wheel and the gas incident. Besides other small incidents, which did not prevent the good follow-up of our journey, another complicadissima situation was the fact that on the last day we had marked an ascension to the Volcano Lascar. However, 2 days before we climbed the Cerro Toco and it was a very difficult ride for us because of the altitude (my fiancé was suffering from headaches throughout the afternoon even taking medication and I with a fast heart), with this we decided to preserve our body and health and request a change from the last day's ride. I tried to contact the agent who came to assist me and she did not receive the messages, when she received I was directed to another number to which I sent the request for a change of ticket. The same number had spoken to me earlier about the ride we would have that night. The number answered me, I asked about 2 specific tours, he informed me, said that some details would need to be confirmed, but gave me an advance of the values, duration, dynamics of the tour, schedule and also informed that we could receive a refund of the difference in values between the tour we had contracted (and already paid) and the new one. The next day we headed for the day's walk, confident that the next day, our last day of trip, was resolved. Our illusion, when we arrived at the hotel and we had access to the Internet we were informed that we had spoken with an AI of the company that passed us all the wrong information. And that was the beginning of chaos. Frustrated and disappointed, I lost an entire afternoon and night until I was able to define with the company what we would actually do. We were not granted the refund of the difference in values (which although it was not provided in the contract we were informed that there would be), we were introduced to solutions that when questioned the logistics they said that would not give and we had the owner of the company going to our hotel without warning for 2 times. One we were not and the other we were already lying in pyjamas and we did not attend. The next day we went for a tour (tour in the region's vineyard) which we considered extremely expensive because it was what I had for that day (this IA had told us that this tour would be between 70 and 100 dollars, they later told us that it was 220 dollars for about 3 hours of tour, which I consider an exorbitant value, especially for the size of the vineyard which is quite small). We still had to hear for a few times from the guide and owner of the company that we "yellowed", which sounded a disrespectful and disguised posture that left us super embarrassed, even because there was another guide in the car. He proposed another tour at the end of the day, which we went, but we had to pay for the entrance to the park. And when he left us at the hotel still tried to sell us the photos and videos he took along the way for a value between 100 and 200 dollars. We chose this agency for the proposal to offer a premium service, in the illusion that we would not have all these problems, but the values showed exorbitant before the service provided. In addition to these highlighted problems, we still had the car without battery in the middle of a road without a phone signal when we returned from Rota dos Solares, following the road by the force of gravity, since it was a descent, and the car being controlled by the brake). If I went back to Atacama I would not return with them, with all this stress at the end of the trip we could not return from the holiday happy, satisfied and relaxed as we hoped. I'm still without words and digesting everything that happened...

review_text: Lake Llanquihue is not the largest lake in Chile (Lago General Carrera in the Aysen Region of Chile is almost twice as large as Lago Llanquihue), but this is probably one of the most beautiful locations in Chile. Best time to visit is during spring or fall, so one can avoid the tourist crowds and still enjoy decent weather. The lake is pretty just about any day of the year, but it is gorgeous during a sunny, clear day when you can appreciate the whole size of the lake and the incredible view of the surrounding snow-capped volcanoes. Besides visiting P. Varas, it is worth taking a trip to neighbouring Frutillar, Llanquihue town, Puerto Octay, and if you possibly can, take a trip around the whole lake via Las Cascadas and Ensenada where you can see the beautiful Osorno Volcano at close range.

review_text: This review covers a trip to Antarctica in December of 2013. It consisted of two nights in Punta Arenas (the night before and the night after the cruise) and five nights onboard the Ocean Nova. This particular cruise includes flights between Punta Arenas and King George Island, rather than taking the ship across the Drake Passage. We wanted to avoid the rough seas typical of a trip across the Drake Passage. We booked the cruise through Polar Cruises, a travel agency located in Seattle; the land arrangements in Punta Arenas and the air travel to/from King George Island and the shore expeditions to Antarctica were handled by Antarctica XXI; the shipboard operations were handled by Ocean Nova. All three organizations handled their responsibilities very well. Polar Cruises provide good guidance in making the arrangements, preparing for the trip, and handling payment. All of the Antarctica XXI staff were excellent, with good support from the time we arrived at the airport in Punta Arenas until we departed Punta Arenas for our return home. The shipboard Antarctica XXI staff were very knowledgeable about Antarctica and very friendly and helpful. There were two shore expeditions daily, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. Each one lasted 2-3 hours, which is long enough to experience Antarctica, but not so long as to end in exhaustion. Although the weather was cold (especially when riding in the Zodiacs), as long as the pre-departure suggestions for clothing and gear were followed, it was not unpleasant. They also offer (at an additional cost) options for sea kayaking and shoe-shoeing. The Ocean Nova is a great ship for visiting Antarctica: the maximum number of passengers is 68 (we had only 49); the cabins are spacious; the onboard service is very good, the food was great (not overly fancy, but well prepared and plentiful without being overdone); and since the hull is reinforced, it can break through moderate ice. There is a spacious observation deck (fore) and a library (aft) that have panoramic windows. The views were always spectacular. There are six Zodiacs on board, so everyone can go ashore at the same time. The staff are very well trained, so it feels like it is possible to have an exciting and informative expedition, while always feeling safe in a very demanding environment.

review_text: This bronze equestrian statue of José Miguel Carrera Verdugo stands on a marble plinth in Citizenship Park, opposite the Moneda Palace in Santiago de Chile. José Miguel Carrera Verdugo was a Chilean patriot general and dictator who fought Spain for years for Independence and served as head of government when breaks in the fighting allowed. He was a charismatic leader but a short-sighted administrator and an average military leader. Often at odds with Chile's liberator, Bernardo O'Higgins. He was executed in 1821 for conspiring against O'Higgins and Argentine liberator José de San Martín. The conflict between followers of O’Higgins and Carrera continues to some extent to this day, but this does not prevent their equestrian statues from standing next to each other opposite the Moneda Palace in Santiago de Chile. TIP: There are many concrete benches around to sit on but little shade.

review_text: We did the cruise from Puerto Montt to Puerto Natales in march 2012. It is important to know that it is a ferry, not a luxury boat. Your cabins are small (depending on the price you are willing to pay), food is the same for everyone and no continuous entertainement is given. We had the cabin to share (4 people), no window and shared bathroom. As we did not stay in the cabin, it being small was not a problem (but you still have to coordinate with the other people when you need to enter the cabin or use your bag). The food was honestly ok. Breakfast can be light and there is nothing for a snack, so you have to foresee that point (a few biscuits in your bag and it's ok!). Price is quite high, but you are on full board for 3 nights and almost 4 days. We had good weather half the time of the cruise. Those days were really good, enjoying the view and the dolphins, birds or sea lions in the outdoor. We had rain for 2 days so not so funny. Prepare a book to keep you busy just in case. A good thing is that they present flora and fauna power points during the trip. Nicely done and very useful! People can get sick when the boat reaches the ocean as the waves become more important. A little pill can help you have a good night. It allowed us to meet some very nice people who became friends. Prepare to have some good times.

review_text: I GOT ROBBED IN PARQUE FORESTAL A COUPLE MONTHS AGO! This was in broad daylight and there were plenty of people around. The police and the people at the U.S. embassy weren't at all surprised when I told them about it--they had heard the same story many times. Here's how it happened: I was walking through this park taking pictures (so, yes, they were attracted to my camera, an SLR); actually I saw them checking me out and I even wanted to get a shot of them b/c they were such a clearly sinister-looking gang, kinda night-clubby/druggie types with shaved heads (not skinhead-like, rather those sorta fancy shave jobs) all sitting around a picnic table. Just after I passed them a guy who looked like one of them asks me what time it is--this is to hear my voice and establish that I'm a tourist (and it also showed them that I had an iPhone). A few seconds later something soft and wet hits me on the back of my neck--bird crap or something like it. A woman comes up to me and is helping me clean it off--she's got bottle of water and some kleenex; she gets me to take off my jacket so she can clean it off, but then to get my jacket off I have to take off my bag and camera and put them on the park bench next to me (at the embassy they told me it's always a woman doing this part). Then a guy comes up and makes a noise and stares at me (he looked like the rest of them too); this distracts me from the bag and camera; then this little old man tells me my stuff is gone and tells me that they went that-a-way (out of the park) and is running after them and getting me to follow and then telling me that they're getting on this bus that's pulling away. So that's it. Again, totally light out, plenty of people around, very nice area, and happens all the time. So if you get hit my bird crap or whatever, just get out of there. During my 3 weeks in Chile--and before I got hit--i also heard about another tourist who had all his camera gear stolen in Santiago; and in Valparaiso I saw the end of an operation like the one I got hit with: people running onto a bus I was on in a big hurry, all excited, acting like they were looking for somebody (though it wasn't very good acting), and then jumping out of the bus through the back door. So it's definitely not uncommon. I should also add that I'm 5'10", male, a New York City, and a big traveler. So not a particularly obvious target other than the camera and the fact they I was clearly a tourist. All that said, I generally liked Santiago a lot, loved Valparaiso, and loved Patagonia. And Parque Forestal was, ironically, the prettiest and most peaceful place in Santiago. Just be prepared...

review_text: My close friend consider me as a seasoned mountain hiker and a nature enthusiast. Although this was my second trip to Chile, I visited Torres del Paine for the first time. On my arrival, I was mesmerized by the beauty of the Canadian Rockies and the Norwegian coast as well as the history of Wild West - everything put in one place: Region de Magallanes. Because of time constraints, my trip to Torres del Paine fell within the shoulder season, so - as expected - the weather did not want to cooperate and the bus service from Puerto Natales to the Park was quite infrequent. To make the things even worse - my budget was really tight. But I was very lucky to use the 'Go Calafate Chalten!' travel agency and managed to do a very exciting full-day trip of the National Park. For the next day, Ivan (the owner) together with Fernando (the guide) suggested me to take another full-day trip including individual hikes to two selected Miradores (Condor and Cuernos). And finally, on the third day I did the hike that leads to the Base del Torres. Not only does the Torres del Paine National Park look magnificent, but it also smells nice with Nothofagus Antarctica! These hikes whetted my appetite for the famous W-hike or the Loop, which I hope to complete on my next trip to Chile.

review_text: My girlfriend and I hiked the W Hike in early January of 2011 (OK, we did more of an “N” hike instead of the official “W” – more on that later, but it worked out great). We flew into Punta Arenas around 11:45Am and rented an economy car from Europcar at the airport counter and made what seemed to be about a 5-6 hour drive to the Las Torres hotel (be sure to get gas on the way in Puerto Natales – we had read there was a gas station in Cerro Castillo, but when I asked around in Cerro for it - yes I speak Spanish – 2 people at the local store said there was none – I was later told they say this so the locals can save the fuel for local use – which I have no issue with). The local store did have gas canisters for our camping stove. We were concerned about the dirt roads that lead into and around the park, but our little econobox held up and so did the tires (it did fill with dust while driving…but life is sometimes a dusty adventure). Stop at the park entrance and pick up your hiking/park pass (about $50/person) and then enjoy the rickety old one lane bridge that leads to the hotel. Las Torres hotel is in a great location – right near the trailheads – has beautiful views – and free range horse running around (we heard munching outside our window and opened the curtain to find a horse chowing right there). The rooms are clean with few amenities, but the location is why you are there – and their front desk has good info on trails/buses/etc. We readied our backpacks/camping gear for the next 4 days, ate from the satisfying but less expensive bar menu and prepared for the next day. Next day we stored our remaining baggage in our rental and left it in the hotel lot (we asked and they said this is perfectly fine as we would be returning to the hotel in 4 days. We hit the trail (it's right next to the hotel) and started the approx. 6 mile hike to Campamiento Las Torres – it’s a bit of an uphill climb but you get there eventually. You can also stop at Refuge Chileno on the way and grab some snacks/drinks. We set up camp (u arrive and pick a spot – there seemed to be plenty but they filled up as evening fell) – there are a few toilets, but you have to filter your own water. It was clear, so we were advised to head up to the Las Torres viewpoint as the weather changes quickly and you might miss them the next day. We hiked up with a day pack/water/lunch (it’s about an hour away – up thru a large rock field) and…wow…what a view…when the towers come into sight they are amazing. We scrambled around the area to get the best views and some seclusion and headed back (bring hiking sticks up there – you will definitely enjoy them on the way down – it’s slippery dust/pebbles in many areas). Next day we got up early for the looooong 12 or so mile trek to Cuernos Cabanas (you have to reserve a cabin ahead of time..and it’s worth it). We were concerned about finding the shortcut that leads you in the right direction (instead of having to backtrack all the way to the Las Torres Hotel) – but it was signed and seemed easy to find. The scenery to the right is amazing with the mountains – and keeps getting better. The trail rises and falls most of the way, with some steadier climbs towards the end. There are plenty of places to filter water, in fact, you’ll find some of the water crossings interesting (again, you’ll appreciate hiking sticks and your ability to balance). Waterproof boots will also help. As you approach Cuernos Cabanas the views of the Cuernos and approaching French Valley are pretty cool. The Cabanas are very basic (2 beds/linens – with a communal bathroom for the cabanas) – but very welcome after a night in a tent. The cabanas have great views of the lake/mountains. There’s even a wood burning hottub for the Cabana guests. Meals (we reserved dinner and breakfast ahead of time) were just so-so and are in a communal hall – and most importantly, they sell beer and snacks! Next morning we awoke for the approx. 6 mile hike to Campamiento Brittanico…the weather looked…well, ominous. After breakfast we hit the trail and started into the valley – the trail is mostly flat at first, but then begins climbing (the trail can be occasionally steep/slippery in sections and rocky in others – again hiking sticks helped a lot). For a brief time the sky turned nasty gray and it opened up on us with rain/high winds…but died down after about 20 minutes. The views to the left are postcard amazing – the glaciers hanging over the mountains with occasional avalanches thundering down make for a stunning walk. One of the best views I’ve ever seen (also - there are plenty of places to filter water along the trail). As you finish most of the climb you get to an exposed viewpoint with even better views – and in our case blasting winds. Once off there you head into the woods and the wind dies down. The trail winds thru the woods (OK – they are beautiful, but the trees are a little creepy at the same time…kinda like a haunted forest – with no sounds…and very few people hike this far). The 6 miles seemed longer than 6 – but you eventually make it to Campo Brittanico and find a camping spot – we saw around 10-15 scattered about in the woods (most stayed empty) – you’ll know them by the twig/log wind breaks built in front of each. This seemed to be an omen so we tied down our tent, ate dinner and went to sleep. Fortunately the wind didn’t re-appear that night… FYI – no restrooms, but worth the seclusion. In the morning we packed up and headed for the roughly 8 mile trek to Refuge Pehoe. Good news – it’s mostly downhill with the same amazing mountain views. The trail opens up with fewer trees (and less shade) and winds its way to Pehoe (this was the less scenic part of the trail, but we’re not complaining, it still has good views over your shoulder). We we’re on a schedule to grab the 12:30PM catamaran to Pudeto and made it with plenty of time (it was about $30/person). The refuge looks pretty new and has a good food/snack shop. The backpackers/dayhikers boarded the boat (plenty of room on board) and we were off to Pudeto. Some nice views from the rear deck. We arrived at Pudeto and found 3-4 large buses waiting. We found the bus back to Hotel Las Torres and hopped on (bring $ - be sure it’s paper money to reduce your pack weight). There seemed to be plenty of seats – the bus was less than half full. The bus drops you at the park entrance where you initially had to buy your passes. Here you get transferred to a shuttle to the hotel (this also cost $ - which didn’t seem right, but we were glad to pay it so we would be closer to a shower). We were surprised that the shuttle doesn’t take you all the way to the hotel and you have to walk the last ½ mile (something about they are not allowed to go the last ½ mile due to it being private land) – but again…a hot shower and beer awaited. We re-checked in – got our bag from the car and enjoyed a long shower and clean clothes. Next day we packed up and drove to Hosteria Lago Gray for the 2PM glacier boat tour (a little over $100/person) to complete our “W” (can’t remember how long the drive was, but the hotel can tell you). The reason we called it the “N” instead of the “W” hike is because we didn’t hike the last section up to Refugio Gray and back – we figured we would get better views of the glacier from the boat. We were glad we did - the views from the boat are awesome (and so are the Pisco Sours made with glacier ice) – the glaciers have cool/vibrant blue colors and you can see calving if you’re lucky. That’s about it – enjoy and bring a big memory card for your "N" hike experience. Buena Suerte!

The rooms are clean with few amenities, but the location is why you are there – and their front desk has good info on trails/buses/etc. We readied our backpacks/camping gear for the next 4 days, ate from the satisfying but less expensive bar menu and prepared for the next day. Next day we stored our remaining baggage in our rental and left it in the hotel lot (we asked and they said this is perfectly fine as we would be returning to the hotel in 4 days. We hit the trail (it's right next to the hotel) and started the approx. 6 mile hike to Campamiento Las Torres – it’s a bit of an uphill climb but you get there eventually. You can also stop at Refuge Chileno on the way and grab some snacks/drinks. We set up camp (u arrive and pick a spot – there seemed to be plenty but they filled up as evening fell) – there are a few toilets, but you have to filter your own water. It was clear, so we were advised to head up to the Las Torres viewpoint as the weather changes quickly and you might miss them the next day. We hiked up with a day pack/water/lunch (it’s about an hour away – up thru a large rock field) and…wow…what a view…when the towers come into sight they are amazing. We scrambled around the area to get the best views and some seclusion and headed back (bring hiking sticks up there – you will definitely enjoy them on the way down – it’s slippery dust/pebbles in many areas). Next day we got up early for the looooong 12 or so mile trek to Cuernos Cabanas (you have to reserve a cabin ahead of time..and it’s worth it). We were concerned about finding the shortcut that leads you in the right direction (instead of having to backtrack all the way to the Las Torres Hotel) – but it was signed and seemed easy to find. The scenery to the right is amazing with the mountains – and keeps getting better. The trail rises and falls most of the way, with some steadier climbs towards the end. There are plenty of places to filter water, in fact, you’ll find some of the water crossings interesting (again, you’ll appreciate hiking sticks and your ability to balance). Waterproof boots will also help. As you approach Cuernos Cabanas the views of the Cuernos and approaching French Valley are pretty cool. The Cabanas are very basic (2 beds/linens – with a communal bathroom for the cabanas) – but very welcome after a night in a tent. The cabanas have great views of the lake/mountains. There’s even a wood burning hottub for the Cabana guests. Meals (we reserved dinner and breakfast ahead of time) were just so-so and are in a communal hall – and most importantly, they sell beer and snacks! Next morning we awoke for the approx. 6 mile hike to Campamiento Brittanico…the weather looked…well, ominous. After breakfast we hit the trail and started into the valley – the trail is mostly flat at first, but then begins climbing (the trail can be occasionally steep/slippery in sections and rocky in others – again hiking sticks helped a lot). For a brief time the sky turned nasty gray and it opened up on us with rain/high winds…but died down after about 20 minutes. The views to the left are postcard amazing – the glaciers hanging over the mountains with occasional avalanches thundering down make for a stunning walk. One of the best views I’ve ever seen (also - there are plenty of places to filter water along the trail). As you finish most of the climb you get to an exposed viewpoint with even better views – and in our case blasting winds. Once off there you head into the woods and the wind dies down. The trail winds thru the woods (OK – they are beautiful, but the trees are a little creepy at the same time…kinda like a haunted forest – with no sounds…and very few people hike this far). The 6 miles seemed longer than 6 – but you eventually make it to Campo Brittanico and find a camping spot – we saw around 10-15 scattered about in the woods (most stayed empty) – you’ll know them by the twig/log wind breaks built in front of each. This seemed to be an omen so we tied down our tent, ate dinner and went to sleep. Fortunately the wind didn’t re-appear that night… FYI – no restrooms, but worth the seclusion. In the morning we packed up and headed for the roughly 8 mile trek to Refuge Pehoe. Good news – it’s mostly downhill with the same amazing mountain views. The trail opens up with fewer trees (and less shade) and winds its way to Pehoe (this was the less scenic part of the trail, but we’re not complaining, it still has good views over your shoulder). We we’re on a schedule to grab the 12:30PM catamaran to Pudeto and made it with plenty of time (it was about $30/person). The refuge looks pretty new and has a good food/snack shop. The backpackers/dayhikers boarded the boat (plenty of room on board) and we were off to Pudeto. Some nice views from the rear deck. We arrived at Pudeto and found 3-4 large buses waiting. We found the bus back to Hotel Las Torres and hopped on (bring $ - be sure it’s paper money to reduce your pack weight). There seemed to be plenty of seats – the bus was less than half full. The bus drops you at the park entrance where you initially had to buy your passes. Here you get transferred to a shuttle to the hotel (this also cost $ - which didn’t seem right, but we were glad to pay it so we would be closer to a shower). We were surprised that the shuttle doesn’t take you all the way to the hotel and you have to walk the last ½ mile (something about they are not allowed to go the last ½ mile due to it being private land) – but again…a hot shower and beer awaited. We re-checked in – got our bag from the car and enjoyed a long shower and clean clothes. Next day we packed up and drove to Hosteria Lago Gray for the 2PM glacier boat tour (a little over $100/person) to complete our “W” (can’t remember how long the drive was, but the hotel can tell you). The reason we called it the “N” instead of the “W” hike is because we didn’t hike the last section up to Refugio Gray and back – we figured we would get better views of the glacier from the boat. We were glad we did - the views from the boat are awesome (and so are the Pisco Sours made with glacier ice) – the glaciers have cool/vibrant blue colors and you can see calving if you’re lucky. That’s about it – enjoy and bring a big memory card for your "N" hike experience. Buena Suerte!

review_text: I went to Vina del Mar as a side excursion to a tour of the port of Valparaiso (9kms from Vina Del Mar.. Vina del Mar is a small coastal resort town equipped with a nice beach, a choice of excellent seafood restaurants & a casino to tempt visitors. Other attractions for visitors include an archaelogical & history museum (Museo Fonck) boasting mainland Chile's only moai (large Easter Island stone statue); Reloj de Flores, a famous clock made from flowers. &, of course, the Quinta Vergara Amphitheater. The amphitheatre is situated within a large heavily-wooded park which is also the home of the grand Palacio Vergara (currently closed due to recent earthquake damage). The Quinta Vergara Amphitheater annually hosts the biggest International Song Festival in South America, which has drawn many international performers like Elton John, Morrissey, Julio Iglesias and Sting; It is an interesting construction, very much open air, based on the Ancient Greek model, but with a particular distinctive feature, a 'roof' comprising multiple vertical poles suspended from the air!

Thomas selected a wonderful small hotel (Wood Residence Hotel), a lovely resurrected old house - like a B&B with a delicious breakfast and a convenient location. We could not walk as much as we'd have liked (physically) and Thomas more than made up for the fact that Valparaiso is all hills by taking us to places we could walk, and making sure we saw all the sights from the art to the plaza. We lacked for nothing. Thomas was able to accommodate each change and re-decision I made with aplomb and panache (!). He is a great guy and a wonder guide. You will not be disappointed.

review_text: There are many touroperators for this tour in San Pedro de Atacama, they offer more or less the same tour. The tour will take you south of San Pedro and will visit the flamingo reserve first. At the flamingo reserve you will walk for about 400-800m through a salt flat, not like in the 'marble' flat surface but more like an area full of salt rocks. You are NOT allowed to walk on the salt (stick to the path!), other tours will only visit (a different) salt flat where you can walk (but they do not include the flamingos). In the background you will see the Lascar Vulcano (one of many active vulcanoes) At the end of the salt path you will see some beautiful lagoons with many flamingos (depending on time, early morning/late afternoon there will be most of them). Also some other birds can be easily spotted. There is a map with pictures of the species of birds. After the flamingo park the bus will continue for about 90 minutes to Miscantie & Minique Lagoon. Again a short walk here with some pretty views of both lagoons. Because of Vicuñas and some birds you can't visit the lagoon itself but still it's a nice view. About 45 minutes by bus to a small village where a lunch is served (with local ingredients) and again 45 minutes later a stop at Toconao Village is included. This village is somewhat disappointing (there is a church you can visit and mainly souvenir shops). That's the end of the tour (well, after the ride back to San Pedro of course) The tour is good value for money. Please keep in mind entrance fees are not included with most tour operators. Also the lagoons are at 4300m above sea level, it's better to spend some time in San Pedro (2500m) first to get used to the altitude. We booked our tour with Desert Adventures but we're transfered to 'LaYana' because not enough people joined the tour.

review_text: We did the circuit Arica - Codpa (one night) - Putre (two nights) - Arica (one night). Its VERY recommendable to start the trip in Codpa, which is located at 1850 meters, before moving to Putre (3500 meters) Salar de Surire (4000 meters) and Lago Chungara (4500 meters). Its very recommendable to rent a 4WD and take 20 liters extra fuel. This considering we rented a car with a tank capacity of 80 liters, some only have 50 - 60 liters. You CAN do the whole trip in a 2WD, but it just adds the risk of getting stuck, which is not a good scenario in places where you may be the only car passing during a given day. Also bring water and drink lots of water to help you getting used to the altitude. We found that arriving in Codpa in late afternoon, one day to travel from Codpa to Putre (two nights in Codpa) Day two travel to Salar de Surire, with thermal bath at the extreme south-east side of the lake, driving around the lake and hitting back towards Putre, but halfway on the way back towards the highway swinging right (taking the A95) to Lago Chungara was the perfect way to go. Last day either Socoroma or Azapa and a relaxed afternoon in Arica.

review_text: I loved the tour. The scenery with the dark mountains, the telescopes and the endless Atacama sky was simply perfect. The Canadian guide did a great job explaining the basics of astronomy and showing the most important objects in the night sky. On the other hand he was also able to answer more detailed astronomy questions if you were interested. The telescopes were good too. We saw galaxies, nebulae, star clusters and Mars. However, please don't expect to see Hubble-like images of outer space objects or the surface of Mars. The telescopes that are used to take those pictures play in a completely different league (even though their 70cm telescope is said to be the biggest touristic telescope in South America). The true magic of the tour lies in seeing the objects by yourself. Afterwards you will have the chance to take a picture of the moon through the telescope. Highly recommended tour.

review_text: If you're looking for an authentic Chilean cooking experience, look no further. My girlfriend and I had a blast as Rodrigo took us around to different local markets while teaching us about local ingredients, customs, and history. Have you ever seen an Anthony Bourdain show where he gets guided around by a local and gets to experience things as a normal person living in the city? That's what this felt like. After touring the markets, Rodrigo took us back to the cooking workshop where we first learned how to make pisco sours at their custom-built bar. Next, we went to the kitchen to meet Luis, who is one of their resident chefs. With Luis' guidance, we made granado bean stew, sopaipillas, pebre, braised beef empanadas, and pears poached in wine. Everything was quite delicious and we left with our bellies full! Rodrigo and Luis were fun, professional, and hospitable. review_text: Placed in the heart of downtown, Santa Lucía hill gives a break to stroll under its trees. Originally called Huelén by the pre-colonization inhabitants, it is the remnant of a volcano 15 million years old. It has an altitude of 629 m and a height of 69 m over the surrounding area. The whole park comprises a 65,300 square metre, adorned with elegant facades, stairways and squares, interior roads, balconies, statues, fountains, paths and even a small church, an amphitheater and even a castle. There is a Statue of Mapuche Indian whixh is a replica of that in Central Park. Many lookouts allow to enjoy great panoramic views of Santiago, especially after a rainy day that clears the smog away. At the highest point there is a viewpoint popular with tourists visiting the city. Traditionally, a cannon shot is fired exactly at noon. You can shop for handicrafts at the native artisanal market.Visits finishes by 7PM.

review_text: Kingston was at the top of my list of vineyards to visit because the wine they make matches my passion for Pinot and Sauvignon Blanc. I also like the fact that they are very small and you get a lot of personal attention. You won’t see a line of buses here transporting hundreds of people to drink swill. We didn’t travel 5000 miles for crowds and swill. Kingston is right sized and classy. No swill here. When I initially contacted them they were very responsive. I actually had the Marriott book the tour because I was unsure about the transportation before I left for the trip. I agree with some of the other reviews. The view atop a hill overlooking the valley is worth the visit and it looks like you are on a movie set. It was both relaxing and awesome. You are also looking down below at Casas Del Bosque (which we’d visit the following day). We elected for the premium tasting and lunch. Although we were a little late, Kingston was very cool and flexible. When we arrived we were greeted by Haley our guide. Upon arrival we were handed a glass of cold Rose to start. Haley was very friendly and gave us a great tour. A lot of great information and history of the vineyard. We had a spectacular lunch with ceviche to start along with beef and a carrot purée and the. Dessert. The pairing was awesome. The building where we had lunch and the tasting has spectacular views. The 2nd part of the pairing included some cheese and chocolate. From what we were told the building just opened that week so we were some of the first people to Christen the building. Very modern and the facility was immaculate. Honestly I could have stayed there all day long to hang out. It is very relaxing and the view is breathtaking. The only thing lacking was a gift shop. Kingston has a structured way for you to purchase wine though. Since they have a distribution center in Napa they are able to ship the wine to Places in the US. On their form you choose your wine and even tell them when to ship so your wine shows up when you are back in the states. This isn’t the typical over crowded vineyard. It is modeled very similar to vineyards in California and it is owned by Americans. They cater to Americans and most of all of the tour guides are American. I think we tasted about 8 wines. All were great. When I return to Chile I’ll revisit Kingston. The ambience along with the food and wine were off the charts awesome. Without the wine, I could sit atop that hill and continue to soak in the extravagant view. With the wine it was one of the highlights of our trip. Thanks to our guide Haley and Kingston Family Vineyards. Job well done!! I’d highly recommend this vineyard. Fantastic experience. Thank you for coming to visit us at Kingston Family Vineyards. We're glad to hear that you enjoyed your afternoon with Haley. We're in the process of building out our gift shop in our new Tasting Salon and we hope you'll come back to visit once we're done!

review_text: This museum covers the political oppression under General Pinochet between 11 September 1973 to 1990. The museum's exhibits literally start on the day of the coup d'etat in 1973. There no information on the events leading up to the overthrow of Allende, nor barely a mention of the life histories of this man or Pinochet. I spoke to one of the museum guides about this noticeable gap and she said that the museum aims to be apolitical and rather present the evils of human rights abuses, whether it be from a left or right-leaning government. I was impressed to see the number of school groups going through, and at least three children in one group were moved to tears. One can only hope that some of the lessons of history will be learnt. The museum is modern and the exhibits good but you must have an English audio guide. At the end of my visit I learnt that there are two English-speaking guides, who give free tours. She said that all you have to do is ask at the front desk and if they are available, they'll give you a tour. However, during the week, they tend to be booked up a lot giving school tours. She also said you can book a tour on the museum web site, but as I cannot speak Spanish, I could not find the information. If you can get a guide, you will have a more meaningful visit.

review_text: Traveling in Catholic countries can get you a little worn down on churches. But when they all start to blur together, this church stands out from the repetitive Baroque style found in the region. The blue ceiling with white trim make it feel open, as if outside on a sunny day. Stained glass is found not only on the windows, but also on the chandeliers that are shaped like cut gems. On either side of the altar hang a Chilean and Vatican flag, hinting at a bit of unity of church and state which may or may not say something about the region, but gets the brain juices going in any case. In the background, music reminiscent of Gregorian Chant plays just loudly enough to break the silence and set the mood. Great church.

review_text: I want to detail a robbery scam that largely wrecked our otherwise great trip to Valparaiso and, because it involved the loss of a passport, resulted in the cancellation of a week's trip to Patagonia. I was familiar with this scam in one form or another years ago but this time had let my guard down and was too trusting in the goodness of locals. Here's how the scam worked: Was lost trying to find our hostel near Calle Templeman and got down a dead end in my rental car. Followed into the dead end by another car whose driver got out and offered directions. While backing out I heard a pop and was soon aware I had a badly leaking tire. (I'm certain the second person in the car was able to slip something under the wheel). As we worked our way down the switchback streets the tire went completely flat. As I was making preparations to change the spare and English-speaking "Good Samaritan" appeared on foot telling us the spot was unsafe because another demonstration was about the begin and riot police were going the close the road. I went around the corner to the "safer" location, which in hindsight was in heavy traffic, and out of the range of CCTV. The man instructed me on the mandatory use of the yellow vest and reflective triangles, which afforded him time to see inside the car, including glove box and trunk. While I was setting up the jack a car drove by, nearly hitting me and crushing the reflective triangles. Later, and too late, we realized this was the same car that followed us into the dead end previously and the two men were working together. The man instructed my companion to stand warning traffic coming up from behind of the tire changing and while her back was turned the two men lifted our daypacks from our car and took off. They were the epitome of well-dressed and apparently courteous people who relieved us of a passport, camera, medicines and even eyeglasses. Trust in people, but never let your guard down.

review_text: Where to start? I was so excited to go on this trip. It sounded like the ideal way to see Chile. Boy was I wrong. First of all, bus....not a bus, we had a group of eight people on vehicle somewhere between a mini- van and a dodge sprinter. Room to spread out? Laughable. At the end of the first day my legs hurt and I was aching to get off the tour. Too bad, no refunds, you have to 're-sell' you ticket. Anyway I digress, keep in mind the amount of time the description uses the word "possibility" No choices in hostels, or hotels. Drive all day past the country you paid so much to see, only to stop at a pricey, poorly located hostels, or hotels. In Bahia Inglesia we asked to camp and were told it would be more costly than splitting a room with another individual. No explanation..not to mention being in a fenced in area with no access to the beach. We found a hole in the fence to crawl through and encouraged others to do so as well, as there was no other way to get out. When we asked the guide about it, he blamed the owners for not unlocking the gate. Awful. In antofagasta, we were put into a hotel called hotel brasil. Easily the worst, more rude hotel i stayed at in Chile. After asking if we could crack a few beers open like it says on the website, or eludes to, we were denied. Without explanation. Again. The more I re-read the concept and FAQ's page the more disappointed I become. This was probably the most poor representation of Chile I experienced during my 3 months. After Pachamama, I will never take another tour. Being shuffled on and off a bus, being told where to point your camera, how long, and when you can is NOT TRAVELING. We stopped more time for cigarette breaks than sight seeing. I will not bring the guide into this review because as I understand he was not the biggest fan of his contract with the company. So in short, if you want to travel all day, witnessing the country you worked so hard to come to out the window of a van. Only to arrive at night to your destination without a choice where to stay. And repeat this process day after day for close to $400 USD, have fun. I will never do this again worst tour ever.

review_text: The observatory is good and we spent a good time looking at the various celestial objects. The group was small and there were two good / qualified and experienced guides/astronomers to explain what we saw. Impressive! However, the experience was significantly tainted by the transfer. We were driven up to the observatory (30-40 minutes drive) in a smallish car (no problem) by an incredibly unsensitive driver. One of his issues was lacking the courtesy to consider that not everybody enjoys death-metal music and kept the radio running the whole time. Even when asked to turn the radio off, he did not. He was further reticent with apparently no interest at all regarding the work he was doing and reluctant to maintain even the most elementary civil conversation, be it regarding the observatory or any other aspects. Going up was one thing, it was extremely anoying, however, we were looking forward observing the stars. Going down was an insult. We were tired, full of great experiences and had to endure the outragously dull noises from his radio for the whole trip down. He really managed to destroy an otherwise perfect evening. All members of our group thought so. We were upset and felt messed around. If you plan to do the tour (but do not love death metal), make sure that the team commits to send a normal driver who would understand and comply with the most basic social conventions. It seems appropiate to specify that the transfert to the observatory was performed by a private taxi company not affiliated to the observatory. We called them that night because our own vehicule was unavailable (maintenance service cannot always coincide with Full Moon phases!). In a private mail we gave you the references of that company, so I hope you can clear with them the reason why the drivers felt he was not treated with courtesy. Meanwhile we thank you for your review : indeed we remenber how much you appreciate the Astro Tour so, as a compensation for the "transfert experience", I propose to get you a free pass to the observatory for some friend of yours that may come to Chile some day : they just have to mention your reference and we'll receive them... and that should be aboard the observatory vehicule !...

review_text: After a business meeting in Santiago, we wanted to visit Valparaiso before going to the Lake District. Fortunately for us when we contacted him the evening prior, Hector was available not only to give us a wonderful tour of his native city but also to make arrangements for an excellent guide in Puerto Varas. He is courteous, knowledgeable, and quick to cater to our interests. Since he lived in New York for ten years, his English is quite good. When he picked us up at our hotel, I mentioned that we had not seen much of Santiago while working so he took us on an impromptu circuit to major sites around the city, filling us in on the history from colonial times to the present day. On the way to Valparaiso, Hector took us to a lookout point in the Coast Range above the Casablanca Valley and explained the unusual origins of the Carmenere wine industry. In Valparaiso, he gave us many personal insights as we ventured on back roads, rides on the bus and ascensores, and strolls on cobblestone streets and hillside stairs. We had a wonderful view as we lunched on seafood at Oda Pacifico restaurant near Pablo Neruda's home. And we enjoyed seeing the colorful buildings and street murals in the various neighborhoods. With Hector's narration, we quickly became enchanted with this fascinating town. Hector got us back to the Santiago airport in time for our flight and, along the way, put us in touch with a colleague, Nelly Carrasco Garay, who gave us similarly personalized experience around Puerto Varas and Chiloe. If you want a private guide, we highly recommend HecTour for its excellent service.

review_text: We took the trip flying from Punta Arenas on Dec 19th to Frei Station to board the Hebridean Sky for 5 days. Things started well: boot fitting in Punta Arenas, welcome dinner (ok if not great) and the flight on the 19th appeared to run on time and was to regular airline standards including a mostly edible airline meal. The walk of about a mile across the airfield to the beach while carrying our hand-luggage was a bit unpleasant but we'd been warned about it, and about the potential choppiness of the Zodiac trip from the beach to the ship. We thought the Hebridean Sky to be very good: comfortable cabin, good lounge space, excellent meals and very helpful restaurant and cabin staff. Unfortunately the weather was poor throughout our visit, and one of the staff let slip that we actually did not do a single one of the excursions originally planned. But the expedition staff managed to find alternatives on various islands including one landing on the Antarctic mainland. These and the Zodiac cruises were as good as we expected, with huge numbers of penguins to see at close quarters, as well as many other birds, a few seals and whales, and in places lots of shapely icebergs. Expedition staff were good at this, and we had no concerns over our safety or their competence. It was a pity that we didn't get the chance to visit Deception Island which looked good on the map and from its reputation since we sailed very close to it at one point, but we accepted that the weather affected our itinerary. Some small disappointments: the ship's senior officers (Captain, Engineer, Doctor, etc.) introduced themselves on the first night but were then just about never seen, they were never in the bar or restaurant. We've been on other small cruises where they are willing to mix with passengers much more. Also the talks by the various expredition staff were good but not as many as we'd expected, and the subject matter didn't venture much beyond the local wildlife. There was, for example, not a single mention throughout of topics like climate change, the ozone hole, or the effect of tourism on the local environment. Perhaps the staff didn't want to risk alienating Trump-supporters among the passengers - if there were any. Or maybe there was some other reason. A more serious disappointment came on the 23rd Dec when we went out on a morning Zodiac cruise with the expectation of a beach landing in the afternoon - expedition staff were said to be exploring ready for it. Around 13:45 we were suddently ordered to assemble in the lounge to be told that because of adverse weather being forecast for 24th Dec (our scheduled return date) we had to return home that same day, i.e. a day early. We were given barely 20 minutes to pack our bags and get dressed for the zodiacs. Mike Hann, the expedition leader, who had been ubiquitous up to that point simply vanished. It was clear that the company knew about this change of plan from early that morning as they had also notified all those on the next group who got their flight a day early and were already on their way. There seemed no reason for keeping us in the dark throughout and we got no apology at all over this, and have had no satisfactory explanation. This made it a very abrupt and unpleasant departure - we got no time at all to express our thanks to our excellent cabin steward or any of the ship's staff. When we signed up we knew that flights to/from Antarctica were weather-dependent but they warned us about delays rather than early departures. We all felt that the sudden departure was not well managed. There had been several spare seats on the flight out so we we did not dash across the runway to be early onto the plane home, but it turned out to be completely full (some ships crew returning, I think), so we didn't even manage to get two seats together which didn't make the return trip any more pleasant. If it hadn't been for the badly managed departure 1 day early, I would have given this a much higher mark. As it is: potential fly-cruisers should beware that there can be schedule changes in both directions. In the end we spent as many nights in a hotel in beautiful downtown Punta Arenas as we did on the ship; not quite what we had expected. With a bit more notice we might have been able to arrange to fly home a day earlier, as it was there was no chance of doing this. Dear astronomer-at-large, Many thanks for your review of your Antarctic air-cruise. I am happy to read that you mostly enjoyed your experience and that you would have rated the trip with a much higher mark had it not been for the early departure from Antarctica. I hope I can clarify that point. At multiple touchpoints prior to and during the reservation process, we inform our guests about the variable nature of the Antarctic weather. We explain that the weather can impact itineraries and we outline the contingency plans that we have in place for those situations. The information is transparent and tries to address all possible scenarios, including the scenario experienced by your trip. The Contingency Plan section of our 2019-20 Antarctic Air-Cruises brochure (page 30) states: “In case the return flight to Punta Arenas is moved forward - In those cases when the forecast suggests the likelihood of unfavorable weather conditions in Antarctica persisting for several days, the flight back to Punta Arenas may be moved forward to the previous evening as a way to avoid a protracted delay in Antarctica.” The forecast for the day of your scheduled return flight from Antarctica indicated unfavorable weather conditions at King George Island, the location of our Antarctic airfield. Our flight plan had to remain flexible as we looked for a flying window within those variable conditions. To avoid the very likely possibility that you would experience a long delay in Antarctica, we decided to fly the day before, December 23, when a window of good weather became available in the afternoon. Things were touch and go, with a lot of uncertainty as we waited for the right conditions and for confirmation of the flight. As things turned out, after that day no more flights could be operated until the afternoon of December 27. So had we not returned as we did, you would have been stuck in Antarctica for four more days, with all the implications that would have had on your ongoing travel arrangements during the busy holiday season. We regret that the circumstances surrounding the departure from Antarctica impacted your enjoyment of the experience. Antarctica21 is a community of caring individuals deeply committed to the satisfaction of our guests. We hope that you can cherish the good memories from your trip while accepting that we acted to protect your overall travel experience, avoiding the complications that would have resulted from a long delay returning from Antarctica. Please do not hesitate to contact our office if you need further details. Best regards, Jamie Ensey Director of Marketing

review_text: Our trip to the geysers began at 5:30 am so that we could see the sunrise. Guess what--the sky was crystal clear as always! We climbed from San Pedro de Atacama at about 2200 meters to the Geyser del Tatio at 4300 meters. So, that's high for most of us, but we did well once again at high altitude. There are two geyser fields and you can hike around each one, so that's fun. Some geysers are high, some occur on a periodicity of 18 min and some just bubble. It's always windy at that site, so you must dress warmly. Even though we were there a week before summer begins, it was cold and windy--sustained winds of at least 30 mph. But, worth it! If you visit this region, this trip is a must. On the way back, we stopped at a local village that was notable for lots of solar panels, street lights and cable connections. A cell phone tower was nearby. It's great to see how modern technology has covered every inch of the globe.

review_text: We did the "W Plus Trek Program" and had such an amazing week we couldn't give this any less than 5 stars. HOWEVER as we found it very hard to find reviews on the "Riverside Camp" accommodation provided by Chile Nativo, we wanted to write a detailed review to help everyone else out. The first section will be on the company/program, and the second section will be on the accommodation. 1. CHILE NATIVO PROGRAM We did the 4 nights / 5 days program which loosely followed the W Trail. But instead of staying each night at a different campsite, you're driven back to the same camp each night where the accommodation standard is much better and away from the crowds. Overall the program was amazing, one of the coolest things we have ever done. In rough order: a. The guide (Felipe) was the best guide we have ever had, anywhere in the world. Extremely knowledgeable. Perfect english. High energy (even when we weren't), great vibes and an always positive attitude. Always looked after and took good care of us. Planned each day's schedule to perfection. Went above and beyond every hour of every day for 5 days. b. The booking experience was very easy. Once I sent the initial email I was assigned an agent (Ale) who was friendly, informative, and always replied within 24 hours (despite a 14 hour time difference). This was very different to other tour companies in South America... c. The program was overall fantastic. French valley, torres hike, lasso-weber and grey lake/glacier were all perfect days. The only negative was the wildlife day - getting up at 4am to drive to the Puma spot but there were no pumas felt a bit silly. Apparently this happens a lot so I would consider scrapping this. d. The staff (other than Felipe) were all pleasant and friendly and you just get the impression it's a very well-run company with low staff turnover and good processes and systems. 2. RIVERSIDE CAMP ACCOMODATION The first thing to note is that from December 2023 onwards the Riverside Camp has MOVED so the description and pictures (which remain on the Chile Nativo website as at late Jan 2024) are not correct. The new camp is across the other side of the river and is very much within the "Serrano Village" so less secluded, albeit with nicer facilities. If I were just rating the accommodation it would get a 4 star review given the price - see below. The good: - The tents are new, spotless and really nice. It really is glamping, with enough room for two beds, bedside tables, an end of bed (for suitcase/clothes) and some reticulation space. - Proper, real beds! super comfortable and luxe. - The tents have electricity and wifi which felt like such a luxury given the location. - Each tent is set on a wooden platform and next to a separate hut which serves as the private bathroom for the tent. The bathroom is cosy but has full sink, cabinet, toilet, shower and heated towel rack. - Nice new linen sheets and towels - Breakfast and dinner is served in a separate, even bigger tent attached to a kitchen. This is a beautiful space with views of the mountain range, a fire place, couches and dining tables for eating. - Lunch is provided each day in the form of a lunch box to take out hiking. Every day was something different and each day it was delicious! - The location is very convenient - next to the park but not inside it. You have a lovely view of the mountains from the site and you can walk to the river bank in a few minutes. BUT note that you're not technically on the river (you have to leave the grounds and cross a road) and many other accommodation properties are within eyeshot. Some other guests were disturbed by noise from a party one night, but we didn't hear any of this. The bad: - The camp is powered by a fuel generator which is LOUD. You notice it when you arrive and you can hear it when you go to bed at night. This really does detract from the feeling of being in nature. The company should really look at ways to reduce this sound. - The tents can only be configured as two single beds (not a double). This doesn't suit couples like us. - As it's new, the space around the tents isn't great - some of it is grass, some of it is just dirt and some of it feels like it's still a construction site. As there is zero vegetation, there isn't much visual privacy as you move between the tent and bathroom. This didn't bother us, but other guests maybe? - While they are aiming for a gourmet food experience (with a waiter for dinner, nice wine etc) the quality was a bit hit and miss. The bread for breakfast each day was stale (don't know why when an excellent bakery is located in the village) and some of the dinners weren't very nice (but you're there for the nature not the food). Overall this gets 5 stars for sure and i would TOTALLY recommend it, but speak to the company before booking if you're concerned about any of the accommodation issues listed above. Review of: W Trek Torres del Paine

review_text: My wife and I recently did a half day fishing trip with our guide Paul. He arrived at our hotel at 8:00 am with his wooden boat on a trailer and we proceeded to drive to the river. My wife wanted to try fly fishing so Paul took the time to teach her how to do this before we set off. Paul was an excellent guide, always instructing us were to put our lines, how fast to reel in and when to stop trying to fish as it was not a good spot. He did a great job rowing the boat to the best spots for fish. He was very polite with a very calming personality. He brought us a nice little lunch to have along the way. The scenery along the trip is beautiful and that alone is worth the trip. As far as fishing goes we caught three trout, two were small but one was a good size that you would have kept if that was allowed. We did see some salmon jump at one location and tried to get them to bite but with no success. This is a great way to spend part of a day and I highly recommend it if you are in the area.

review_text: The purpose of this review is to provide information and tell us about our experience on this trip, as previously I could not find enough information to be able to travel in a better way. To make the crossing to Chile by route 7 I left from Buenos Aires and stayed overnight in Luján de Cuyo, recommended for what was coming. Upon reaching the border, on the Argentine side it is called Christ the Redeemer International Passage, but on the Chilean side it is called Los Libertadores International Passage. The day we crossed there were too many trucks. And here comes the first problem, confusion due to lack of information from the Argentine authorities. A single toll booth we find no other end. Line of stationary trucks mixed with private cars, until a car passes us all on the left and puts itself first in line. The trucks were not passing because on the Chilean side was the entrance for them stopped, but not for the cars. But on the Argentine side, nobody reports anything. The car drives by and everyone who came by car back. We paid 300 pesos in that cabin and left all the trucks behind. We crossed the tunnel and arrived in Chile. The road inevitably takes you to Chilean Customs, not so when you return (later I tell them). Migration procedures, I previously did everything online from the AFIP website and also printed it. Form OM-2261 "Temporary Departure and Admission of Vehicles", all useless, because when you arrive in Chilean Migrations, they make you fill it out again so that you have the letterhead of them... "in case"... well... If you have to declare something when you leave, for example the GO PRO that you bought in Ciudad del Este two years ago, there is the form OM-121, which I guess you will present when you return to the country, I do not know because for me it was not necessary. Immigration procedure at the Chilean Customs in three steps, I recommend you although no one does it like this, is that you do not go ahead and sit in your car, because your car can not pass over those in front of you even if you can. When your time comes, you get out of your car and do all the paperwork. They have scanner and the customs staff very kindly make you get everything, absolutely everything out of the car. They even lifted the rugs out of my trunk and made me pull out the emergency wheel, and not because I looked suspicious, they did it to all cars. All bags, bags, lumps, backpacks, all by scanner. They give you a series of papers stamped by them that recommend you do not lose them, because they will serve you to get out, do not lose them. We leave the dock and here comes a very important part if you did not leave Argentina with Chilean pesos, there is a small booth just before leaving, at the end of the parking sector that is a currency exchange. I exchanged dollars for Chilean pesos, the exchange was not so bad. But why is it important to have Chilean pesos if you go by car to Chile with Argentina patent?because there is a toll before you arrive in Santiago that is only paid in cash, and if you are going to circle beyond Santiago, also the tolls are effective, between 2,000 and 4,500 Chilean pesos. So it's better to have cash. As soon as the descent of Los Caracoles is over, you have the first toll, but you pay it on the return, in the first leg you continue long. As I said you leave Chilean Customs and begins the road of Los Caracoles, spectacular, very spectacular the problem is trucks. We made the trip on a business Monday and had a two-hour delay, by route 60 until connecting the 57 that is highway that takes you to Santiago. Route 60 is the one that takes you down from the international crossing and you don't have a single and long enough stretch to be able to overtake a truck, so 60 km until you connect route 57 that is highway. Customs was a sigh next to 60 km in almost 3 hours. Once up the highway you have the first toll, 4,500 Chilean pesos and then, already in Santiago, there is something that I found a little confusing. There is a sign on the highway that says cars with foreign patents had to pay an "extra" toll but it seemed that they made you exit to the right, so I went on long, because I didn't want to leave, it was still quite a few kilometers to reach my destination. But when I look past the cockpits, it wasn't an exit, you'd pay and re-enter the highway. Nobody informs you anything!! Then I thought, well I'll pay for it at some TAG Chile office, no, neither. When I approached a road brokers’ office at Shopping Arauco, they told me they don’t know what to do with cars with foreign patents. Then it's like they ask you to pay, I don't know, it doesn't seem like a good system, since nobody informs you anything, you come traveling by highway from the north at 120 kmh and suddenly a sign appears that makes you leave, but no, it asks you to pay... I don't know, I don't think. Santiago has 5,507 highways. Some elevated, others underground, you can cross Santiago from north to south and east to west. But there is not a single toll booth, it is all with TAG Chile system and patent reading. And as I already mentioned, they don’t know what to do with foreign patents, so with your patented car in Bernal you can use all the highways in Santiago, only those in Santiago without paying a single peso. I didn’t think it was right, so I set up the Maps so that on all routes I would avoid tolls and that’s it. Then I did a tax exercise and said to myself: since VAT they charge you on every Chilean peso you leave them, because I didn't find a single TAX FREE anywhere, I could have used them perfectly without having an ethical-moral problem, but good. Same Santiago is a beautiful city and came very well to do the roads by streets and avenues and not by underground highways. Then we continue our tour to the beaches of Matanzas, all in cash tolls. And then to Viña to finish. Return to Buenos Aires with 5 bags full of shopping. All roads in excellent condition, but had it not been for the Maps, with the few indicative signs they have, it would have been a hell of a trip. The return, before entering the road of Los Caracoles, the last toll on the Chilean side. Chilean migrations on Chilean soil NO HAY, you do it in Los Horcones, now I tell you. You pass through the side of where you entered Chile and continue straight to the tunnel. One million three hundred and forty-three trucks in line waiting to enter Chile, the same as for entry two weeks ago. You continue through the tunnel and return to Argentina. The same cabin that used to charge you 300 pesos to leave, now asks how many members travel in the car and gives you a little paper. You are warned that you have to enter the Argentine customs office that is in Los Horcones 15 kilometers ahead. Don’t throw it away and don’t lose it, it’ll help you and pay attention to the signs on the way to customs, since the entrance is on the left side of the road, so you have to cross lanes to enter, Argentina.... you wouldn’t understand. You arrive at the Argentine customs office, you enter, the system is very similar to the one we made when entering Chile, do not get out of the car until your turn, it will reach you, calm, I did not see anyone living there, so calm. In three steps you will be submitting the different forms. But the not subtle difference from Chile is control, they ask you what you bought and it depends only on the goodwill of your answers. They check what you told them you bought, they don't check much further. Although I think if it came with 30 boxes of sneakers, some kind of explanation would have given. And one more thing that seems to me to be very important, is the fact that there is NO scanner in the Argentine Customs in Los Horcones, it is not good. Once all the procedures are completed, we exit to route 7 and about 40 km there is a Gendarmerie post, exactly in Punta de Vacas. There you are arrested and asked for the first piece of paper you were given in the "toll booth" just outside the international tunnel. And ready, you're back. Some additional information, the departure from Argentina and the entry to Chile was done on a Monday at noon, towards the end of October 2024 and the return also on a Monday at noon, but in mid-November 2024. As it is my first and only experience of this international step, I do not know if it is always like this or just that day. The fuel tank, whenever you can, full. Arm yourself with patience because there are many, many many trucks on all routes, I stayed overnight, both on the way and back, in Mendoza. Route 7 in Mendoza and San Luis is a highway. Cordoba, he owes you. And Buenos Aires only to or from Chacabuco. That's what it is. On Chile's side, they're better off. Many more highways, it is true that they are fewer kilometers of territory, but they made them. The internal routes are very good. They have many mountains, hills, mountains, then you spend all the time going up and down with curve and against curve. And what I noticed in Chile, I'm not saying it's better or worse, is just an observation, is that they don't have routes, en route, that they don't have populations. All the time there are populations, small, large, medium, houses, sets of houses, all the time civilization on the side of the road. Here between Laboulaye and Vicuña Mackenna there are almost 100 kilometers and you barely cross two villages. The trip is worth it, if you like to drive, you will not have major drawbacks, if you can not become a little tedious. I hope I've been helpful. The reason is that wildlife is most active at this time. On our way back, we saw Vicunas, Llamas, and Flamingos in large numbers. It was fantastic. High altitude, so be ready for that.

review_text: This tour was amazing! Frankly, given the quality and quantity of reviews on TripAdvisor, I decided to book through Jorge rather than investigate cheaper options. Jorge is extremely knowledgeable and runs an amazing tour.

review_text: Floating in this place was fun, interesting and unmissable. But every scratch picked up over the previous week stung like hell. There's a wind in the afternoon, usually, so be smart and stay on the downwind side of the lagoon where the warm water accumulates. It's much colder in the deep water. It's quite a walk from the changing facilities to the lagoon, so take sandals, and put sunscreen on. The showers are cold, but you absolutely have to get that salt off. Yes, there are quite a lot of tour buses here, but it's quite big and plenty of room for everyone. The tour we did ended with pisco sour which was deliciously prepared by our fantastic tour guide (knowledgable, interested, energetic and considerate) from Turistour. There were a couple of other nice stops to look at various salt lake features as well.

review_text: While not one of the more beautiful cathedrals we have ever seen, it is certainly one of the most unique. Originally built in 1856 as a church, it was later used as a theater and army barrack! In 1896 it was reconsecrated as a church. When the then Pope created the Diocese of Puerto Montt in 1939 it was named as a cathedral in honor of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. The architectural style and Doric columns are believed to have been inspired by the Parthenon. The cathedral is built of alerce wood, a type of cypress tree native to the Andes mountains. The copper cupola and use of rectangular pieces of stained glass add to the uniqueness. The interior is interesting in its simplicity, rows of Doric columns on either side of the nave, lovely murals, a neo-Gothic chapel. I would not go out of my way to see the church but it is worth a visit if in the area. Check the hours.... I think it is only open in the morning or early afternoon.

review_text: We got to Puerto Montt in a cruise and wanted to do the whitewater rafting through the company, not the cruise so we texted with Colin (Al Sur team/photographer) and he let us know they were already booked through the cruise line (by the way, very responsive to our email/texts) so there was no way around it. We went ahead and booked through our cruise ship. We were very lucky there was still space and we got excellent weather compared to all the rain and freezing cold we've been getting. We drove through Puerto Varas and were able to see a clear view of the volcano. We got to their place, it took about 45 minutes and changed into wetsuits they provided along with shoes, helmet and life jacket. We change in one big changing room (2 total changing rooms, one for men one for women). There is also one bathroom on site. Once in the river area the walk down to the river is tricky, slippery and ashy (yes, a lot of ash mixed with the sand from the eruption back in April). Once at the river Cristobal (main guide) went over commands, rules and procedures. In the water we practiced what we had just learned. We sat on the second row in the raft. Being first timers we didn't know what to expect but it was fantastic! Cristobal asked if we wanted to go down the river again and the group said yes so we went at it a second time. Note: the second time around we went in the first row and it sure made a difference on the whole experience PLUS the river had changed and was much faster than the first time. It was a blast. I recommend this to anyone who loves adventure and nature. Beautiful sites from the river of all 3 volcanoes in the area. Once back the group had a cold beer, coffee, water and snacks and then left back to the pier. When in the area, we would do it all over again. Money well spent. Review of: Half-Day Small-Group Rafting Experience in Petrohué River

We went ahead and booked through our cruise ship. We were very lucky there was still space and we got excellent weather compared to all the rain and freezing cold we've been getting. We drove through Puerto Varas and were able to see a clear view of the volcano. We got to their place, it took about 45 minutes and changed into wetsuits they provided along with shoes, helmet and life jacket. We change in one big changing room (2 total changing rooms, one for men one for women). There is also one bathroom on site. Once in the river area the walk down to the river is tricky, slippery and ashy (yes, a lot of ash mixed with the sand from the eruption back in April). Once at the river Cristobal (main guide) went over commands, rules and procedures. In the water we practiced what we had just learned. We sat on the second row in the raft. Being first timers we didn't know what to expect but it was fantastic! Cristobal asked if we wanted to go down the river again and the group said yes so we went at it a second time. Note: the second time around we went in the first row and it sure made a difference on the whole experience PLUS the river had changed and was much faster than the first time. It was a blast. I recommend this to anyone who loves adventure and nature. Beautiful sites from the river of all 3 volcanoes in the area. Once back the group had a cold beer, coffee, water and snacks and then left back to the pier. When in the area, we would do it all over again. Money well spent. Review of: Half-Day Small-Group Rafting Experience in Petrohué River
